topic: Ischemic Heart Disease and Angina Pectoris
clinical_hallmarks: Retrosternal pressure or squeezing lasting 2-15 minutes
provoked by physical exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin.
pertinent_negatives: no tenderness on chest wall palpation
content: Angina pectoris presents as retrosternal pressure, heaviness, or burning sensation lasting 2 to 15 minutes, typically provoked by physical exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or sublingual nitrates. Pain may radiate to the left shoulder, left arm, neck, or lower jaw. Pertinent negatives include absence of pleuritic chest pain or sharp focal tenderness. Diagnostic workup: 12-lead ECG (ST depressions or T-wave inversions), High-sensitivity Cardiac Troponin (hs-cTnI/T) to rule out NSTEMI, Echocardiography, and Treadmill Stress Test (TMT) or Coronary Angiography.

topic: Congestive Heart Failure (Acute Decompensated Heart Failure)
content: Heart failure exacerbation presents with exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, bilateral lower limb pitting edema, nocturnal cough, and rapid weight gain from fluid retention. Auscultation reveals S3 gallop, basilar pulmonary crackles, and raised JVP. Diagnostic workup: Serum NT-proBNP or BNP, 12-lead ECG, 2D Echocardiography (Ejection Fraction calculation), Chest X-Ray (cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines), and serum electrolytes/renal function.

topic: Atrial Fibrillation with Rapid Ventricular Response
clinical_hallmarks: and exercise intolerance. High thromboembolic stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc score).
content: Atrial fibrillation is characterized by irregularly irregular tachycardia, palpitations, fatigue, and presyncope. Key clinical risk is left atrial appendage thrombus formation causing embolic ischemic stroke. Diagnostic workup: 12-lead ECG (absent P waves, fibrillatory baseline, irregular R-R intervals), Holter monitor, 2D Echocardiogram (rule out mitral valve disease and LA thrombus), and Thyroid function panel (TSH/free T4).

clinical_hallmarks: and nocturnal cough triggered by cold air
or allergens. Reversible airway obstruction on spirometry.
pertinent_negatives: no high fever with purulent rusty sputum
content: Asthma exacerbation is characterized by episodic wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and nighttime cough. Symptoms are triggered by cold air, viral respiratory infections, dust, or allergens. Key diagnostic markers: prolonged expiratory phase, bilateral polyphonic wheezes on auscultation, and reduced Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR). Pertinent negatives include absence of unilateral absent breath sounds (rules out pneumothorax) and absence of high fever with purulent rusty sputum (rules out lobar pneumonia). First line workup: Bedside PEFR measurement, Pulse Oximetry, Chest X-ray, and Nebulization with Beta-2 agonists.

clinical_hallmarks: Chronic progressive exertional dyspnea and cough with increased sputum volume or purulence (Anthonisen criteria). Strong smoking or biomass fuel exposure history.
pertinent_negatives: no sudden sharp pleuritic unilateral chest pain
content: Acute exacerbation of COPD presents with increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and sputum purulence in long-term smokers or patients with biomass fuel exposure. Physical signs include barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, coarse rhonchi, and prolonged expiration. Diagnostic workup: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG to evaluate PaO2 and PaCO2 acidosis), Chest X-Ray (hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm), Spirometry with post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70, and Complete Blood Count.

clinical_hallmarks: productive cough with yellowish or rusty sputum
and localized bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles on auscultation.
content: Community-acquired pneumonia presents with fever, productive cough with purulent sputum, chills, and localized pleuritic chest pain. Clinical examination reveals tachypnea, focal crepitations/crackles, increased vocal resonance, and dullness to percussion. Risk stratification via CURB-65 or PSI score. Diagnostic workup: Chest X-Ray PA view (lobar consolidation or air bronchograms), Complete Blood Count (leukocytosis with neutrophilic left shift), C-reactive protein (CRP), and Sputum Gram stain & culture.

red_flags: acute right heart strain on ECG (S1Q3T3)
clinical_hallmarks: Sudden onset dyspnea and sharp pleuritic chest pain in a patient with DVT risk factors (recent surgery
pertinent_negatives: no chronic cough with purulent sputum
content: Acute pulmonary embolism is a life-threatening vascular emergency presenting with abrupt dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and occasional hemoptysis. Physical exam may show unilateral calf swelling/tenderness (DVT) and tachypnea. Risk stratification via Wells Score and Geneva Score. Diagnostic workup: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA - gold standard), Quantitative D-dimer assay, Bedside Echocardiography (McConnell's sign), 12-lead ECG, and Lower Extremity Venous Doppler.

clinical_hallmarks: Retrosternal burning pain (heartburn) and acid regurgitation occurring after meals or when recumbent
relieved by antacids. No association with physical exertion.
pertinent_negatives: no radiation to left arm or jaw
content: GERD presents with retrosternal pyrosis (heartburn) and acid regurgitation, frequently exacerbated post-prandially or in the recumbent/supine position. Relief is often achieved with antacids or warm water. Must be distinguished from cardiac ischemia: GERD pain typically lacks radiation to the jaw or diaphoresis and does not correlate with physical exertion. Warning red flags (dysphagia, hematemesis, unintentional weight loss) warrant urgent Upper GI Endoscopy. Workup: Empirical trial of Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI), H. pylori antigen test, and Upper GI Endoscopy if alarm symptoms are present.

clinical_hallmarks: Burning or gnawing epigastric pain. Duodenal ulcers characteristically produce pain 2-3 hours post-prandially or at night
content: Peptic ulcer disease typically presents with gnawing or burning epigastric pain. Duodenal ulcers characteristically produce pain 2-3 hours after meals or at night, relieved by food or antacids. Gastric ulcer pain is exacerbated by food ingestion. History of NSAID use or H. pylori infection is frequent. Sudden board-like abdominal rigidity suggests acute perforation. Diagnostic workup: Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (gold standard), Complete Blood Count (to detect occult bleeding anemia), and H. pylori stool antigen test.

clinical_hallmarks: Visceral periumbilical dull pain that shifts and localizes within 12-24 hours to the Right Iliac Fossa (McBurney's point)
accompanied by anorexia (hamburger sign) and nausea.
pertinent_negatives: no bilateral lower quadrant pelvic tenderness with vaginal discharge
content: Acute appendicitis characteristically starts as vague periumbilical visceral pain that over 12-24 hours migrates and localizes to the Right Lower Quadrant (McBurney's point). Accompanied by anorexia, low-grade fever, nausea, and vomiting. Physical signs include McBurney's point tenderness, Rovsing's sign, Psoas sign, and rebound tenderness. Alvarado score stratifies probability. Workup: Complete Blood Count (leukocytosis with left shift), Ultrasonography of Abdomen/Pelvis, or Contrast-enhanced CT Abdomen.

red_flags: ascending cholangitis (Charcot triad: fever, jaundice, RUQ pain)
Reynold pentad with hypotension and confusion
clinical_hallmarks: Severe Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ) or epigastric pain radiating to the right shoulder/infrascapular region
triggered 1-2 hours after fatty food ingestion. Positive Murphy's sign on deep inspiration.
content: Acute cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by gallstone cystic duct obstruction. Presents with severe RUQ pain radiating to the right scapula, fever, nausea, and leukocytosis. Physical examination shows arrest of inspiration on deep RUQ palpation (Murphy's sign). Diagnostic workup: Ultrasonography of Abdomen (gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening > 4mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign), Liver Function Tests (elevated bilirubin, ALP, AST/ALT), and Lipase/Amylase.

red_flags: Cullen's sign / Grey Turner's sign (retroperitoneal hemorrhage)
clinical_hallmarks: epigastric boring pain radiating straight through to the back
characteristically partially relieved by sitting upright and leaning forward
content: Acute pancreatitis presents with intense epigastric abdominal pain boring through to the back, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and tachycardia. Common etiologies include gallstones (biliary) and alcohol consumption. Diagnosis requires 2 of 3 Atlanta criteria: typical abdominal pain, serum lipase or amylase > 3x upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging findings. Diagnostic workup: Serum Lipase (highly sensitive/specific), Serum Amylase, Contrast-enhanced CT Abdomen (after 48-72h for necrosis staging), Calcium, and Triglycerides.

red_flags: severe dehydration (sunken eyes, delayed skin turgor, anuria)
clinical_hallmarks: and low-grade fever following contaminated food or water consumption.
pertinent_negatives: no localized rebound tenderness in RIF
content: Acute gastroenteritis presents with rapid-onset watery diarrhea, cramping abdominal colic, nausea, and vomiting. Assessment of hydration status (mild, moderate, severe) is critical. Viral pathogens (Rotavirus, Norovirus) and bacterial pathogens (E. coli, Salmonella, Campylobacter) are primary causes. Diagnostic workup: Stool Routine & Microscopy (fecal leukocytes, parasites), Stool Culture (if dysenteric or immunocompromised), Serum Electrolytes and Renal Function (BUN/Creatinine), and Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) protocol.

clinical_hallmarks: and dull suprapubic aching without systemic signs or flank pain.
pertinent_negatives: no flank tenderness or CVA punch tenderness
no vaginal or urethral purulent discharge
content: Acute uncomplicated cystitis presents with painful burning urination, pollakiuria (frequency), urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. Absence of fever and costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness distinguishes lower UTI from acute pyelonephritis. Pyelonephritis features high spiking fevers, chills/rigors, nausea, and flank pain with positive renal angle tenderness. Workup: Urine Routine & Microscopy (pyuria, bacteriuria, leukocyte esterase), Urine Culture & Sensitivity, Complete Blood Count, and Renal Ultrasound if pyelonephritis or obstruction is suspected.

red_flags: obstructive uropathy with infected hydronephrosis (fever + calculus = urological emergency)
clinical_hallmarks: paroxysmal colicky flank pain radiating along the ureter to the groin
or labia. Patient is characteristically restless
and unable to find a comfortable position.
pertinent_negatives: no peritoneal rebound tenderness or rigid abdomen
no chronic burning with frequency only
content: Renal and ureteral colic occurs when urinary calculi obstruct the urinary tract. Presents with abrupt, excruciating paroxysmal flank pain radiating to the ipsilateral groin or genitalia, associated with microscopic or gross hematuria, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnostic workup: Non-contrast Helical CT Abdomen and Pelvis (NCCT KUB - gold standard), Ultrasonography KUB (hydronephrosis detection), Urine Routine (RBCs/crystalluria), and Serum Creatinine/Electrolytes.

red_flags: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (Kussmaul deep breathing, fruity acetone breath, vomiting, confusion)
clinical_hallmarks: Classical triad of osmotic symptoms: polyuria
and recurrent cutaneous or fungal infections.
content: Type 2 Diabetes commonly presents with osmotic symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, unintentional weight loss, and recurrent fungal or urinary tract infections. Acute complications include Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS), signaled by vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, or altered sensorium. Diagnostic workup: Fasting Blood Glucose (FBG >= 126 mg/dL), Random Blood Glucose (>= 200 mg/dL with symptoms), Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c >= 6.5%), and Serum Electrolytes with Urine Ketones.

red_flags: myxedema coma (hypothermia, severe bradycardia, hypoventilation, altered sensorium)
clinical_hallmarks: and delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes.
pertinent_negatives: no heat intolerance or palpitations (rules out hyperthyroidism)
content: Hypothyroidism is a systemic metabolic deficiency predominantly caused by autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis or post-surgical/radioiodine ablation. Features include fatigue, sluggishness, cold intolerance, dry coarse skin, periorbital puffiness, non-pitting pretibial edema, and menstrual irregularities (menorrhagia). Diagnostic workup: Serum Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH - elevated in primary hypothyroidism), Free Thyroxine (FT4 - low), and Anti-TPO antibodies.

red_flags: SNOOP criteria: Systemic fever, Neurological focal deficits, Onset thunderclap (peak < 1 min), Older age > 50, Papilledema/positional change
clinical_hallmarks: Recurrent episodic headache attacks lasting 4-72 hours
pertinent_negatives: no neck stiffness or Kernig sign
no unilateral limb weakness or facial droop
content: Migraine typically presents with recurrent, unilateral, throbbing or pulsating headache of moderate-to-severe intensity lasting 4 to 72 hours. Classically aggravated by routine physical activity and accompanied by photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, or vomiting. Red flags (SNOOP criteria: Systemic symptoms, Neurological deficits, Onset sudden thunderclap, Older age > 50, Papilledema) require non-contrast Brain CT/MRI. Workup: Detailed neurological exam, fundoscopy, and trial of triptan / NSAID abortive therapy.

red_flags: nocturnal awakening headache with projectile vomiting
clinical_hallmarks: pressing or tightening ('vise-like' or tight band around the head) sensation of mild-to-moderate intensity
not aggravated by routine physical activity
content: Tension-type headache is the most prevalent primary headache disorder, presenting as a diffuse, bilateral, tight band-like or pressing headache. It is closely linked to stress, sleep deprivation, and myofascial pericranial muscle tenderness. Does not worsen with routine physical activity like walking. Diagnostic workup: Clinical diagnosis, physical palpation of pericranial and trapezius musculature, and reassurance with stress-reduction or simple analgesics.

topic: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) & Acute Ischemic Stroke
red_flags: ANY positive FAST sign (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty)
sudden ataxia or loss of balance
sudden diplopia or visual field cut
clinical_hallmarks: Acute focal neurological deficit corresponding to a cerebral vascular territory (MCA
content: Acute ischemic stroke is a medical emergency where rapid reperfusion (IV thrombolysis with rtPA within 4.5h or mechanical thrombectomy within 6-24h) determines neurological survival. Evaluated with Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale / FAST. Diagnostic workup: Non-contrast Brain CT STAT (to rule out intracranial hemorrhage), Brain MRI with Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI), Blood Glucose (rule out hypoglycemia mimic), and 12-lead ECG.

red_flags: HINTS exam showing central vertigo (normal head impulse, skew deviation, direction-changing nystagmus)
clinical_hallmarks: Brief episodes (< 1 minute) of intense spinning vertigo provoked specifically by changes in head position relative to gravity (turning over in bed
looking upward). Associated with torsional nystagmus.
pertinent_negatives: no hearing loss or tinnitus (rules out Meniere disease)
content: BPPV is the most frequent cause of peripheral vertigo, caused by otolith displacement into the semicircular canals (predominantly posterior canal). Characterized by sudden rotational vertigo lasting under 60 seconds triggered by head repositioning. Diagnostic workup: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver (confirmatory: produces transient upbeat torsional nystagmus with latency), HINTS test, and therapeutic Epley Particle Repositioning maneuver.

red_flags: Cauda Equina Syndrome: urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bilateral progressive motor weakness
clinical_hallmarks: Lumbosacral pain radiating down the posterolateral aspect of the leg following L4
or sneezing. Positive Straight Leg Raise (SLR).
pertinent_negatives: no unexplained fever or weight loss
no bowel or bladder sphincter loss
content: Mechanical low back pain involves lumbosacral musculoligamentous strain, exacerbated by flexion or lifting and relieved by lying flat. Lumbar radiculopathy presents with radiating lancinating pain following dermatomal distribution (L4, L5, S1) below the knee, often with positive Straight Leg Raise (SLR). Cauda Equina Syndrome is a surgical emergency characterized by saddle anesthesia, bilateral lower limb weakness, and bowel/bladder incontinence. Diagnostic workup: Clinical neuro-deficit examination, Lumbosacral spine X-ray, and Non-contrast MRI Lumbosacral Spine if radiculopathy or red flags are present.

red_flags: hot swollen erythematous joint with fever (septic arthritis emergency)
inability to bear weight after acute trauma
clinical_hallmarks: activity-related joint pain that worsens with weight-bearing (walking
stairs) and improves with rest. Short-lived morning stiffness (< 30 minutes) and coarse crepitus.
pertinent_negatives: no prolonged morning stiffness > 1 hour (rules out rheumatoid arthritis)
no cutaneous erythema or warm effusion
content: Knee osteoarthritis is degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation. Common in patients > 50 years, featuring joint crepitus, restricted range of motion, and varus deformity. Diagnostic workup: Weight-bearing Bilateral Knee X-rays (AP and lateral views demonstrating joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes), and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR).

clinical_hallmarks: acute monoarthritis reaching peak intensity within 12-24 hours
classically affecting the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra). The joint is dusky red
content: Gout is crystal-induced inflammatory monoarthritis triggered by monosodium urate monohydrate crystal deposition in joints with hyperuricemia. Rapid overnight onset with severe erythema resembling cellulitis. Diagnostic workup: Arthrocentesis and Synovial Fluid Analysis under polarized light microscopy (negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals - definitive), Serum Uric Acid (note: may be normal during acute attack), and X-ray of the affected joint.

clinical_hallmarks: Erythematous pharynx and tonsils with exudates
and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy without cough.
content: Acute sore throat with fever, tonsillar exudates, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Centor criteria evaluate likelihood of Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS): fever (+1), tonsillar exudates (+1), tender cervical nodes (+1), absence of cough (+1). Score 0-1 suggests viral etiology; score 3-4 indicates potential bacterial infection warranting testing or empirical antibiotics. Red flag: trismus or uvular deviation indicates peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy). Workup: Throat swab for Rapid Antigen / Culture, Throat examination, and supportive analgesia.

red_flags: post-auricular swelling, erythema, and tenderness with ear protrusion (acute mastoiditis)
clinical_hallmarks: Rapid onset of severe unilateral otalgia (earache)
and conductive hearing dampening following an upper respiratory tract infection.
pertinent_negatives: no pain on pulling the pinna or tragus (rules out otitis externa)
content: Acute otitis media is bacterial or viral infection of the middle ear space, most prevalent in infants and young children. Otoscopy reveals an erythematous, bulging, opaque tympanic membrane with reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, sometimes with spontaneous perforation and purulent otorrhea. Diagnostic workup: Otoscopic examination, Tympanometry, and temperature assessment.

topic: Dengue Fever with Warning Signs Triage
red_flags: WHO warning signs: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding (epistaxis/gum bleed), clinical fluid accumulation (ascites/pleural effusion), lethargy, rapid drop in platelets with rising hematocrit
content: Dengue virus infection transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes presents with sudden high fever, retro-orbital pain, severe myalgia, and bone aches. Strict triage into Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, and Severe Dengue (plasma leakage shock, severe bleeding, or severe organ impairment). Diagnostic workup: Dengue NS1 Antigen (Days 1-5), Dengue IgM/IgG ELISA (Day 5 onwards), Serial Complete Blood Count (hematocrit hemoconcentration and platelet count), and Liver Function Tests.

red_flags: ileal perforation with peritonitis (sudden severe abdominal pain, guarding)
clinical_hallmarks: Insidious onset of step-ladder pattern fever
content: Enteric fever caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi or Paratyphi presents with progressive daily step-ladder fever rising in the second week, relative bradycardia (pulse rate disproportionately slow for fever height), abdominal discomfort, and rose spots on trunk. Diagnostic workup: Blood Culture (gold standard, highest yield in Week 1), Widal Serology (significant titers only in Week 2+), Complete Blood Count (leukopenia or normal WBC despite high fever), and Stool Culture.

clinical_hallmarks: Classical malarial paroxysm occurring in three sequential stages: cold stage (shivering and rigors for 1-2h)
hot stage (high fever > 40C with burning skin for 3-4h)
and sweating stage (drenching diaphoresis with rapid defervescence).
pertinent_negatives: no localized neck rigidity (unless cerebral malaria)
content: Malaria caused by Plasmodium infection (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale) transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. Falciparum carries high risk of multi-organ failure and cerebral malaria. Paroxysms occur tertian (every 48h for vivax/falciparum) or quartan (72h for malariae). Diagnostic workup: Peripheral Blood Smear (Thick and Thin blood films stained with Giemsa - gold standard), Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT for Pf-HRP2 and pLDH antigens), Complete Blood Count, and Serum Bilirubin.

red_flags: eczema herpeticum (widespread punched-out umbilicated vesicles with high fever - HSV emergency)
secondary bacterial superinfection (impetiginization with honey-colored crusts)
clinical_hallmarks: chronic relapsing eczematous skin lesions with xerosis (dry skin). Typical flexural distribution (antecubital and popliteal fossae
wrists) in older children and adults; facial/extensor in infants.
pertinent_negatives: no mucosal blistering or Nikolsky sign
content: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, pruritic inflammatory skin disorder linked to skin barrier breakdown (filaggrin mutations) and personal/family history of atopy (allergic rhinitis, asthma). Key symptom is intractable pruritus ('the itch that rashes'). Diagnostic workup: Hanifin and Rajka criteria, clinical dermatological examination, and avoidance of triggers.

clinical_hallmarks: hypotension or end-organ dysfunction after allergen exposure
content: Anaphylaxis is an acute, potentially fatal multi-system syndrome caused by sudden release of mast cell and basophil mediators. Hallmarks include urticaria, angioedema (lips/tongue), bronchospasm, and hemodynamic collapse. Immediate statutory treatment is intramuscular Epinephrine (1:1000) 0.5mg in mid-anterolateral thigh, supplemental oxygen, and rapid IV fluid resuscitation.

clinical_hallmarks: metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap
content: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) results from absolute insulin deficiency with glucagon excess. Characterized by triad of uncontrolled hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and ketonemia. Patients present with polyuria, polydipsia, rapid deep Kussmaul respirations, nausea, and fruity acetone breath odor. Management requires STAT IV isotonic saline, IV regular insulin infusion, and vigilant potassium monitoring.

Croup is an acute viral infection of upper respiratory tract common in infants 6 months to 3 years. Key features include sudden onset harsh barking seal-like cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness, often worse at night. Treatment involves oral dexamethasone (0.15-0.6 mg/kg), cool mist or humidified air, and nebulized racemic epinephrine for moderate-to-severe stridor.

Life-threatening supraglottic inflammation predominantly caused by Hib or Streptococcus. Medical emergency requiring ENT and anesthesia STAT. Do not examine throat with tongue depressor in non-controlled setting as it may trigger fatal laryngospasm. Immediate airway management, STAT IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin.

clinical_hallmarks: rhinorrhea followed by fine bilateral expiratory crackles and wheeze
content: Viral lower respiratory tract infection primarily due to Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in infants. Supportive management with gentle nasal suctioning, warm humidification, and hydration. Bronchodilators and systemic steroids are NOT routinely recommended by AAP guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: generalized tonic-clonic convulsion associated with rapid fever spike > 38.5C
duration < 15 min for simple febrile seizure
content: Benign generalized seizures in young children triggered by rapid temperature spikes. Excellent long-term prognosis. Parent reassurance, antipyretics for comfort (paracetamol/ibuprofen), identification and treatment of source infection (viral illness, otitis media).

clinical_hallmarks: triad of fever, altered mental status, and neck stiffness
cloudy CSF with neutrophilic pleocytosis and high protein
content: Life-threatening leptomeningeal infection. Statutory medical emergency. Obtain blood cultures and start empiric IV ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone immediately without delaying for lumbar puncture if signs of sepsis or elevated ICP are present.

clinical_hallmarks: severe debilitating bilateral symmetrical polyarthralgia predominantly involving wrists, hands, and ankles
stooped posture due to joint agony
content: Aedes mosquito-borne alphavirus infection prevalent in India. Characterized by high fever and severe, debilitating symmetrical joint pains that may persist for months. Treatment is supportive: hydration, paracetamol, and NSAIDs once dengue has been ruled out.

clinical_hallmarks: prodromal anorexia and nausea followed by icterus/jaundice
pertinent_negatives: no biliary duct dilation on ultrasound
content: Enterically transmitted acute hepatic viral infection (fecal-oral water contamination common in monsoon season). Self-limiting course in majority. High risk of fulminant hepatic failure in pregnant females with Hepatitis E. Supportive care, avoid hepatotoxic medications, monitor LFTs and PT/INR.

clinical_hallmarks: intense subconjunctival suffusion without purulent exudate
triad of jaundice, renal failure, and bleeding (Weil syndrome)
history of wading in floodwaters or rodent exposure
content: Zoonotic spirochetal infection transmitted through water contaminated by rodent urine. Biphasic illness: bacteremic phase followed by immune phase. Mild disease treated with oral doxycycline; severe pulmonary/renal leptospirosis requires IV penicillin G or ceftriaxone.

clinical_hallmarks: cigarette-burn pathognomonic eschar with black crust and erythematous halo (in axilla, groin, beltline)
pertinent_negatives: no typical typhoid step-ladder pulse dissociation
content: Vector-borne rickettsial infection transmitted by larval trombiculid mites (chiggers) in agricultural and brush regions. High clinical index of suspicion in unexplained acute febrile illness in India. Drug of choice: oral Doxycycline 100mg BID for 7 days or Azithromycin in pregnancy/children.

clinical_hallmarks: facial pain or pressure over cheeks or forehead
symptoms > 10 days without improvement or 'double sickening' pattern
content: Inflammation of nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. Majority start as viral upper respiratory infections. Bacterial infection diagnosed when symptoms last >= 10 days without improvement or worsen after initial improvement. First-line: amoxicillin-clavulanate, nasal saline rinses, intranasal fluticasone.

red_flags: malignant otitis externa in elderly diabetic
clinical_hallmarks: intense ear canal pain exquisitely triggered by pushing on tragus or pulling on pinna
erythematous and edematous external ear canal
content: Superficial infection of external auditory canal skin, usually caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus following water exposure or mechanical cleaning. Treatment: thorough aural toilet, topical ciprofloxacin/dexamethasone otic drops, keep ear dry.

red_flags: unilateral purulent discharge (rule out foreign body)
clinical_hallmarks: pale bluish edematous boggy turbinates on rhinoscopy
content: IgE-mediated inflammatory disease of nasal mucosa triggered by aeroallergens (dust mites, pollens, mold). First-line pharmacological therapy: intranasal corticosteroid spray (fluticasone, mometasone) plus second-generation oral antihistamines (cetirizine, fexofenadine).

clinical_hallmarks: diffuse conjunctival hyperemia sparing the limbus
watery discharge with preauricular node (viral adenovirus)
pertinent_negatives: pupils equally round and reactive to light
content: Acute inflammation of ocular conjunctiva. Viral conjunctivitis is self-limiting and highly contagious. Bacterial conjunctivitis responds to broad-spectrum topical antibiotic drops (moxifloxacin or tobramycin). Strict hand hygiene to prevent family transmission.

Ophthalmic emergency caused by pupillary block impeding aqueous humor drainage. Permanent optic nerve necrosis can occur within hours. STAT ophthalmology consult, topical timolol, apraclonidine, pilocarpine, and IV acetazolamide or mannitol to lower IOP immediately.

red_flags: corneal infiltrate or white spot (microbial keratitis)
clinical_hallmarks: intense foreign body sensation exacerbated by blinking
bright yellow-green fluorescein uptake on cobalt blue wood lamp examination
content: Traumatic disruption of corneal epithelial surface. If patient wears contact lenses, must cover for Pseudomonas with topical fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin or moxifloxacin) and avoid eye patching. Standard non-contact lens abrasions heal in 24-48 hours with topical erythromycin/tobramycin.

clinical_hallmarks: lower urinary tract symptoms (hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, nocturia)
smooth, enlarged, non-tender symmetrical prostate on DRE
pertinent_negatives: no hard prostate nodules (rules out prostate cancer)
content: Age-related non-malignant adenomatous enlargement of prostate periurethral transitional zone causing bladder outflow obstruction. First-line medical therapy: alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin 0.4mg) for rapid smooth muscle relaxation, and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride) for prostate volume reduction.

red_flags: sudden onset agonizing pain with high-riding transverse testicle (testicular torsion emergency)
clinical_hallmarks: gradual onset unilateral scrotal pain and swelling
indurated tender epididymis posterolateral to testis
pain relief with scrotal elevation (positive Prehn sign)
increased color Doppler blood flow on ultrasound
pertinent_negatives: testis is normally oriented in scrotum
content: Inflammation of epididymis and testis. In men < 35 years: predominantly sexually transmitted (Chlamydia / Gonorrhea); in men > 35 years: coliform enterics (E. coli). Critical duty is to exclude acute testicular torsion. Ceftriaxone + Doxycycline for STI; Fluoroquinolones for enteric organisms.

red_flags: nausea and vomiting with scrotal pain
clinical_hallmarks: absent testicular perfusion on color Doppler ultrasound
pertinent_negatives: no relief with elevation (negative Prehn sign)
no prior lower urinary tract symptoms
content: Mechanical twisting of spermatic cord cutting off testicular venous and arterial supply. True surgical emergency. Golden window for surgical detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy is < 6 hours from onset (90% salvage). STAT urology consult; do not delay for imaging if clinically evident.

clinical_hallmarks: triad of fever/chills, flank/costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness, and lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria/frequency)
pyuria with white blood cell casts in urine microscopy
pertinent_negatives: no peritoneal rebound tenderness in right/left lower quadrants
content: Bacterial infection ascending to renal pelvis and parenchyma. Common pathogen: uropathogenic E. coli. Outpatient management for mild cases: oral ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin; inpatient admission with IV ceftriaxone for patients with intractable vomiting, pregnancy, or hemodynamic instability.

red_flags: hyperkalemia > 6.0 mEq/L (peaked T waves on ECG)
clinical_hallmarks: persistent reduction in eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2 for >= 3 months
small echogenic kidneys on bilateral renal ultrasound
content: Progressive, irreversible loss of renal function primarily driven by long-standing diabetes and hypertension. Management focuses on slowing progression with ACEi/ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, blood pressure control (<130/80 mmHg), dietary protein restriction, and treating anemia/mineral bone disorders.

clinical_hallmarks: sudden surge of intense fear reaching peak within 10 minutes
somatic symptoms (trembling, sweating, tachycardia, carpopedal spasm from respiratory alkalosis)
medical workup including ECG and cardiac enzymes is completely normal
content: Discrete episodes of sudden, overwhelming autonomic arousal and fear of dying or losing control. Medical mimic exclusion (thyroid disease, pheochromocytoma, arrhythmia) is mandatory. Acute management: calm reassurance, slow diaphragmatic breathing. Maintenance: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram) and CBT.

topic: Major Depressive Episode & Suicide Risk Triage
red_flags: active suicidal ideation with plan and intent
clinical_hallmarks: SIGECAPS criteria (Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicide)
depressed mood or loss of interest for at least 2 consecutive weeks interfering with daily functioning
pertinent_negatives: no prior manic or hypomanic episodes (rules out bipolar)
content: Pervasive mood disturbance affecting cognitive and neurovegetative functions. Primary safety gate is rigorous statutory suicidal risk assessment. First-line pharmacotherapy: SSRIs or SNRIs combined with structured cognitive behavioral psychotherapy.

topic: Acute Delirium in Geriatric Inpatient / OPD
clinical_hallmarks: inattention (inability to focus or sustain attention)
disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness (CAM criteria)
frequently triggered by underlying UTI, electrolyte disturbance, or polypharmacy
pertinent_negatives: no chronic gradual 3-year cognitive decline without fluctuation
content: Acute, transient global cognitive impairment and attentional fluctuation. Medical emergency reflecting systemic decompensation in vulnerable brains. Key: identify and treat underlying somatic cause (urinary tract infection, pneumonia, anticholinergic medications, sodium disturbance).

keywords: painful blisters on one side of rib cage
burning nerve pain followed by vesicles
red_flags: Hutchinson sign (vesicles on tip of nose - risk of Zoster Ophthalmicus & corneal blindness)
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy with ear canal vesicles)
clinical_hallmarks: unilateral dermatomal distribution strictly respecting anatomical midline
grouped erythematous papules progressing to clear fluid-filled vesicles
content: Reactivation of latent Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) in dorsal root or cranial sensory ganglia. Prompt initiation of oral antivirals (Valacyclovir 1000mg TID or Acyclovir 800mg 5x/day) within 72 hours of rash onset significantly reduces duration and severity of post-herpetic neuralgia.

red_flags: secondary bacterial impetigo with glomerulonephritis risk
clinical_hallmarks: intense pruritus severely aggravated at night
pathognomonic intraepidermal serpiginous burrows in interdigital web spaces, flexor wrists, axillae, and genitalia
content: Ectoparasitic mite infestation transmitted via prolonged direct skin-to-skin contact. First-line therapy: topical 5% Permethrin cream applied neck down overnight and washed off after 8-14 hours, repeated in 7 days. Simultaneous treatment of all household contacts and washing bedding in hot water is mandatory.

clinical_hallmarks: evanescent character (individual lesions resolve completely within 24 hours without leaving scar or bruising)
pertinent_negatives: individual wheals do not persist beyond 24 hours (rules out urticarial vasculitis)
content: Mast cell degranulation with histamine release in superficial dermis. Triggered by viral infections, medications (NSAIDs, antibiotics), foods, or insect stings. First-line: second-generation non-sedating H1 antihistamines (levocetirizine, bilastine, fexofenadine) at up to four-fold standard dose.

red_flags: erythrodermic psoriasis (>90% body surface area shedding)
clinical_hallmarks: sharply demarcated erythematous plaques covered by coarse silvery-white micaceous scales
predilection for extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, scalp, lumbosacral)
positive Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding upon scraping scale)
content: Chronic immune-mediated hyperproliferative skin disorder driven by IL-23/IL-17 axis. Associated with psoriatic arthritis and metabolic syndrome. Limited disease treated with high-potency topical corticosteroids + vitamin D analogues (calcipotriene); moderate-severe requires phototherapy or biologics.

red_flags: tinea incognito from misuse of topical steroid creams (e.g. Betnovate/clobetasol)
clinical_hallmarks: annular erythematous scaly plaques with active expanding raised vesicular borders and central clearing
potassium hydroxide (KOH) wet mount showing branching fungal hyphae
content: Superficial dermatophyte infection of keratinized epidermis (Trichophyton rubrum). Widespread in tropical India due to heat, humidity, and rampant over-the-counter topical steroid misuse. Treatment: topical allylamines (terbinafine) or imidazoles (clotrimazole, luliconazole) for 2-4 weeks. Strictly avoid steroid combinations.

red_flags: forehead movement preserved (rules out Bell's palsy - indicates central stroke / intracranial lesion)
clinical_hallmarks: acute unilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness involving both upper AND lower face (inability to wrinkle forehead or close eye fully)
Bell's phenomenon (eyeball rolls upward on attempted eye closure)
content: Acute idiopathic peripheral neuropathy of cranial nerve VII, likely triggered by HSV-1 reactivation. Key distinction from central stroke: Bell's palsy affects forehead wrinkling; stroke spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation. Treatment: oral prednisolone 60mg/day for 10 days started within 72 hours, artificial tears, and nighttime eye taping.

keywords: absent breath sounds on one side
red_flags: tracheal deviation away from affected side
clinical_hallmarks: one-way valve pleural air trapping causing mediastinal shift and superior vena cava compression
content: Fatal thoracic emergency. Clinical diagnosis: do NOT wait for chest radiography. Immediate needle decompression with large-bore 14G cannula in 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line (or 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line), followed immediately by tube thoracostomy (chest drain).

keywords: epigastric pain boring through to back
red_flags: organ failure (respiratory PaO2/FiO2 < 300, renal creatinine > 2.0, shock)
clinical_hallmarks: severe persistent epigastric pain radiating to back relieved by leaning forward
serum lipase or amylase >= 3 times upper limit of normal
content: Premature intracellular activation of pancreatic proenzymes causing autodigestion of gland. Common causes: alcohol abuse and gallstones. Early goal-directed IV fluid hydration with Ringer's lactate, adequate analgesia, and early oral refeeding once pain improves. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.

red_flags: fever with localized peritoneal rigidity (strangulated bowel necrosis)
clinical_hallmarks: cardinal tetrad: colicky abdominal pain, bilious/feculent vomiting, marked distension, absolute constipation (obstipation)
step-ladder air-fluid levels on erect abdominal x-ray
content: Mechanical arrest of intestinal contents. Common etiologies: post-operative adhesions (small bowel) or sigmoid volvulus / colorectal carcinoma (large bowel). Initial management: 'drip and suck' (aggressive IV fluids + nasogastric decompression). Immediate laparotomy if signs of strangulation/ischemia are present.

clinical_hallmarks: suppressed serum TSH with elevated free T4 and T3
smooth diffuse goiter with vascular bruit (Graves disease)
content: Hypermetabolic syndrome from elevated circulating thyroid hormones. Graves disease is the most common etiology. Medical emergency when presenting as Thyroid Storm: treated with IV beta-blockers (propranolol), antithyroid thionamides (propylthiouracil/methimazole), Lugol's iodine, and IV hydrocortisone.

red_flags: fever with joint effusion (septic arthritis must be excluded by arthrocentesis)
clinical_hallmarks: rapid monoarticular inflammation peaking in < 24 hours
exquisite erythema and warmth over 1st MTP joint (podagra)
negatively birefringent needle-shaped urate crystals under polarized light
content: Crystal-induced arthritis from monosodium urate precipitation. Triggered by purine-rich diet, alcohol, dehydration, or thiazide diuretics. First-line acute flare therapy: oral Colchicine (1.2mg then 0.6mg 1 hr later), NSAIDs (indomethacin/naproxen), or oral steroids. Urate-lowering therapy (Allopurinol) should not be stopped if already on it.

keywords: recent long haul flight leg swelling
red_flags: sudden shortness of breath / chest pain (pulmonary embolism)
phlegmasia cerulea dolens (massive limb ischemia / pale blue leg)
clinical_hallmarks: unilateral calf swelling (> 3cm difference compared to asymptomatic leg)
pitting edema and tenderness along deep venous system
non-compressible femoral/popliteal vein on compression duplex ultrasound
pertinent_negatives: no bilateral symmetrical edema from heart/liver/renal disease
content: Thrombus formation in deep leg veins. Virchow triad: stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability. High risk of fatal pulmonary embolism. Prompt diagnostic confirmation with compression ultrasonography. Anticoagulation with DOACs (Apixaban or Rivaroxaban) or LMWH bridge to Warfarin.

red_flags: unexplained iron deficiency in adult male or post-menopausal female (mandates bidirectional endoscopy to rule out occult GI malignancy)
clinical_hallmarks: microcytic hypochromic indices (low MCV < 80 fL, low MCH)
low serum ferritin (< 30 ng/mL) with elevated TIBC
mucocutaneous pallor, fatigue, brittle nails, angular stomatitis
pertinent_negatives: no jaundice / hemolysis (normal LDH and unconjugated bilirubin)
content: Most common nutritional anemia globally, highly prevalent in Indian women of reproductive age. Caused by blood loss (menorrhagia, occult GI bleeding) or impaired absorption. Treatment: oral elemental iron (ferrous ascorbate/fumarate) or IV ferric carboxymaltose for rapid replenishment. Always investigate underlying source of blood loss.

topic: Suppurative Otitis Media with Tympanic Perforation
keywords: sudden relief of earache with pus
clinical_hallmarks: abrupt relief of intense throbbing otalgia immediately accompanied by purulent bloody otorrhea
visible perforation on otoscopy with pulsating discharge
pertinent_negatives: no mastoid bone tenderness or fluctuance
content: Spontaneous rupture of tympanic membrane due to purulent middle ear pressure in acute otitis media. Majority heal spontaneously within 2-6 weeks. Systemic oral amoxicillin-clavulanate, keep water out of ear, avoid aminoglycoside otic drops due to ototoxicity risks.

red_flags: free air under dome of diaphragm on erect chest x-ray
clinical_hallmarks: sudden, catastrophic, agonizing epigastric pain spreading across entire abdomen
absence of liver dullness on percussion (obliteration by subdiaphragmatic air)
content: Life-threatening surgical catastrophe resulting from full-thickness erosion of gastric or duodenal wall. Leakage of acid, bile, and food causes acute chemical peritonitis progressing to bacterial sepsis. STAT resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, nasogastric suction, and emergent exploratory laparotomy with Graham omental patch repair.

topic: Acute Viral Upper Respiratory Tract Infection (Common Cold / Nasopharyngitis)
red_flags: inability to swallow liquids / severe throat pain
signs of lower respiratory distress or chest pain
clinical_hallmarks: gradual onset of clear to cloudy rhinorrhea and nasal stuffiness
mild sore or scratchy throat typically preceding nasal symptoms by 24 hours
frequent sneezing and low-grade or absent fever in adults
mild malaise, self-limiting course typically resolving within 7 to 10 days
pertinent_negatives: absence of high fever with shaking chills (rules out influenza/pneumonia)
no purulent tonsillar exudates or anterior cervical lymphadenopathy (Centor criteria)
no localized facial bone tenderness or purulent discharge > 10 days (rules out acute bacterial sinusitis)
no wheezing or dyspnea on exertion
content: The common cold (acute nasopharyngitis) is a benign, self-limiting viral infection of the upper respiratory mucosa, most commonly caused by Rhinoviruses (30-50%), Coronaviruses, and Adenoviruses. Clinical hallmarks include clear-to-cloudy nasal discharge (rhinorrhea), sneezing, nasal congestion, mild scratchy throat, and occasional low-grade malaise. Antibiotics are strictly ineffective and contraindicated in uncomplicated viral colds. Management is supportive: adequate oral hydration, warm saline steam inhalations, saline nasal drops/sprays, oral paracetamol/ibuprofen for body aches, and short-term oral/topical decongestants if severe nasal obstruction is present. Patients should seek immediate care if high fever >102F develops, breathlessness occurs, or symptoms fail to improve after 10-14 days.

pertinent_negatives: absence of unilateral wheezing (suggests foreign body)
content: Croup is a common viral infection of the upper airway, primarily caused by parainfluenza viruses, leading to subglottic inflammation. It typically presents in children aged 6 months to 3 years with a characteristic barking, seal-like cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor, often preceded by mild URI symptoms and low-grade fever. Physical examination focuses on assessing respiratory effort, stridor severity (at rest vs. with agitation), and air entry. Pertinent rule-outs include epiglottitis (high fever, drooling, toxic appearance), bacterial tracheitis, and foreign body aspiration. Diagnosis is primarily clinical. A neck X-ray showing a 'steeple sign' is supportive but not routinely required. Severity is assessed using the Westley Croup Score. Management involves humidified air, corticosteroids (dexamethasone), and nebulized epinephrine for moderate-to-severe cases, aligned with international guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: preceding URI symptoms in infants <2 years
pertinent_negatives: absence of high fever (suggests bacterial pneumonia)
absence of focal lung findings (suggests lobar pneumonia)
absence of sudden onset (suggests foreign body aspiration)
content: Acute bronchiolitis is a viral infection of the lower respiratory tract, predominantly affecting infants under 2 years, with Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) being the most common cause. It typically begins with upper respiratory symptoms, progressing to cough, tachypnea, wheezing, crackles, nasal flaring, and intercostal/subcostal retractions. Physical examination involves assessing respiratory rate, effort, oxygen saturation, and auscultating for diffuse wheezes and crackles. Key rule-outs include asthma, pneumonia, and foreign body aspiration. Diagnosis is clinical, based on age and characteristic findings. RSV testing (nasal swab) is useful for infection control and cohorting but not essential for diagnosis. Chest X-ray is generally not recommended unless the presentation is atypical or severe. Management is supportive, focusing on hydration, oxygen supplementation, and airway clearance, as per WHO and AAP guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: duration <15 minutes, single episode within 24 hours
associated with fever (≥38°C), age 6 months to 5 years
pertinent_negatives: absence of signs of increased intracranial pressure
content: Simple febrile seizures are common, benign events occurring in children aged 6 months to 5 years, associated with a fever (≥38°C) not caused by an intracranial infection or metabolic imbalance. They are typically generalized tonic-clonic, brief (<15 minutes), and occur as a single episode within 24 hours. The physical examination should focus on identifying the source of fever and ruling out signs of central nervous system infection (meningitis/encephalitis) or other neurological abnormalities. Pertinent rule-outs include complex febrile seizures, afebrile seizures, and CNS infections. Lumbar puncture is indicated if meningeal signs are present, in infants <12 months, or if immunization status is incomplete. EEG and neuroimaging are not routinely recommended for simple febrile seizures. Management involves fever control and parental reassurance, with emphasis on recognizing red flags for urgent evaluation.

clinical_hallmarks: vesicular rash on hands, feet, and buttocks
typically caused by Coxsackievirus A16 or Enterovirus 71
pertinent_negatives: absence of neurological signs (unless severe EV71 infection)
content: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) is a common viral illness in young children, primarily caused by Coxsackievirus A16 and Enterovirus 71. It presents with fever, malaise, and sore throat, followed by characteristic painful oral ulcers (enanthem) and a non-pruritic vesicular rash on the palms, soles, and sometimes buttocks (exanthem). Physical examination involves inspecting the oral cavity for ulcers and the skin for the typical rash distribution. Pertinent rule-outs include herpangina (oral lesions only), chickenpox (generalized rash), and measles. Diagnosis is typically clinical. Laboratory confirmation (e.g., PCR) is usually reserved for severe or atypical cases, especially during outbreaks of EV71. Management is supportive, focusing on hydration, pain relief, and monitoring for complications, particularly neurological involvement with EV71, as per national and international public health guidelines.

red_flags: jaundice within first 24 hours of life
signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia, arching)
clinical_hallmarks: yellow discoloration of skin and sclera
elevated serum bilirubin levels, age-dependent severity
pertinent_negatives: absence of dark urine/pale stools (suggests cholestasis)
content: Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, or jaundice, is common in newborns. Physiological jaundice appears after 24 hours, peaks at 3-5 days, and resolves within 1-2 weeks. Pathological jaundice is characterized by onset within 24 hours, rapid rise in bilirubin, high levels, or prolonged duration. Physical examination involves assessing the degree of jaundice (Kramer's rule), looking for signs of bilirubin encephalopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, pallor, and signs of infection. Pertinent rule-outs include ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, sepsis, hypothyroidism, and biliary atresia. Diagnostic workup includes total and direct bilirubin, blood group, Coombs test, CBC, reticulocyte count, and G6PD screen. Management involves phototherapy for indirect hyperbilirubinemia, exchange transfusion for severe cases, and addressing underlying causes, following established AAP and Indian Academy of Pediatrics guidelines to prevent kernicterus.

topic: Pediatric Dehydration (WHO Plan A, B, C)
red_flags: signs of shock (tachycardia, weak pulse, prolonged capillary refill, hypotension)
clinical_hallmarks: sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor, dry mucous membranes
pertinent_negatives: absence of significant electrolyte imbalance (unless severe dehydration)
content: Pediatric dehydration, often secondary to gastroenteritis, is classified by the WHO into Plan A (no dehydration), Plan B (some dehydration), and Plan C (severe dehydration). Assessment involves evaluating general condition (alert, irritable, lethargic), eyes (normal, sunken), tears (present, absent), mucous membranes (moist, dry), skin turgor (normal, slow, very slow), and thirst. Physical examination includes vital signs, weight, and a comprehensive hydration status assessment. Pertinent rule-outs include other causes of shock (e.g., septic shock) or metabolic derangements like diabetic ketoacidosis. Diagnostic workup may include electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, and urine specific gravity in moderate to severe cases. Management follows WHO guidelines: Plan A (home oral rehydration solution - ORS), Plan B (ORS in a clinical setting), and Plan C (rapid intravenous fluid resuscitation) to prevent mortality.

red_flags: signs of fluid overload (pulmonary edema, heart failure)
pertinent_negatives: absence of chronic kidney disease history
content: Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is an immune-mediated renal disease occurring 1-3 weeks after Group A Streptococcus infection (pharyngitis or impetigo). It presents acutely with edema (often periorbital), hypertension, gross hematuria (cola-colored urine), and oliguria. Physical examination focuses on blood pressure, edema, and signs of fluid overload. Pertinent rule-outs include IgA nephropathy, Henoch-Schönlein Purpura nephritis, and other causes of acute kidney injury. Diagnostic workup involves urinalysis (RBC casts, proteinuria), serum creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, C3 complement (typically low), ASO titer, and anti-DNase B titer. Renal biopsy is usually not required unless the presentation is atypical or there's progressive renal dysfunction. Management is supportive, including fluid and salt restriction, antihypertensives, and diuretics to manage symptoms and prevent complications, adhering to national nephrology guidelines.

pertinent_negatives: absence of other systemic vasculitis signs (e.g., ANCA-associated)
content: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP), now termed IgA vasculitis, is the most common vasculitis in children, characterized by IgA deposition. The classic clinical tetrad includes palpable purpura (non-thrombocytopenic) on dependent areas, arthritis/arthralgia (large joints), colicky abdominal pain (potentially with GI bleeding or intussusception), and renal involvement (hematuria, proteinuria). Physical examination should assess skin, joints, abdomen, and urine. Pertinent rule-outs include ITP (thrombocytopenia), other vasculitides, and sepsis with purpura. Diagnostic workup includes CBC (normal platelets), ESR/CRP (elevated), urinalysis, stool occult blood, and renal function tests. Skin biopsy showing IgA deposition is confirmatory but often not needed. Management is supportive; corticosteroids may be used for severe abdominal pain or progressive renal disease, following international consensus guidelines.

red_flags: signs of heart failure (tachycardia, gallop rhythm, respiratory distress)
large or giant coronary artery aneurysms
clinical_hallmarks: fever >5 days + 4 of 5 criteria: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), peripheral extremity changes (edema, erythema, desquamation), polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy
pertinent_negatives: absence of other clear infectious source for fever
absence of other causes for rash/lymphadenopathy
content: Kawasaki Disease is an acute systemic vasculitis primarily affecting medium-sized arteries, notably the coronary arteries, in young children. Diagnosis requires fever lasting ≥5 days plus at least four of five principal clinical features: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), peripheral extremity changes (erythema, edema, desquamation), polymorphous rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Physical examination involves a meticulous assessment of all criteria and cardiac auscultation. Pertinent rule-outs include measles, scarlet fever, adenovirus, and drug reactions. Diagnostic workup includes CBC (leukocytosis, thrombocytosis), ESR/CRP (elevated), LFTs, urinalysis, and crucially, an echocardiogram to assess for coronary artery aneurysms. Management with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and high-dose aspirin is critical to prevent cardiac complications, guided by American Heart Association and Indian Academy of Pediatrics protocols.

clinical_hallmarks: colic: 'rule of 3s' (crying >3 hrs/day, >3 days/week, >3 weeks in healthy infant)
GER: frequent effortless spitting up/vomiting, irritability during/after feeds
pertinent_negatives: absence of signs of intestinal obstruction
content: Infantile colic is characterized by excessive, inconsolable crying in an otherwise healthy infant, typically following the 'rule of threes' (crying >3 hours/day, >3 days/week, for >3 weeks). Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) is common, involving effortless spitting up. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) implies complications like poor weight gain, esophagitis, or respiratory issues. Physical examination must assess growth parameters, abdominal exam, and neurological status, ruling out organic causes. Pertinent rule-outs include cow's milk protein allergy, intestinal obstruction (e.g., pyloric stenosis, intussusception), urinary tract infection, and corneal abrasion. Diagnosis is clinical after excluding red flags. Diagnostic workup is usually not needed for typical colic or GER. pH probe or endoscopy may be considered for severe GERD. Management involves parental reassurance, feeding adjustments, burping techniques, positioning, and anti-reflux medications for GERD, as per IAP and ESPGHAN guidelines.

red_flags: joint pain with skin lesions (psoriatic arthritis suspicion)
clinical_hallmarks: well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales
Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding after scale removal)
pertinent_negatives: absence of systemic symptoms (fever, malaise) in typical cases
no acute blistering or epidermal detachment
no history of recent drug exposure (to rule out drug eruption)
absence of severe pruritus (less common than eczema)
content: Psoriasis Vulgaris presents as chronic, well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered with silvery scales, typically on extensor surfaces, scalp, and lumbosacral region. Patients may report pruritus, though often less severe than eczema. Physical examination reveals characteristic plaques, often with Koebner phenomenon (lesions at sites of trauma) and Auspitz sign. Nail involvement (pitting, onycholysis, oil spots) and joint pain (suggesting psoriatic arthritis) should be assessed. Pertinent rule-outs include seborrheic dermatitis, tinea corporis, lichen planus, and drug eruptions. Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Biopsy may be performed in atypical cases to confirm psoriasiform dermatitis. No specific lab tests are diagnostic, but inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) may be elevated in severe or psoriatic arthritis cases. Screening for metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular risk factors is recommended due to systemic associations.

red_flags: widespread erythema with pustules/vesicles (eczema herpeticum suspicion)
signs of secondary bacterial infection (purulent discharge, crusting)
severe sleep disturbance due to pruritus
clinical_hallmarks: eczematous lesions (erythema, papules, vesicles, crusting, lichenification)
typical distribution (flexural folds in adults, extensor/face in infants)
personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis)
pertinent_negatives: absence of well-demarcated, silvery scales (rules out psoriasis)
no acute blistering or epidermal detachment (rules out bullous pemphigoid, SJS/TEN)
no specific contact allergen identified (rules out allergic contact dermatitis)
absence of systemic symptoms like fever or weight loss (unless secondary infection)
content: Atopic Dermatitis presents with intense pruritus, xerosis, and eczematous lesions varying by age. Infants typically show erythematous, weeping papulovesicles on the face and extensor surfaces, while adults exhibit lichenified plaques in flexural areas (antecubital, popliteal fossae). The "itch-scratch cycle" is central. Physical examination reveals erythema, papules, vesicles, crusting, excoriations, and lichenification. Assessment for secondary bacterial (Staphylococcus aureus) or viral (Herpes simplex - eczema herpeticum) infections is crucial. Pertinent rule-outs include seborrheic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, psoriasis, and scabies. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on established criteria (e.g., Hanifin and Rajka). Skin swabs for bacterial culture and sensitivity are indicated for suspected secondary infection. Viral PCR may be considered for atypical or rapidly worsening vesicular lesions. Allergy testing (skin prick, specific IgE) may identify triggers but is not diagnostic for AD itself.

topic: Acute and Chronic Urticaria with Angioedema
clinical_hallmarks: individual lesions resolve within 24 hours without scarring
angioedema (non-pitting, deeper swelling of dermis/subcutaneous tissue)
often affecting face, lips, eyelids, genitals, extremities
associated with intense itching or burning sensation
pertinent_negatives: absence of fixed lesions lasting >24 hours (rules out urticarial vasculitis)
no epidermal detachment or blistering (rules out SJS/TEN, bullous pemphigoid)
no fever or systemic illness (unless anaphylaxis or specific underlying cause)
absence of purpura or petechiae within lesions
content: Urticaria presents as transient, intensely pruritic, erythematous wheals (hives) that blanch with pressure and typically resolve within 24 hours without scarring. Angioedema involves deeper dermal and subcutaneous swelling, often affecting the face, lips, eyelids, and extremities, and can be painful or burning rather than itchy. Acute urticaria lasts less than 6 weeks, while chronic urticaria persists beyond this. Physical examination confirms the characteristic wheals and assesses for angioedema, particularly in critical areas like the airway. Urgent assessment for anaphylaxis (dyspnea, hypotension) is paramount. Pertinent rule-outs include urticarial vasculitis (lesions last >24h, leave bruise), drug eruptions, and other inflammatory dermatoses. Diagnosis is largely clinical. For acute cases, identifying triggers (foods, drugs, infections) is key. For chronic cases, a thorough history and basic labs (CBC, ESR, CRP, thyroid function, autoantibodies like anti-TPO, C4, C1 esterase inhibitor levels for angioedema) may be pursued to rule out underlying causes, including autoimmune or hereditary forms. Skin biopsy is rarely needed but can differentiate urticarial vasculitis.

red_flags: signs of systemic infection (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy)
severe pain or tenderness at infection sites
clinical_hallmarks: excoriated papules, vesicles, and characteristic burrows
typical distribution (finger webs, wrists, elbows, axillae, navel, genitals, buttocks)
pertinent_negatives: absence of well-demarcated, silvery plaques (rules out psoriasis)
no history of recent drug exposure (rules out drug eruption)
absence of flexural lichenification without burrows (rules out typical atopic dermatitis)
no transient, migratory wheals (rules out urticaria)
content: Scabies presents with intense, often nocturnal, pruritus and a polymorphic rash including erythematous papules, vesicles, and pathognomonic burrows. Typical sites include finger webs, wrists, elbows, axillae, navel, genitals, and buttocks. Secondary impetigo, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, manifests as honey-colored crusts, pustules, and erosions, often due to excoriation. Physical examination should meticulously search for burrows and assess the extent of impetiginization and any signs of cellulitis. Pertinent rule-outs include atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, insect bites, and papular urticaria. Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic identification of mites, eggs, or fecal pellets (scybala) from skin scrapings, ideally from a burrow. In cases with extensive impetigo, bacterial culture and sensitivity of exudates are crucial to guide antibiotic therapy. Family members and close contacts should also be examined and treated empirically due to high contagiousness.

red_flags: widespread, rapidly spreading lesions in immunocompromised patients
signs of secondary bacterial infection (pus, fever)
failure to respond to appropriate antifungal therapy
systemic symptoms (rare, but consider if extensive)
clinical_hallmarks: typical locations: trunk, limbs (corporis); groin, inner thighs (cruris)
pertinent_negatives: absence of well-demarcated, silvery scales (rules out psoriasis)
no transient, migratory wheals (rules out urticaria)
no burrows or intense nocturnal pruritus (rules out scabies)
absence of vesicles/bullae (rules out contact dermatitis, herpes)
content: Tinea Corporis presents as annular, erythematous, scaly plaques with raised, often vesicular borders and central clearing, commonly known as "ringworm." Tinea Cruris ("jock itch") affects the groin and inner thighs, manifesting as erythematous, pruritic, often bilateral plaques with well-demarcated, scaly borders. Both are caused by dermatophytes and are typically pruritic, especially with warmth and moisture. Physical examination confirms the characteristic morphology and distribution. Differentiation from other annular lesions like psoriasis, eczema, or granuloma annulare is crucial. Pertinent rule-outs include psoriasis, pityriasis rosea, eczema, and candidiasis (especially in intertriginous areas). Diagnosis is confirmed by potassium hydroxide (KOH) microscopy of skin scrapings, revealing hyphae and spores. Fungal culture may be performed for species identification, especially in recalcitrant cases or if KOH is negative but suspicion remains high. No specific blood tests are usually required unless systemic involvement or immunocompromise is suspected.

red_flags: ocular involvement (Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus - vision loss risk)
facial palsy (Ramsay Hunt Syndrome - hearing loss, facial paralysis)
clinical_hallmarks: unilateral, painful, vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution
preceding prodromal pain/paresthesia in the affected dermatome
lesions progress from papules to vesicles, pustules, and crusts
postherpetic neuralgia (persistent pain >3 months after rash resolution)
pertinent_negatives: absence of bilateral or generalized rash (rules out disseminated HSV, chickenpox)
no central clearing or raised borders (rules out tinea)
absence of intense pruritus without pain (rules out eczema, scabies)
content: Herpes Zoster presents as a painful, unilateral, vesicular rash confined to a single dermatome, preceded by prodromal pain, tingling, or burning. Lesions evolve from erythematous papules to vesicles, pustules, and then crusts over 7-10 days. Postherpetic Neuralgia (PHN) is persistent pain lasting more than 3 months after rash resolution. Physical examination confirms the dermatomal distribution and assesses for complications like ocular involvement (HZO), facial nerve palsy (Ramsay Hunt), or motor weakness. Pertinent rule-outs include Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) infection (often recurrent, less dermatomal), contact dermatitis, and insect bites. Diagnosis is primarily clinical. If atypical or severe, Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells) or PCR for Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) from vesicle fluid can confirm. No specific blood tests are diagnostic, but immunocompromised status should be evaluated if disseminated zoster occurs. Early antiviral therapy (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir) within 72 hours of rash onset is crucial to reduce severity and PHN risk.

red_flags: signs of systemic infection (fever, malaise) with severe cysts
rapidly worsening, painful, coalescing lesions (acne fulminans)
extensive scarring or disfigurement affecting mental health
associated hirsutism or irregular menses (PCOS suspicion)
severe psychological distress or suicidal ideation
clinical_hallmarks: presence of deep-seated, painful nodules and cysts
often associated with significant scarring (atrophic, hypertrophic, keloidal)
pertinent_negatives: absence of other systemic symptoms (rules out rosacea with systemic features)
no transient, migratory wheals (rules out urticaria)
no dermatomal distribution (rules out herpes zoster)
absence of intense pruritus as primary symptom (rules out eczema, scabies)
content: Grade III/IV Nodulocystic Acne Vulgaris presents with numerous inflammatory lesions including deep-seated, painful nodules and cysts, often coalescing, alongside comedones, papules, and pustules. It primarily affects the face, chest, and back, leading to significant scarring (icepick, boxcar, rolling, hypertrophic, keloidal) and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Physical examination involves assessing the type, number, and distribution of lesions, and the extent of scarring. Psychological impact should also be evaluated. Pertinent rule-outs include rosacea (lacks comedones, telangiectasias prominent), folliculitis (often monomorphic, lacks comedones), and drug-induced acne. Diagnosis is clinical. No specific lab tests are routinely required for typical acne. However, in females with severe, recalcitrant acne, hirsutism, or menstrual irregularities, hormonal workup (e.g., testosterone, DHEA-S, LH/FSH ratio) may be indicated to rule out polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) or other endocrine disorders. Bacterial culture from cysts is rarely needed unless secondary infection is suspected.

red_flags: rapid progression to alopecia totalis or universalis
associated systemic autoimmune disease symptoms (e.g., thyroid, vitiligo)
significant psychological distress or suicidal ideation due to hair loss
signs of scarring alopecia (follicular atrophy, inflammation)
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset of well-demarcated, smooth, non-scarring patches of hair loss
scalp is most commonly affected, but any hair-bearing area can be involved
presence of 'exclamation mark' hairs at the periphery of patches
nail pitting or trachyonychia (rough nails) may be present
pertinent_negatives: absence of scaling, erythema, or pustules (rules out tinea capitis, folliculitis)
no signs of follicular atrophy or scarring (rules out scarring alopecias like DLE, lichen planopilaris)
no diffuse thinning without distinct patches (rules out telogen effluvium, androgenetic alopecia)
absence of hair shaft abnormalities (rules out trichorrhexis nodosa, monilethrix)
content: Alopecia Areata presents as sudden, often asymptomatic, well-demarcated, smooth, non-scarring patches of hair loss, most commonly on the scalp. It can progress to total scalp hair loss (alopecia totalis) or complete body hair loss (alopecia universalis). Physical examination reveals characteristic patches, often with "exclamation mark" hairs (short, broken hairs that are wider distally and narrower proximally) at the periphery. Nail changes like pitting or trachyonychia may be observed. Pertinent rule-outs include tinea capitis (scaling, broken hairs, positive KOH), trichotillomania (irregular patches, broken hairs of varying lengths), telogen effluvium (diffuse shedding), and scarring alopecias (follicular atrophy, inflammation). Diagnosis is primarily clinical. A dermoscopic examination can aid in identifying exclamation mark hairs and yellow dots. A scalp biopsy may be performed in atypical or recalcitrant cases to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other alopecias. Blood tests for associated autoimmune conditions (e.g., thyroid function tests, ANA) may be considered, though not routinely diagnostic for AA itself.

red_flags: signs of secondary bacterial infection (pus, fever, cellulitis)
severe facial or genital involvement with significant swelling
rapidly spreading lesions with systemic symptoms (anaphylaxis suspicion)
compromised airway due to angioedema-like swelling
clinical_hallmarks: erythematous, pruritic, often vesicular or bullous rash
lesions confined to areas of contact with an allergen or irritant
irritant CD often presents with burning/stinging, allergic CD with intense itching
pertinent_negatives: absence of well-demarcated, silvery scales (rules out psoriasis)
no burrows or intense nocturnal pruritus (rules out scabies)
no transient, migratory wheals (rules out urticaria)
absence of dermatomal distribution (rules out herpes zoster)
content: Contact Dermatitis presents as an erythematous, pruritic, often vesicular or bullous rash confined to areas of skin exposure to an irritant or allergen. Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD) is more common, caused by direct tissue damage (e.g., strong acids, solvents), often presenting with burning and stinging. Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD) is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., nickel, poison ivy), typically intensely pruritic. Physical examination reveals lesions sharply demarcated to the contact area, ranging from erythema and edema to papules, vesicles, bullae, and crusting. Chronic exposure can lead to lichenification. Pertinent rule-outs include atopic dermatitis, tinea, psoriasis, and cellulitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history of exposure and morphology. Patch testing is the gold standard for identifying specific allergens in suspected ACD. Skin biopsy is rarely needed but can differentiate from other inflammatory dermatoses. Bacterial culture of exudates is indicated if secondary infection is suspected. No specific blood tests are diagnostic.

topic: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SJS/TEN Alert)
red_flags: rapidly spreading painful erythema and blistering
positive Nikolsky's sign (epidermal detachment with lateral pressure)
mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital) with erosions
skin detachment >10% BSA (SJS/TEN overlap) or >30% BSA (TEN)
signs of sepsis or organ failure
clinical_hallmarks: widespread erythematous or purpuric macules rapidly progressing to flaccid blisters
severe involvement of at least two mucosal sites (oral, ocular, genital, anal)
pertinent_negatives: absence of transient, migratory wheals (rules out urticaria)
no well-demarcated, silvery scales (rules out psoriasis)
no burrows or intense nocturnal pruritus (rules out scabies)
absence of chronic, localized eczematous lesions (rules out typical eczema)
content: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) are severe, life-threatening mucocutaneous reactions, most commonly drug-induced. SJS involves <10% body surface area (BSA) epidermal detachment, SJS/TEN overlap 10-30%, and TEN >30%. Patients present with prodromal flu-like symptoms, followed by rapid onset of widespread, painful, erythematous or purpuric macules that quickly evolve into flaccid blisters and extensive epidermal detachment (positive Nikolsky's sign). Severe involvement of at least two mucosal sites (oral, ocular, genital) with erosions is characteristic. Physical examination requires urgent assessment of BSA detachment, mucosal involvement, and systemic signs of sepsis or organ failure. Pertinent rule-outs include bullous pemphigoid (autoimmune, less acute, less mucosal), erythema multiforme (target lesions, less detachment), and widespread cellulitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by a skin biopsy showing full-thickness epidermal necrosis with sparse inflammatory infiltrate. Urgent admission to a burn unit or ICU is critical. Labs include CBC, electrolytes, renal/hepatic function, inflammatory markers, and blood cultures to monitor for complications. Identifying and discontinuing the culprit drug is paramount.

red_flags: acute severe pain with fever (septic arthritis)
clinical_hallmarks: reduced range of motion (ROM), often with varus/valgus deformity
pertinent_negatives: absence of systemic inflammatory signs (e.g., fever, rash)
absence of severe, rapidly progressive neurological deficits
content: Knee osteoarthritis presents with insidious onset of activity-related pain, morning stiffness, and functional limitation. Patients often report crepitus and swelling. Physical examination reveals joint line tenderness, effusion, reduced active and passive range of motion, and potential varus or valgus deformity. Gait may be antalgic. Crucial rule-outs include septic arthritis, inflammatory arthropathies, meniscal tears, and fractures. Diagnostic workup begins with weight-bearing plain radiographs (AP, lateral, skyline views) to assess joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and cysts, which are graded using the Kellgren-Lawrence scale. MRI is reserved for atypical presentations, complex cases, or surgical planning to evaluate cartilage, menisci, and ligaments. Laboratory tests (ESR, CRP) are typically normal but may be ordered to rule out inflammatory or infectious etiologies, aligning with Indian and international orthopedic guidelines for diagnosis and staging.

red_flags: cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction)
clinical_hallmarks: radiating leg pain below the knee in a dermatomal pattern
dermatomal sensory loss and/or myotomal weakness
pertinent_negatives: absence of rapidly progressive motor weakness
absence of constitutional symptoms (fever, chills, unexplained weight loss)
content: Lumbar spondylosis with radiculopathy presents as chronic low back pain radiating into the leg, often exacerbated by prolonged sitting or standing. Patients describe sharp, shooting pain, numbness, or tingling in a dermatomal distribution. Physical examination typically reveals a positive straight leg raise test, motor weakness (e.g., foot drop for L5, calf weakness for S1), sensory deficits, and diminished deep tendon reflexes corresponding to the affected nerve root. Critical rule-outs include cauda equina syndrome, spinal tumor, infection (discitis/osteomyelitis), and fracture. Initial diagnostic workup involves plain radiographs (AP, lateral, oblique views) to assess degenerative changes and instability. MRI of the lumbar spine is the gold standard for visualizing nerve root compression, disc herniation, and spinal stenosis. Electromyography/nerve conduction studies (EMG/NCS) may be used to confirm nerve root involvement and rule out peripheral neuropathies, aligning with international guidelines.

red_flags: upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity, Babinski)
clinical_hallmarks: radiculopathy: dermatomal pain/paresthesia, myotomal weakness, diminished reflexes
myelopathy: gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, spasticity, positive Hoffman's sign
pertinent_negatives: absence of gait instability or balance issues
absence of constitutional symptoms (fever, unexplained weight loss)
content: Cervical spondylosis can manifest as radiculopathy (neck pain radiating to the arm with sensory/motor deficits) or myelopathy (spinal cord compression causing gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, and weakness). Presentation is often insidious. Physical examination for radiculopathy includes a positive Spurling's test, dermatomal sensory loss, and myotomal weakness. Myelopathy signs include hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Hoffman's sign, inverted supinator reflex, and a wide-based, spastic gait. Critical rule-outs are spinal tumor, infection, multiple sclerosis, and ALS. Diagnostic workup begins with plain radiographs (AP, lateral, oblique, flexion-extension views) to assess degenerative changes and instability. MRI of the cervical spine is essential for visualizing spinal cord compression, disc herniation, osteophytes, and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy.
