EMG/NCS can confirm radiculopathy and differentiate it from peripheral neuropathies, adhering to Indian and international neurological and orthopedic guidelines.

red_flags: fever, chills, severe systemic illness (septic arthritis)
polyarticular involvement with systemic symptoms (other inflammatory arthritis)
skin breakdown or ulceration over affected joint
clinical_hallmarks: acute onset of severe monoarticular pain, redness, swelling, and warmth
most commonly affects the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra)
pertinent_negatives: absence of bacterial growth in synovial fluid culture
absence of other crystal types (e.g., calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate)
absence of systemic signs of infection (unless septic arthritis is co-occurring)
content: Acute gouty arthritis, often presenting as podagra, is characterized by a sudden, excruciating onset of monoarticular pain, typically in the first MTP joint. The affected joint becomes intensely red, swollen, hot, and exquisitely tender, often waking the patient from sleep. Physical examination reveals classic signs of acute inflammation. Critical rule-outs include septic arthritis (a medical emergency), pseudogout, and cellulitis. Diagnostic workup involves synovial fluid aspiration and analysis, which is the gold standard, revealing negatively birefringent, needle-shaped urate crystals and ruling out bacterial infection. Serum uric acid levels are often elevated but can be normal during an acute attack. Plain radiographs may show soft tissue swelling initially, with chronic cases demonstrating characteristic 'punched-out' erosions with overhanging edges. ESR and CRP may be elevated. Management aligns with international rheumatology guidelines.

red_flags: acute monoarticular flare with fever (septic arthritis)
rapidly progressive joint destruction or deformity
unexplained weight loss or constitutional symptoms
clinical_hallmarks: symmetrical polyarthritis, primarily affecting small joints (MCP, PIP, MTP, wrists)
positive Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and/or Anti-CCP antibodies
pertinent_negatives: absence of other specific autoimmune disease markers (e.g., ANA for SLE)
absence of psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease
content: Seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) presents with insidious onset of symmetrical polyarthritis, predominantly affecting the small joints of the hands and feet, wrists, and knees. Patients experience prolonged morning stiffness (>30 minutes), fatigue, and joint swelling. Physical examination reveals tender, swollen joints, limited range of motion, and in chronic cases, characteristic deformities like ulnar deviation, boutonnière, or swan neck deformities. Key rule-outs include other inflammatory arthropathies (e.g., psoriatic arthritis, SLE), osteoarthritis, and septic arthritis. Diagnostic workup includes elevated ESR and CRP, positive Rheumatoid Factor (RF), and Anti-CCP antibodies (highly specific). Plain radiographs of hands and feet show periarticular erosions and joint space narrowing. Ultrasound or MRI can detect early synovitis and erosions, guiding early diagnosis and treatment according to ACR/EULAR criteria and Indian rheumatology guidelines.

red_flags: acute severe back pain with neurological deficits (fracture, cauda equina)
clinical_hallmarks: inflammatory back pain (insidious onset, worse with rest, better with activity, nocturnal, morning stiffness >30 mins)
reduced spinal mobility (Schober's test, chest expansion)
pertinent_negatives: absence of mechanical back pain features (worse with activity, better with rest)
absence of other inflammatory arthritis (e.g., RA, PsA)
content: Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the axial skeleton, presenting with inflammatory back pain: insidious onset, worse with rest, better with exercise, nocturnal exacerbation, and prolonged morning stiffness. It commonly affects young males. Peripheral joint involvement, enthesitis, and acute anterior uveitis are common extra-articular manifestations. Physical examination reveals reduced spinal mobility (e.g., positive Schober's test), sacroiliac joint tenderness, and decreased chest expansion. Critical rule-outs include mechanical back pain, disc herniation, and other spondyloarthropathies. Diagnostic workup includes elevated ESR/CRP and positive HLA-B27 (in ~90%). Imaging is crucial: X-rays of the sacroiliac joints show sacroiliitis, and later, spinal X-rays may reveal squaring of vertebrae, syndesmophytes, and the characteristic 'bamboo spine'. MRI of the SI joints is sensitive for early inflammatory changes. Diagnosis follows ASAS criteria, aligning with international rheumatology guidelines.

red_flags: acute severe pain after trauma (fracture, massive rotator cuff tear)
signs of infection (fever, erythema, septic arthritis)
clinical_hallmarks: progressive global restriction of active and passive shoulder range of motion (ROM)
pain, often worse at night, followed by stiffness
characteristic 'capsular pattern' of ROM loss (external rotation > abduction > internal rotation)
often associated with diabetes or thyroid dysfunction
pertinent_negatives: absence of neurological deficits (e.g., C5 radiculopathy)
absence of significant rotator cuff tear on imaging
content: Adhesive capsulitis, or frozen shoulder, is characterized by insidious onset of shoulder pain followed by progressive global stiffness, limiting both active and passive range of motion. It typically progresses through painful, freezing, and thawing stages, often lasting 12-18 months. It is frequently associated with diabetes mellitus and thyroid disorders. Physical examination reveals a characteristic 'capsular pattern' of motion loss, with external rotation being most restricted, followed by abduction and internal rotation. Critical rule-outs include rotator cuff tear, subacromial impingement, glenohumeral arthritis, and cervical radiculopathy. Diagnostic workup usually starts with plain radiographs (AP, axillary, outlet views) to rule out fracture, arthritis, or calcific tendinitis. MRI is often performed to exclude rotator cuff tears and can show capsular thickening, but the diagnosis is primarily clinical, aligning with international orthopedic guidelines.

red_flags: signs of systemic disease (e.g., inflammatory arthritis affecting wrist)
clinical_hallmarks: numbness, tingling, and pain in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, radial half of ring finger)
positive Tinel's sign at the wrist
pertinent_negatives: absence of cervical radiculopathy symptoms (neck pain, shoulder pain)
absence of other peripheral neuropathies (e.g., polyneuropathy)
absence of pronator teres syndrome symptoms
content: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) results from median nerve compression at the wrist, presenting with numbness, tingling, and pain in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger. Symptoms are often worse at night or with repetitive hand activities. Patients may report dropping objects due to weakness or sensory loss. Physical examination reveals positive Tinel's sign (percussion over carpal tunnel) and Phalen's test (wrist flexion). Sensory deficits in the median nerve distribution and thenar muscle weakness/atrophy may be present in severe cases. Critical rule-outs include cervical radiculopathy, pronator teres syndrome, and polyneuropathy. Diagnostic workup primarily involves Electromyography/Nerve Conduction Studies (EMG/NCS), which are the gold standard to confirm diagnosis, localize compression, and assess severity. Plain radiographs of the wrist may be taken to rule out bony pathology. Ultrasound can visualize median nerve swelling, aligning with international neurological and orthopedic guidelines.

red_flags: severe pain out of proportion to injury
tenderness over medial malleolus or base of 5th metatarsal
clinical_hallmarks: acute pain and swelling over the lateral malleolus after an inversion injury
localized tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)
positive anterior drawer test (indicating ATFL instability)
pertinent_negatives: absence of bony tenderness (as per Ottawa Ankle Rules)
content: Acute lateral ankle sprain, commonly involving the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), typically results from an inversion injury. Patients present with acute pain, swelling, and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus, often reporting difficulty bearing weight. Physical examination reveals localized tenderness over the ATFL, swelling, and pain with inversion. An anterior drawer test may reveal ankle instability. The Ottawa Ankle Rules should be applied to determine the need for radiographs to rule out fracture. Critical rule-outs include ankle fracture (fibula, talus, 5th metatarsal), syndesmotic injury (high ankle sprain), and peroneal tendon injury. Diagnostic workup involves plain radiographs (AP, lateral, mortise views) if Ottawa Ankle Rules are positive. MRI is generally not required for acute sprains but may be considered for persistent pain, suspected syndesmotic injury, or osteochondral lesions, aligning with international sports medicine and orthopedic guidelines.

red_flags: acute severe pain with complete inability to lift arm (massive tear)
signs of infection (fever, erythema, septic arthritis)
clinical_hallmarks: pain with overhead activities and/or night pain (especially lying on affected side)
weakness with abduction and/or external rotation
positive empty can test (supraspinatus) or external rotation lag sign (infraspinatus)
pertinent_negatives: absence of significant trauma (for chronic tears)
content: Supraspinatus tendinitis or rotator cuff tear presents with shoulder pain, often exacerbated by overhead activities or at night. Patients may report weakness, catching, or clicking sensations. Acute tears often follow trauma, while chronic tears are typically degenerative. Physical examination reveals a painful arc of motion, tenderness over the greater tuberosity, and weakness with resisted abduction (empty can test for supraspinatus) or external rotation (infraspinatus). Critical rule-outs include adhesive capsulitis, subacromial impingement, biceps tendinitis, cervical radiculopathy, and glenohumeral arthritis. Diagnostic workup begins with plain radiographs (AP, axillary, outlet views) to rule out fracture, arthritis, and assess acromial morphology. Ultrasound is a useful screening tool for tears. MRI of the shoulder is the gold standard for confirming rotator cuff tears, assessing tear size, retraction, and muscle atrophy, guiding management according to international orthopedic and sports medicine guidelines.

Acute Suppurative Otitis Media (ASOM) presents with acute onset otalgia, fever, irritability (especially in children), and conductive hearing loss. Physical examination via otoscopy is crucial, revealing a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane (TM) with loss of normal landmarks, and potentially purulent discharge if spontaneous perforation has occurred. Pertinent rule-outs include otitis externa, foreign body in the ear canal, and dental pain. Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Tympanometry can confirm middle ear effusion. Laboratory tests or imaging (e.g., CT temporal bone) are generally not indicated unless complications such as mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy, or intracranial spread are suspected, which mandate urgent ENT consultation and potential surgical intervention. Management focuses on analgesia and appropriate antibiotic therapy.

topic: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM Safe vs Unsafe)
content: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) is characterized by chronic ear discharge (>6 weeks) and a persistent tympanic membrane perforation. "Safe" CSOM (tubotympanic type) involves a central perforation with mucoid discharge, generally without bone erosion. "Unsafe" CSOM (atticoantral type) involves a marginal or attic perforation, often with cholesteatoma, foul-smelling discharge, and potential for bone erosion and intracranial complications. Physical examination via otoscopy identifies perforation type, discharge characteristics, and presence of cholesteatoma or granulations. Rule-outs include otitis externa, foreign body, and active ASOM. Workup includes audiometry to assess hearing loss, microbiology of discharge, and crucially, a high-resolution CT temporal bone for unsafe CSOM to delineate disease extent and identify complications, guiding surgical planning.

Acute Rhinosinusitis (ARS) is inflammation of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. Viral ARS is common, self-limiting. Bacterial ARS is suspected if symptoms persist beyond 10 days without improvement, or worsen after initial improvement (double sickening) after 5-7 days. Presentation includes nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, facial pain/pressure, hyposmia/anosmia, and cough. Physical examination via anterior rhinoscopy may show mucosal edema and purulent discharge. Tenderness over affected sinuses can be elicited. Pertinent negatives include absence of orbital cellulitis or neurological deficits. Diagnosis is clinical. Imaging (CT sinuses) is reserved for refractory cases, suspected complications (e.g., orbital or intracranial spread), or before surgical intervention, not for routine diagnosis.

pertinent_negatives: no signs of deep neck space infection
content: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy) is a collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and superior constrictor muscle, typically following acute tonsillitis. Patients present with severe unilateral sore throat, odynophagia, dysphagia, fever, malaise, trismus (difficulty opening mouth), and a characteristic "hot potato" voice. Physical examination reveals a markedly swollen, erythematous soft palate and uvula deviation to the contralateral side. Rule-outs include severe tonsillitis, parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal abscess, and epiglottitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Needle aspiration of pus is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Imaging, such as a CT neck with contrast, is indicated if the diagnosis is uncertain, if deep neck space infection is suspected, or if aspiration fails, to delineate the extent of the abscess.

Epistaxis, or nosebleed, is classified as anterior or posterior. Anterior epistaxis (90%) originates from Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior nasal septum, typically unilateral and manageable. Posterior epistaxis is less common but more severe, often from the sphenopalatine artery, presenting with profuse bleeding that may flow posteriorly into the pharynx, potentially bilateral. Presentation is visible nasal bleeding. Physical examination involves anterior rhinoscopy to identify the bleeding source and assess severity. Pertinent rule-outs include systemic coagulopathies, severe hypertension, nasal trauma, and nasal tumors. Workup includes vital signs, complete blood count, and coagulation profile if on anticoagulants or a bleeding disorder is suspected. Nasal endoscopy may be required for posterior bleeds. Management ranges from direct pressure and cautery to nasal packing.

red_flags: severe unremitting vertigo with neurological signs
pertinent_negatives: no signs of central nervous system pathology
no other identifiable cause for symptoms
content: Meniere's Disease is an inner ear disorder characterized by endolymphatic hydrops. It presents with a classic triad of episodic vertigo (lasting 20 minutes to 24 hours), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus or aural fullness, typically unilateral. Attacks can be debilitating and unpredictable. Physical examination during an acute attack may reveal nystagmus; otherwise, otoscopy is usually normal. Pertinent negatives include absence of focal neurological deficits or continuous vertigo, which would suggest central pathology. Rule-outs include BPPV, vestibular migraine, vestibular neuritis, and acoustic neuroma. Diagnostic workup includes audiometry, which demonstrates fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and caloric testing. MRI brain with contrast is essential to rule out retrocochlear lesions like acoustic neuroma.

clinical_hallmarks: otalgia exacerbated by tragal pressure/pinna traction
pertinent_negatives: no systemic signs of severe infection (typical OE)
content: Otitis Externa (OE), or "Swimmer's Ear," is an inflammation or infection of the external auditory canal (EAC), commonly bacterial (Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus). Patients present with otalgia, itching, otorrhea, and hearing loss. Pain is exacerbated by tragal pressure or pinna traction. Physical examination reveals an edematous, erythematous EAC, often with purulent discharge. Malignant Otitis Externa (MOE) is a severe, invasive form, typically affecting immunocompromised individuals (e.g., diabetics), characterized by severe unremitting pain, granulation tissue in the EAC (especially at the bone-cartilage junction), and potential cranial nerve palsies. Rule-outs: ASOM (intact TM), foreign body, furuncle. Workup: Clinical diagnosis for OE. For MOE, culture of discharge, CT temporal bone to assess bone erosion, and ESR/CRP are crucial.

Nasal Polyposis involves benign, pale, glistening, grape-like growths in the nasal cavity, often associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. Deviated Nasal Septum (DNS) is a structural abnormality where the nasal septum is displaced. Both conditions cause chronic nasal obstruction, reduced sense of smell (hyposmia/anosmia), and post-nasal drip. Physical examination via anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy reveals the polyps or the septal deviation. Pertinent negatives include absence of unilateral epistaxis, orbital involvement, or neurological deficits, which could suggest malignancy. Rule-outs: Nasal tumors (e.g., inverted papilloma, malignancy), turbinate hypertrophy, foreign body. Workup: Nasal endoscopy is essential. CT sinuses is crucial for polyposis to assess extent, rule out malignancy, and plan surgical intervention.

topic: Vocal Cord Nodules & Hoarseness of Voice
clinical_hallmarks: bilateral, symmetrical lesions on vocal folds
pertinent_negatives: no history of significant smoking/alcohol abuse
content: Vocal Cord Nodules are benign lesions on the vocal folds, typically bilateral and symmetrical, caused by chronic vocal abuse or misuse ("singer's nodules"). Hoarseness (dysphonia) is the primary symptom, characterized by a breathy voice, vocal fatigue, and occasional voice breaks. Physical examination via laryngoscopy (flexible or rigid) is paramount to visualize the vocal folds, confirm the presence of nodules, and crucially, rule out other causes of hoarseness such as polyps, cysts, granulomas, vocal cord paralysis, or malignancy. Pertinent negatives include absence of dysphagia, odynophagia, stridor, or a history of significant smoking/alcohol use, which would raise suspicion for laryngeal malignancy. Workup includes laryngoscopy, voice assessment, and stroboscopy for detailed vocal fold vibration analysis.

clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset severe unilateral eye pain
pertinent_negatives: absence of significant photophobia (distinguishing from uveitis)
content: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma presents as a sudden, severe, unilateral eye pain often accompanied by blurred vision, halos around lights, headache, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, the affected eye typically shows conjunctival injection, a hazy or edematous cornea, and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil that is non-reactive to light. Intraocular pressure (IOP) is markedly elevated, often >30 mmHg. This is a true ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate intervention to prevent irreversible vision loss. Pertinent rule-outs include acute iritis, corneal ulcer, and migraine. Diagnostic workup involves tonometry, gonioscopy (to confirm angle closure), and anterior segment OCT. Management includes topical miotics (e.g., pilocarpine), topical beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and systemic osmotics (e.g., mannitol) to lower IOP, followed by peripheral iridotomy.

clinical_hallmarks: discharge (purulent for bacterial, watery for viral)
content: Conjunctivitis, commonly known as "pink eye," presents with conjunctival injection, ocular irritation, and discharge. Bacterial conjunctivitis typically features thick, purulent discharge, often unilateral initially, with eyelids matted upon waking. Viral conjunctivitis, frequently associated with an upper respiratory infection, presents with watery discharge, follicular conjunctivitis, and often bilateral involvement, sometimes with preauricular lymphadenopathy. Both are highly contagious. Pertinent rule-outs include acute iritis, acute glaucoma, and corneal abrasion/ulcer, which present with more severe pain and vision changes. Diagnosis is primarily clinical; cultures are rarely needed unless severe, recurrent, or unresponsive to treatment. Treatment for bacterial involves topical antibiotics (e.g., moxifloxacin), while viral is supportive (cold compresses, artificial tears), though severe cases may warrant topical steroids (under specialist supervision) or antivirals for herpes simplex.

Corneal ulcer, or keratitis, is an ophthalmic emergency characterized by severe eye pain, photophobia, foreign body sensation, and blurred vision. It often presents with circumcorneal injection and a visible corneal infiltrate or opacity, which stains with fluorescein. Bacterial ulcers typically appear as a dense, grayish-white infiltrate, often with an overlying epithelial defect, and can progress rapidly. Fungal ulcers may have a feathery border, satellite lesions, and a slower, indolent course, often following trauma with vegetative matter or in immunocompromised individuals. Pertinent rule-outs include corneal abrasion, acute iritis, and viral keratitis (e.g., HSV). Diagnosis requires a thorough slit-lamp examination and corneal scraping for Gram stain, KOH prep, and cultures (bacterial and fungal) to guide specific antimicrobial therapy. Prompt initiation of broad-spectrum topical antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones) or antifungals is crucial to prevent vision loss.

Diabetic Retinopathy is a microvascular complication of diabetes, often asymptomatic in early stages (Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy - NPDR). Symptoms, when present, include blurred vision, floaters, or sudden vision loss, particularly with Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) or Diabetic Macular Edema (DME). NPDR manifests with microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, and cotton wool spots. PDR is characterized by neovascularization (new, fragile blood vessels) which can lead to vitreous hemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment. DME involves retinal thickening and fluid accumulation in the macula, causing central vision impairment. Pertinent rule-outs include other causes of vision loss like retinal vein occlusion or age-related macular degeneration. Diagnosis relies on dilated fundus examination, optical coherence tomography (OCT) for macular edema, and fluorescein angiography for neovascularization. Regular screening for all diabetics is paramount. Treatment includes strict glycemic and blood pressure control, laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF injections, and vitrectomy for advanced PDR complications.

red_flags: sudden vision loss (unrelated to cataract progression)
red eye (suggesting acute glaucoma or uveitis)
clinical_hallmarks: visible lens opacification on slit-lamp exam
content: Senile cataract is a progressive, painless clouding of the natural lens of the eye, leading to gradual vision impairment. Patients typically report blurred or hazy vision, increased glare sensitivity (especially at night), halos around lights, and reduced contrast sensitivity. Color perception may also be affected. Cataracts are classified by their location (e.g., nuclear, cortical, posterior subcapsular) and maturity (immature, mature, hypermature). Immature cataracts cause mild symptoms, while mature cataracts significantly impair vision. Pertinent rule-outs include other causes of vision loss like glaucoma, macular degeneration, or diabetic retinopathy. Diagnosis is made through a comprehensive eye examination, including visual acuity testing, slit-lamp biomicroscopy to visualize the lens opacity, and dilated fundus examination to assess retinal health. Surgical removal and intraocular lens implantation remain the definitive treatment, indicated when vision impairment affects daily activities.

red_flags: recurrent chalazion in elderly (rule out malignancy)
clinical_hallmarks: localized painful, red, swollen lump on the eyelid (stye)
painless, firm, non-tender nodule on the eyelid (chalazion)
content: A stye (hordeolum) is an acute, localized bacterial infection of an eyelid gland, presenting as a painful, red, tender lump, often at the eyelid margin (external hordeolum, affecting Zeis or Moll glands) or within the eyelid (internal hordeolum, affecting meibomian glands). A chalazion is a chronic, painless, firm, non-tender nodule resulting from sterile inflammation and blockage of a meibomian gland, often developing after a stye. Pertinent rule-outs include preseptal or orbital cellulitis (which involve more diffuse swelling, pain, and systemic symptoms), sebaceous cell carcinoma (for recurrent chalazia in older patients), and other eyelid lesions. Diagnosis is clinical. Treatment for styes involves warm compresses, gentle massage, and sometimes topical antibiotics. Chalazia also benefit from warm compresses; persistent lesions may require intralesional corticosteroid injection or surgical incision and curettage. Good eyelid hygiene is crucial for prevention.

clinical_hallmarks: chronic foreign body sensation, burning, stinging
conjunctival injection, reduced tear break-up time
content: Dry Eye Disease (DED), or keratoconjunctivitis sicca, is a multifactorial disease of the ocular surface characterized by a loss of homeostasis of the tear film, accompanied by ocular symptoms, in which tear film instability and hyperosmolarity, ocular surface inflammation and damage, and neurosensory abnormalities play etiological roles. Patients typically report chronic foreign body sensation, burning, stinging, grittiness, redness, and sometimes paradoxical reflex tearing. Symptoms often worsen with prolonged visual tasks or in dry environments. Pertinent rule-outs include allergic conjunctivitis, blepharitis, and early corneal pathology. Diagnosis involves a comprehensive history, slit-lamp examination, tear film break-up time (TBUT), Schirmer's test, and ocular surface staining (fluorescein, lissamine green) to assess corneal and conjunctival damage. Management includes artificial tears, warm compresses, eyelid hygiene, topical anti-inflammatory agents (e.g., cyclosporine, lifitegrast), punctal plugs, and addressing underlying systemic conditions.

clinical_hallmarks: bright red patch on the sclera
content: Subconjunctival hemorrhage presents as a sudden, striking bright red patch on the white of the eye (sclera) due to a ruptured blood vessel beneath the conjunctiva. It is typically painless, causes no vision changes, and has no associated discharge or photophobia. Common precipitating factors include coughing, sneezing, straining (Valsalva maneuver), vomiting, eye rubbing, or minor trauma. While alarming in appearance, it is usually benign and self-limiting. Pertinent rule-outs include acute conjunctivitis (which has discharge and irritation), acute iritis (pain, photophobia, vision changes), and more serious conditions like orbital trauma or ruptured globe (which would involve pain, vision loss, or other signs of injury). Diagnosis is clinical. Blood pressure should be checked, especially if recurrent or associated with systemic symptoms, to rule out hypertension or coagulopathy. No specific treatment is required; the blood reabsorbs spontaneously within 1-2 weeks.

clinical_hallmarks: miotic pupil, cells and flare in anterior chamber
pertinent_negatives: absence of fixed mid-dilated pupil (ruling out acute glaucoma)
content: Anterior Uveitis, or iritis, is an inflammation of the iris and ciliary body, presenting with acute onset unilateral eye pain, severe photophobia, blurred vision, and redness, often described as a "ciliary flush" (perilimbal injection). On slit-lamp examination, characteristic findings include inflammatory cells and protein (flare) in the anterior chamber, keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium, and a miotic, often irregular, pupil due to posterior synechiae. Intraocular pressure can be low or elevated. Pertinent rule-outs include acute angle-closure glaucoma (fixed mid-dilated pupil, very high IOP), conjunctivitis (no pain/photophobia, discharge), and corneal ulcer (corneal infiltrate). Diagnostic workup may involve systemic evaluation for underlying autoimmune diseases (e.g., HLA-B27 associated spondyloarthropathies, sarcoidosis) or infections. Treatment involves topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and cycloplegic agents (e.g., atropine, cyclopentolate) to relieve pain, prevent synechiae, and stabilize the blood-aqueous barrier.

topic: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO Sudden Vision Loss)
red_flags: sudden, profound, painless monocular vision loss (often counting fingers or worse)
clinical_hallmarks: sudden, profound, painless monocular vision loss
retinal whitening (edema) in the posterior pole
pertinent_negatives: absence of floaters/flashes (ruling out retinal detachment/vitreous hemorrhage)
content: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is an ophthalmic emergency characterized by sudden, profound, and painless monocular vision loss, often to counting fingers or light perception. It results from an embolus or thrombus blocking the central retinal artery, leading to acute retinal ischemia. On dilated fundus examination, classic signs include diffuse retinal whitening (edema) in the posterior pole, particularly prominent in the macula, with a characteristic "cherry-red spot" at the fovea (where the choroidal circulation is visible). An afferent pupillary defect (APD) is typically present. Pertinent rule-outs include retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, and optic neuritis. CRAO is considered an ocular stroke, necessitating urgent systemic workup for underlying cardiovascular risk factors (e.g., carotid artery disease, cardiac emboli, giant cell arteritis) to prevent further cerebrovascular events. Immediate treatment aims to restore retinal perfusion, though often with limited success, and may involve ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis, or vasodilators.

topic: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD Stage 3b-5 & Uremic Syndrome)
pertinent_negatives: absence of acute kidney injury triggers
no rapid decline in GFR over days
no signs of acute urinary obstruction
content: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) Stage 3b-5 presents with progressive decline in renal function, often manifesting as fatigue, anorexia, pruritus, and altered mental status due to uremic toxin accumulation. Physical examination may reveal pallor, peripheral edema, uremic breath, and rarely, uremic frost. Triage focuses on identifying uremic emergencies. Pertinent rule-outs include acute kidney injury (AKI) and obstructive uropathy. Diagnostic workup involves serial serum creatinine and eGFR, electrolytes (monitoring for hyperkalemia), CBC (for anemia), urinalysis, and renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and rule out hydronephrosis. Further evaluation may include kidney biopsy to determine etiology, especially if rapidly progressive. Management involves optimizing comorbidities, dietary modifications, and preparing for renal replacement therapy in advanced stages.

pertinent_negatives: no active urinary sediment (casts, dysmorphic RBCs)
no signs of systemic lupus erythematosus or other secondary causes
content: Nephrotic Syndrome presents with generalized edema, often starting periorbitally and progressing to anasarca, accompanied by foamy urine. Patients may report fatigue and weight gain. Physical examination reveals pitting edema, ascites, and potentially pleural effusions. Triage aims to assess the severity of fluid overload and rule out complications like AKI or thrombosis. Pertinent rule-outs include cardiac or hepatic causes of edema. Diagnostic workup includes 24-hour urine protein collection or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, serum albumin, lipid panel, renal function tests, and urinalysis. Serological tests (ANA, C3/C4, HBV/HCV, HIV) are crucial to exclude secondary causes. A kidney biopsy is often required for definitive diagnosis and classification (e.g., Minimal Change Disease, Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis) to guide specific therapy.

topic: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH with Urinary Retention)
red_flags: acute kidney injury due to hydronephrosis
pertinent_negatives: absence of neurological deficits (r/o neurogenic bladder)
no history of recent pelvic surgery (r/o iatrogenic cause)
no signs of urethral stricture or mass
content: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) with urinary retention typically presents as a sudden, painful inability to void, often in a male with a history of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) like hesitancy, weak stream, or nocturia. Physical examination reveals a distended, tender suprapubic area with a palpable bladder. Digital rectal examination (DRE) usually identifies an enlarged, smooth prostate. Triage prioritizes immediate bladder decompression via catheterization. Pertinent rule-outs include neurogenic bladder, urethral stricture, prostate cancer, or bladder stones. Diagnostic workup includes urinalysis (to rule out UTI), serum creatinine (to assess for acute kidney injury), and a renal ultrasound to evaluate for hydronephrosis. PSA testing may be considered for prostate cancer screening.

red_flags: severe flank pain with persistent vomiting
signs of urinary obstruction (anuria, severe hydronephrosis)
pertinent_negatives: absence of abdominal rigidity (r/o acute abdomen)
no signs of testicular torsion (in males)
content: Acute Pyelonephritis presents with sudden onset of fever, chills, flank pain, and dysuria. Patients often appear acutely ill, with systemic signs of infection. Physical examination typically reveals significant costovertebral angle tenderness (CVAT). Complicated cases involve underlying structural or functional abnormalities, or immunocompromise. Triage focuses on assessing for sepsis and obstruction. Pertinent rule-outs include appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, or nephrolithiasis. Diagnostic workup includes urinalysis (pyuria, bacteriuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites), urine culture and sensitivity, CBC (leukocytosis), CRP, and blood cultures if sepsis is suspected. Renal ultrasound or CT scan is indicated for complicated cases, persistent fever, or suspicion of obstruction or renal abscess.

red_flags: fever with flank pain (suggesting infected obstruction)
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset severe, colicky flank pain radiating to groin
patient restlessness, unable to find comfortable position
pertinent_negatives: absence of abdominal rigidity (r/o acute abdomen)
no signs of testicular torsion (in males)
content: Urolithiasis, particularly a ureteric calculus with hydronephrosis, presents as acute, excruciating, colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and hematuria. The pain typically waxes and wanes. Physical examination may reveal costovertebral angle tenderness, but usually no peritoneal signs. Triage focuses on pain control, assessing for infection, and evaluating for obstruction. Pertinent rule-outs include pyelonephritis, appendicitis, diverticulitis, or aortic aneurysm. Diagnostic workup includes urinalysis (for hematuria and to rule out UTI), serum creatinine (to assess for AKI), and a non-contrast CT KUB, which is the gold standard for detecting stone size, location, and associated hydronephrosis. Renal ultrasound can identify hydronephrosis but may miss smaller stones.

red_flags: severe acute pain with sudden onset (r/o torsion)
high fever with systemic signs of sepsis
scrotal skin necrosis or crepitus (r/o Fournier's gangrene)
testicular torsion cannot be definitively excluded clinically
clinical_hallmarks: gradual onset unilateral scrotal pain and swelling
positive Prehn's sign (pain relief with scrotal elevation)
pertinent_negatives: absence of sudden, severe pain (r/o torsion)
cremasteric reflex present on affected side
content: Epididymo-Orchitis typically presents with gradual onset of unilateral scrotal pain and swelling, often associated with fever, dysuria, or a history of recent UTI/STD. Physical examination reveals an enlarged, tender epididymis and/or testis. The cremasteric reflex is usually present, and Prehn's sign (pain relief with scrotal elevation) may be positive. Crucially, testicular torsion must be ruled out due to its emergent nature. Diagnostic workup includes urinalysis, urine culture, and STD screening (gonorrhea, chlamydia). Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler flow is essential to differentiate from testicular torsion (showing increased blood flow in epididymitis/orchitis versus absent/decreased flow in torsion) and to rule out abscess or tumor.

red_flags: sudden onset severe unilateral scrotal pain
absent cremasteric reflex on affected side
clinical_hallmarks: absent cremasteric reflex on affected side
negative Prehn's sign (no pain relief with elevation)
content: Testicular Torsion is a surgical emergency presenting with acute, sudden onset of severe unilateral scrotal pain, often radiating to the groin, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Physical examination reveals a tender, swollen, high-riding testis with a horizontal lie. The cremasteric reflex is typically absent on the affected side. This condition requires immediate surgical intervention within 4-6 hours to preserve testicular viability. Triage prioritizes rapid diagnosis and surgical consultation. Pertinent rule-outs include epididymo-orchitis, incarcerated hernia, or testicular appendage torsion. Diagnostic workup is primarily clinical; however, scrotal ultrasound with Doppler flow can confirm absent or decreased blood flow to the testis. Do not delay surgery for imaging if clinical suspicion is high.

red_flags: erythema, edema, and crepitus on palpation
skin necrosis, bullae, or dusky discoloration
clinical_hallmarks: severe pain out of proportion to initial physical findings
crepitus on palpation of affected area
pertinent_negatives: absence of localized infection (e.g., simple cellulitis)
content: Fournier Gangrene is a life-threatening, rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, genital, or perianal regions. Patients present with severe pain, swelling, erythema, and tenderness, which quickly progresses to skin necrosis, bullae formation, and crepitus. Risk factors include diabetes, immunosuppression, and local trauma or infection. Physical examination reveals a rapidly spreading, painful, edematous area with signs of tissue necrosis. Systemic signs of sepsis are common. Triage demands immediate recognition and aggressive management. Pertinent rule-outs include cellulitis, abscess, or epididymo-orchitis. Diagnostic workup includes CBC (leukocytosis), CRP, electrolytes, renal function, blood cultures, and imaging (CT scan) to assess the extent of fascial involvement and gas in soft tissues. Immediate wide surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics are critical.

red_flags: suspicion of testicular tumor (solid, non-transilluminating mass)
clinical_hallmarks: Hydrocele: painless scrotal swelling, transilluminates, non-reducible
Varicocele: 'bag of worms' sensation on palpation, increases with Valsalva, decreases when supine
pertinent_negatives: absence of acute pain or tenderness
no signs of inflammation or infection
no solid mass on palpation (r/o tumor)
content: Hydrocele (ICD-10: N43.3) presents as a painless, soft, fluid-filled scrotal swelling that transilluminates and is non-reducible. Varicocele (ICD-10: I86.1) presents as a painless scrotal mass, often described as a 'bag of worms,' typically on the left side, which increases with Valsalva maneuver and decreases when supine. Both are usually benign. Triage focuses on differentiating these from more serious conditions. Pertinent rule-outs include testicular tumor, epididymitis, or inguinal hernia. Diagnostic workup primarily involves physical examination. Scrotal ultrasound is the primary imaging modality to confirm diagnosis, differentiate from other scrotal masses, assess testicular size, and evaluate blood flow (for varicocele). Management is often conservative unless symptomatic or affecting fertility (varicocele).

red_flags: sudden onset incontinence with neurological symptoms
clinical_hallmarks: Stress Incontinence: involuntary leakage with cough, sneeze, laugh, or exercise
Urge Incontinence: sudden, strong urge to void followed by involuntary leakage
often associated with frequency and nocturia (for urge)
pertinent_negatives: no signs of active urinary infection
content: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI, ICD-10: N39.3) is involuntary urine leakage with increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., coughing, sneezing, lifting). Urge urinary incontinence (UUI, ICD-10: N39.46) is involuntary leakage accompanied or immediately preceded by a sudden, strong urge to void, often associated with overactive bladder symptoms like frequency and nocturia. Physical examination includes a pelvic exam (women) to assess pelvic organ prolapse and pelvic floor muscle strength. Triage focuses on identifying the type and ruling out serious underlying causes. Pertinent rule-outs include UTI, neurogenic bladder, bladder outlet obstruction, or bladder cancer. Diagnostic workup includes urinalysis (to rule out infection/hematuria), post-void residual (PVR) volume, and a voiding diary. Urodynamic studies may be performed for complex cases to differentiate types and assess bladder function.

pertinent_negatives: absence of new focal neurological deficits
content: Migraine presents as a recurrent headache disorder, often unilateral and pulsatile, with moderate to severe intensity. It is typically aggravated by physical activity and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. Aura, if present, usually precedes the headache and involves transient visual, sensory, or speech disturbances. Triage focuses on ruling out secondary causes of headache, especially those with red flags like thunderclap onset (suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage), fever/neck stiffness (meningitis), or new focal deficits (stroke, mass lesion). A thorough neurological examination is crucial. Diagnostic workup is primarily clinical, but imaging (CT/MRI brain) and lumbar puncture may be indicated if red flags are present or to exclude other pathologies, aligning with Indian and international guidelines for acute headache management.

clinical_hallmarks: not aggravated by routine physical activity
no nausea/vomiting (or only one of photophobia/phonophobia)
content: Tension-type headache (TTH) is characterized by a bilateral, pressing or tightening pain of mild to moderate intensity, not aggravated by physical activity. It lacks the severe nausea/vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia typical of migraine. Medication overuse headache (MOH) develops from chronic, excessive use of acute headache medications, leading to a daily or near-daily headache that worsens with continued medication. Triage involves a detailed headache history, including medication use frequency, to differentiate TTH from migraine and identify MOH. Red flags necessitate urgent evaluation to rule out secondary causes like intracranial pathology or infection. Physical and neurological examinations are typically normal. Diagnostic workup is primarily clinical; imaging is usually not required unless red flags are present, following established headache society guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: involvement of upper and lower face (inability to wrinkle forehead)
taste disturbance on anterior 2/3 of tongue
pertinent_negatives: absence of rash in ear canal
absence of other cranial nerve deficits
content: Bell's Palsy is an acute, idiopathic unilateral facial nerve paralysis, typically peaking within 72 hours. It affects both the upper and lower face, leading to inability to wrinkle the forehead, close the eye, or smile on the affected side. Patients may report retroauricular pain, altered taste, or hyperacusis. Triage focuses on differentiating Bell's Palsy from other causes of facial weakness, such as stroke (which typically spares the forehead), Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus with vesicles), tumors, or Lyme disease. A comprehensive neurological examination is essential. Pertinent negatives include absence of other focal neurological deficits or systemic symptoms. Diagnostic workup is primarily clinical; imaging (MRI brain with contrast) is reserved for atypical presentations, slow progression, or suspicion of secondary causes, as per international neurology protocols.

clinical_hallmarks: triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, or cold air
pertinent_negatives: absence of sensory loss in face
absence of other cranial nerve deficits
content: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is characterized by sudden, severe, unilateral, brief, stabbing, recurrent episodes of pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve. Pain is often triggered by innocuous stimuli to specific 'trigger zones'. Triage involves a detailed history of pain characteristics and triggers. A thorough neurological examination is crucial to rule out secondary TN, which may present with sensory loss, bilateral pain, or other neurological deficits, suggesting underlying structural lesions (e.g., multiple sclerosis, tumor, vascular compression). Pertinent negatives include absence of sensory deficits or other cranial neuropathies. Diagnostic workup includes MRI brain with contrast, focusing on the cerebellopontine angle to identify neurovascular compression or other structural causes, in line with international pain management guidelines.

pertinent_negatives: absence of early severe autonomic failure
content: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cardinal motor symptoms: resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability. Symptoms typically begin unilaterally. Triage involves a detailed history of motor and non-motor symptoms (e.g., anosmia, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder). A comprehensive neurological examination assesses for these cardinal signs. It is crucial to differentiate PD from atypical parkinsonism syndromes (e.g., MSA, PSP, CBD) and secondary parkinsonism (e.g., drug-induced, vascular), which often present with red flags. Pertinent negatives include absence of cerebellar or pyramidal signs. Diagnostic workup is primarily clinical, supported by a positive response to levodopa. Imaging (MRI brain) is usually performed to rule out structural lesions or vascular causes, aligning with international movement disorder society criteria.

red_flags: organic cause for physical symptoms (e.g., cardiac, thyroid)
clinical_hallmarks: GAD: persistent, excessive worry for >6 months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance.
Panic Attack: sudden surge of intense fear/discomfort, peaking within minutes, with palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, fear of losing control/dying.
pertinent_negatives: absence of acute organic medical conditions (e.g., MI, PE, hyperthyroidism)
content: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive worry about multiple events for at least six months, accompanied by symptoms like restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance. Panic attacks are sudden, intense episodes of fear or discomfort, peaking rapidly, with prominent physical symptoms such as palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, and dizziness, often accompanied by a fear of dying or losing control. Triage involves a comprehensive mental status examination, detailed history of symptoms, and a thorough medical workup to rule out organic causes (e.g., cardiac, thyroid, respiratory conditions) that can mimic anxiety symptoms. Safety assessment for suicidal ideation is paramount. Labs and imaging are guided by suspected medical etiologies, adhering to psychiatric and emergency medicine guidelines.

topic: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD with Suicidal Risk Assessment)
clinical_hallmarks: persistent depressed mood or anhedonia for >2 weeks
pertinent_negatives: absence of manic/hypomanic episodes (to rule out bipolar)
absence of medical condition causing depressive symptoms (e.g., hypothyroidism)
content: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is characterized by a persistent depressed mood or anhedonia for at least two weeks, accompanied by at least four other symptoms such as significant weight changes, sleep disturbance, psychomotor agitation/retardation, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, diminished concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicide. Triage prioritizes a comprehensive suicidal risk assessment, including ideation, plan, intent, and access to means. A thorough mental status examination and history are crucial. It is vital to rule out organic causes (e.g., hypothyroidism, neurological conditions) and substance-induced mood disorders. Pertinent negatives include absence of manic episodes. Diagnostic workup involves screening for medical conditions and substance use. Management focuses on safety planning, pharmacotherapy, and psychotherapy, guided by national and international psychiatric guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: Mania: distinct period of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased activity/energy, lasting ≥1 week, with ≥3 other symptoms (e.g., grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, impulsivity).
pertinent_negatives: absence of medical condition causing mood symptoms (e.g., hyperthyroidism, stroke)
absence of primary psychotic disorder without mood episodes
content: Bipolar Affective Disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of mania/hypomania and depression. Manic episodes involve a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased goal-directed activity/energy, lasting at least one week, with symptoms like grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, and impulsivity. Depressive episodes mirror MDD. Triage requires a thorough history of mood fluctuations, including past episodes and family history. A comprehensive mental status examination is crucial, with immediate assessment for suicidal or homicidal ideation, psychosis, or severe agitation. It is essential to rule out organic causes (e.g., hyperthyroidism, neurological lesions) and substance-induced mood disorders. Diagnostic workup includes labs to exclude medical etiologies. Management focuses on mood stabilization and safety, following international psychiatric guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: AD: insidious onset, progressive memory impairment (episodic), followed by other cognitive deficits (aphasia, apraxia, agnosia), no focal neurological signs early.
VaD: stepwise decline, often associated with stroke history/vascular risk factors, prominent executive dysfunction, focal neurological signs/symptoms.
pertinent_negatives: absence of other neurological conditions (e.g., normal pressure hydrocephalus)
content: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is characterized by an insidious onset and progressive decline in memory, followed by other cognitive domains (aphasia, apraxia, agnosia), without early focal neurological signs. Vascular Dementia (VaD) typically presents with a stepwise cognitive decline, often linked to a history of stroke or significant vascular risk factors, with prominent executive dysfunction and focal neurological deficits. Triage involves a detailed history from patient and collateral sources, focusing on onset, progression, and specific cognitive deficits. Cognitive assessment tools (e.g., MMSE, MoCA) are essential. Red flags like acute confusion suggest delirium, requiring urgent investigation. Diagnostic workup includes comprehensive lab tests (B12, thyroid, syphilis, HIV) to rule out reversible causes, and neuroimaging (MRI brain) to assess for atrophy, infarcts, and white matter changes, adhering to international dementia guidelines.

topic: Delirium / Acute Confusional State (Hyperactive vs Hypoactive)
clinical_hallmarks: acute onset and fluctuating course of inattention
accompanied by disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness
can be hyperactive (agitation, hallucinations) or hypoactive (lethargy, withdrawal)
disorientation to time, place, or person
pertinent_negatives: absence of primary psychiatric disorder (e.g., schizophrenia)
absence of stable, non-fluctuating cognitive impairment
absence of focal neurological deficits (unless underlying stroke)
content: Delirium, or acute confusional state, is characterized by an acute onset and fluctuating course of inattention, accompanied by disorganized thinking or an altered level of consciousness. It can manifest as hyperactive (agitation, hallucinations) or hypoactive (lethargy, withdrawal) states. Triage is an emergency, focusing on identifying and treating the underlying medical cause. A comprehensive history, including medication review and collateral information, is vital. Physical and neurological examinations are crucial to identify signs of infection, metabolic derangement, organ failure, or neurological insult. Diagnostic workup includes CBC, electrolytes, LFTs, RFTs, urinalysis, blood cultures, drug screen, and often neuroimaging (CT head) to rule out structural lesions. The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) can aid diagnosis. Management involves addressing the cause and supportive care, following critical care and geriatric guidelines.

topic: Cirrhosis of Liver with Portal Hypertension & Ascites
clinical_hallmarks: stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider angiomata, palmar erythema)
shifting dullness/fluid thrill on abdominal exam
pertinent_negatives: absence of acute abdominal pain (r/o SBP)
absence of focal neurological deficits (r/o stroke)
absence of significant fever (r/o severe infection without SBP)
content: Cirrhosis is irreversible scarring of the liver, leading to portal hypertension and its complications like ascites. Patients present with fatigue, jaundice, abdominal distension, and signs of decompensation. Physical examination reveals stigmata of chronic liver disease (e.g., spider angiomata, palmar erythema, gynecomastia), hepatosplenomegaly, and ascites (shifting dullness, fluid thrill). Pertinent rule-outs include other causes of ascites (e.g., cardiac, renal, malignancy) and acute liver injury. Diagnostic workup involves liver function tests, INR, albumin, creatinine, electrolytes, and alpha-fetoprotein. Imaging includes ultrasound abdomen (liver size, nodularity, portal vein patency, ascites), CT/MRI. Upper endoscopy is crucial for esophageal varices screening. Management focuses on managing complications and preventing further liver damage.

red_flags: fever with new-onset abdominal pain in cirrhotic patient
clinical_hallmarks: fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites
pertinent_negatives: absence of surgical abdomen signs (guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness suggesting perforation)
absence of localized pain (r/o cholecystitis, diverticulitis)
absence of recent abdominal surgery or instrumentation
content: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an acute infection of ascitic fluid without an obvious intra-abdominal source, predominantly seen in patients with cirrhosis. Presentation often includes fever, new or worsening abdominal pain, altered mental status, and worsening renal function. Physical examination may reveal diffuse abdominal tenderness, signs of ascites, and stigmata of chronic liver disease. It is crucial to rule out secondary peritonitis (e.g., perforated viscus, abscess) which requires surgical intervention. Diagnostic workup involves urgent diagnostic paracentesis (ascitic fluid PMN count > 250 cells/mm³ is diagnostic, with positive culture confirming SBP), blood cultures, LFTs, renal function. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., third-generation cephalosporins) are initiated immediately.

pertinent_negatives: absence of focal neurological deficits (r/o stroke, intracranial bleed)
content: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a neuropsychiatric syndrome occurring in patients with liver dysfunction, ranging from subtle cognitive changes (Grade I) to coma (Grade IV, West Haven Criteria). Precipitating factors include infection, GI bleed, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, constipation, and sedatives. Patients present with confusion, disorientation, lethargy, and personality changes. Physical examination focuses on mental status assessment, asterixis, deep tendon reflexes, and muscle tone. It is vital to rule out other causes of altered mental status such as hypoglycemia, stroke, sepsis, or drug overdose. Diagnostic workup includes ammonia levels (supportive, not diagnostic), LFTs, electrolytes, renal function, blood cultures, urinalysis, and head CT/MRI to exclude structural lesions. Treatment involves lactulose and rifaximin.

clinical_hallmarks: recurrent bloody diarrhea with mucus and urgency
abdominal cramping, often relieved by defecation
continuous mucosal inflammation starting from the rectum
pertinent_negatives: absence of acute infectious colitis (negative stool cultures)
content: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the colon, typically starting in the rectum and extending proximally with continuous mucosal inflammation. Patients present with recurrent bloody diarrhea, urgency, tenesmus, abdominal pain, weight loss, and fatigue. Physical examination may reveal abdominal tenderness, signs of dehydration, and pallor. It is crucial to rule out infectious colitis (bacterial, viral, parasitic), Crohn's disease, and ischemic colitis. Diagnostic workup includes stool studies (culture, C. difficile, O&P), CBC (anemia), ESR/CRP (inflammation), and albumin. Endoscopy with biopsies (colonoscopy is gold standard, but sigmoidoscopy for acute flares to assess severity and avoid perforation risk) confirms diagnosis. Imaging like CT abdomen is used for complications like toxic megacolon.

clinical_hallmarks: chronic right lower quadrant pain with diarrhea (often non-bloody)
pertinent_negatives: absence of continuous colonic inflammation (r/o UC)
absence of acute appendicitis (though can mimic)
absence of acute infectious enteritis (negative stool cultures)
content: Crohn's disease is a chronic transmural inflammatory disease that can affect any part of the GI tract, often with skip lesions. Terminal ileitis, inflammation of the terminal ileum, is a common manifestation. Patients present with chronic abdominal pain (often right lower quadrant), diarrhea (frequently non-bloody), weight loss, fatigue, and fever. Perianal disease (fistulas, abscesses) is common. Physical examination may reveal abdominal tenderness, a palpable mass, signs of malnutrition, and perianal findings. Rule out appendicitis, infectious enteritis, irritable bowel syndrome, and lymphoma. Diagnostic workup includes stool studies, CBC (anemia, leukocytosis), ESR/CRP, albumin, and vitamin levels. Imaging: CT enterography/MRI enterography is gold standard for small bowel. Colonoscopy with ileoscopy and biopsies confirms diagnosis. Capsule endoscopy may be used for small bowel assessment.

clinical_hallmarks: recurrent abdominal pain associated with defecation or change in stool frequency/form
altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or mixed)
pertinent_negatives: absence of alarm symptoms (weight loss, bleeding, fever)
absence of structural abnormalities on imaging/endoscopy
content: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a chronic functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits (IBS-D for diarrhea-predominant, IBS-C for constipation-predominant, IBS-M for mixed). Diagnosis is based on Rome IV criteria after ruling out organic disease. Patients present with abdominal pain, bloating, distension, urgency, and incomplete evacuation. Physical examination is typically normal, though mild diffuse tenderness may be present. It is crucial to rule out IBD, celiac disease, microscopic colitis, and lactose intolerance. Diagnostic workup includes CBC, ESR/CRP, TSH, celiac serology, and stool studies (calprotectin to rule out IBD, O&P). Colonoscopy is generally reserved for alarm symptoms or age > 45-50. Treatment focuses on symptom management, dietary modifications, and stress reduction.

clinical_hallmarks: chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, and weight loss
iron deficiency anemia refractory to oral iron
often a family history of celiac disease or autoimmune disorders
pertinent_negatives: absence of specific infectious agents (r/o giardiasis)
absence of pancreatic insufficiency (normal fecal elastase)
content: Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically predisposed individuals, leading to small intestinal villous atrophy and malabsorption. Presentation is highly variable, including chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, weight loss, fatigue, iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, and neurological symptoms. Dermatitis herpetiformis is a characteristic rash. Physical examination may reveal signs of malnutrition, pallor, and abdominal distension. Rule out other malabsorption syndromes (Crohn's, SIBO, pancreatic insufficiency) and IBS. Diagnostic workup involves serology (tTG-IgA, EMA-IgA, total IgA), and HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing. Gold standard is upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies (showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes) while on a gluten-containing diet. Treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet.

red_flags: severe anal pain with fever (r/o abscess)
signs of anemia from chronic bleeding
pertinent_negatives: absence of abdominal pain/distension (r/o IBD, diverticulitis)
absence of systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss r/o malignancy)
absence of melena (r/o upper GI bleed)
content: Hemorrhoids are swollen veins in the anus/rectum (internal: Grade I-IV; external). Anal fissure is a tear in the anal canal lining. Both cause rectal bleeding and pain. Hemorrhoids typically present with painless bright red bleeding, pruritus, or prolapse. Fissures cause severe sharp pain during/after defecation, often with bright red bleeding. Physical examination involves inspection of the perianal area, digital rectal exam (DRE) (caution with fissure), and anoscopy. It is crucial to rule out colorectal cancer, IBD, proctitis, perianal abscess, and sexually transmitted infections. Diagnostic workup is typically clinical. Anoscopy/proctoscopy for internal hemorrhoids. Colonoscopy is indicated for new-onset bleeding > 50 years or alarm symptoms. Treatment includes fiber, stool softeners, topical creams, sitz baths. Procedures for hemorrhoids include banding, sclerotherapy, or surgery. Fissures may be treated with topical nitrates, calcium channel blockers, or botox.

clinical_hallmarks: absence of structural disease on endoscopy
pertinent_negatives: absence of alarm symptoms (weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia)
absence of peptic ulcer disease on endoscopy
content: Non-ulcer functional dyspepsia is a chronic or recurrent condition characterized by symptoms of epigastric pain, burning, postprandial fullness, or early satiety, without evidence of structural disease after appropriate investigation. Diagnosis is based on Rome IV criteria. Patients present with chronic upper abdominal discomfort, bloating, and nausea. Physical examination is generally normal, though mild epigastric tenderness may be present. It is crucial to rule out peptic ulcer disease, GERD, H. pylori infection, celiac disease, gallbladder disease, pancreatic disease, and gastric malignancy. Diagnostic workup includes H. pylori testing (urea breath test, stool antigen), and upper endoscopy (especially for alarm symptoms or age > 60). Imaging like ultrasound abdomen may be performed to rule out gallstones. Treatment involves lifestyle modifications, dietary changes, acid suppressants (PPIs), prokinetics, and neuromodulators.

red_flags: severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical exam
sudden onset abdominal pain in patient with AFib/atherosclerosis
clinical_hallmarks: severe, diffuse abdominal pain disproportionate to physical findings
rapid onset, often in patients with cardiovascular risk factors (AFib, atherosclerosis)
pertinent_negatives: absence of localized tenderness (r/o appendicitis, diverticulitis)
absence of guarding/rigidity early on (can develop later with infarction)
absence of significant fever early on (can develop with sepsis)
content: Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) is a life-threatening condition caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow to the intestines, leading to ischemia and potentially infarction. Etiologies include arterial embolism (e.g., from atrial fibrillation), arterial thrombosis (e.g., atherosclerosis), venous thrombosis, and non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMIs). Patients present with sudden onset severe, diffuse abdominal pain, often described as 'out of proportion' to physical exam findings. Nausea, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea may follow. Physical examination is initially benign but later develops signs of peritonitis (guarding, rigidity) with bowel infarction. Rule out perforated viscus, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, appendicitis, and diverticulitis. Diagnostic workup includes CBC (leukocytosis), lactate (elevated), metabolic acidosis, and amylase/lipase. CT angiography (CTA) abdomen is the gold standard. Early diagnosis and intervention (surgical revascularization, embolectomy, angioplasty/stenting) are critical for survival.

pertinent_negatives: absence of acute severe dyspnea (unless complicated)
absence of acute pleuritic chest pain (unless pleurisy)
content: Pulmonary Tuberculosis presents with chronic cough, often productive, lasting over two weeks, accompanied by constitutional symptoms like low-grade fever, night sweats, and unexplained weight loss. Hemoptysis may occur in advanced disease. Physical examination may reveal crackles, dullness to percussion, or decreased breath sounds. Pertinent rule-outs include bacterial pneumonia, lung cancer, and fungal infections. Diagnostic workup involves sputum smear microscopy for Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB), GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay for rapid detection and rifampicin resistance, and mycobacterial culture. Chest X-ray typically shows infiltrates, cavitation, or hilar lymphadenopathy. Treatment follows directly observed therapy short-course (DOTS) guidelines, as per WHO and national programs like India's NTEP.

pertinent_negatives: absence of acute purulent discharge from lymph nodes (bacterial)
absence of rapid onset severe chest pain (PE)
content: Extrapulmonary TB manifests in various forms, with tuberculous lymphadenitis and pleural effusion being common. Lymphadenitis typically presents as chronic, painless, matted lymph nodes, often cervical or supraclavicular, with constitutional symptoms. Pleural effusion causes dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and cough, with physical exam revealing dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds. Rule-outs include lymphoma, sarcoidosis, bacterial adenitis, and malignancy. Diagnosis involves biopsy of affected tissue (lymph node, pleura) for histopathology (granulomas, caseation), AFB stain, and culture. Pleural fluid analysis shows exudative effusion with high protein, low glucose, and elevated Adenosine Deaminase (ADA). GeneXpert can be performed on tissue or fluid samples. Treatment aligns with standard anti-tubercular regimens.

pertinent_negatives: absence of acute abdominal pain (malaria, typhoid)
content: Kala-Azar, or Visceral Leishmaniasis, is a parasitic disease characterized by prolonged, irregular fever, massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and progressive weight loss. Patients often present with pallor due to severe anemia, and hyperpigmentation of the skin (kala-azar means 'black fever'). Physical examination reveals a markedly enlarged spleen, often extending below the umbilicus, and liver enlargement. Rule-outs include malaria, typhoid fever, lymphoma, and tropical splenomegaly syndrome. Diagnosis relies on rapid diagnostic tests like the rK39 strip test, or direct visualization of Leishman-Donovan bodies in bone marrow or splenic aspirates. PCR on blood or tissue is also used. Laboratory findings typically show pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and hypergammaglobulinemia. Treatment involves anti-leishmanial drugs like liposomal amphotericin B or miltefosine.

Leptospirosis is a zoonotic bacterial infection presenting as an acute febrile illness, often biphasic. Initial phase involves fever, severe myalgia (especially calves), headache, and conjunctival suffusion. Weil's disease, the severe form, is characterized by jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhagic manifestations. Physical exam may reveal icterus, muscle tenderness, petechiae, and signs of pulmonary hemorrhage (crackles). Rule-outs include dengue, malaria, viral hepatitis, and rickettsial diseases. Diagnosis is confirmed by serology (Microscopic Agglutination Test - MAT, IgM ELISA) or PCR on blood/urine. Laboratory findings include elevated bilirubin, creatinine, liver enzymes, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis. Chest X-ray may show pulmonary infiltrates. Early treatment with penicillin or doxycycline is crucial to prevent severe complications.

Tetanus is a severe neurological disorder caused by Clostridium tetani toxin, characterized by muscle rigidity and painful spasms. It typically begins with trismus (lockjaw) and dysphagia, progressing to risus sardonicus (sardonic smile) and opisthotonus (arching of the back). A history of recent wound, especially contaminated, and inadequate vaccination status are key. Physical examination reveals generalized muscle stiffness, hyperreflexia, and paroxysmal spasms triggered by stimuli. Rule-outs include strychnine poisoning, dystonic reactions, severe hypocalcemia, and meningitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, as wound cultures are often negative. Management involves aggressive wound debridement, administration of Tetanus Immunoglobulin (TIG), metronidazole, muscle relaxants (benzodiazepines), and meticulous airway management, often requiring mechanical ventilation in severe cases.

pertinent_negatives: absence of rapid improvement with antibiotics (bacterial meningitis)
content: Rabies is a fatal viral encephalitis, typically transmitted through animal bites. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is critical for prevention, involving immediate wound care, Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) infiltration around the wound, and a series of rabies vaccines. Once clinical symptoms develop, the disease is almost invariably fatal. Rabies encephalitis presents with prodromal symptoms (fever, headache, malaise) followed by neurological manifestations: furious rabies (agitation, hydrophobia, aerophobia, hypersalivation, seizures) or paralytic rabies (ascending paralysis). Physical exam reveals characteristic neurological signs. Rule-outs include HSV encephalitis, tetanus, and other viral encephalitides. Diagnosis is clinical; ante-mortem tests (PCR on saliva, skin biopsy, CSF) are often inconclusive. Post-mortem brain examination for Negri bodies is definitive.

topic: Amoebic Liver Abscess vs Pyogenic Liver Abscess
content: Differentiating amoebic from pyogenic liver abscess is crucial. Amoebic liver abscess (ALA) typically presents insidiously with right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, fever, and tender hepatomegaly, often without jaundice, and may have a history of dysentery. Pyogenic liver abscess (PLA) usually has an acute onset with high fever, chills, RUQ pain, and often jaundice, frequently associated with biliary tract disease or sepsis. Physical exam reveals RUQ tenderness and hepatomegaly. Rule-outs include acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, and malignancy. Diagnostic workup includes ultrasound or CT abdomen (ALA often solitary, PLA often multiple), serology for Entamoeba histolytica (ALA), and blood cultures (PLA). Abscess aspiration may yield 'anchovy paste' pus for ALA or frank pus for PLA, with microscopy and culture guiding specific therapy.

Herpes Simplex Encephalitis (HSE) is a severe, acute viral encephalitis, primarily affecting the temporal and frontal lobes. Patients present with acute onset fever, altered mental status (confusion, disorientation), focal neurological deficits (e.g., aphasia, hemiparesis), and seizures. Personality changes and behavioral abnormalities are common. Physical examination may reveal signs of meningeal irritation, but these are often subtle. Rule-outs include bacterial meningitis, other viral encephalitides, autoimmune encephalitis, and stroke. Diagnosis is confirmed by CSF analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and normal glucose, with CSF PCR for HSV DNA being the gold standard. EEG may show periodic lateralizing epileptiform discharges (PLEDs), and MRI brain typically reveals temporal lobe edema and hemorrhage. Urgent empiric intravenous acyclovir is life-saving.

clinical_hallmarks: macules to papules to vesicles to crusts
pertinent_negatives: absence of rapid progression to necrosis (necrotizing fasciitis)
content: Varicella (chickenpox) in adults and immunocompromised individuals can be severe, often complicated by pneumonia, encephalitis, or disseminated disease. Initial presentation includes a prodrome of fever and malaise, followed by a highly pruritic, generalized vesicular rash. The hallmark is a polymorphic rash with lesions in various stages of development (macules, papules, vesicles, crusts), often described as 'dewdrop on a rose petal'. Physical examination reveals widespread rash, including mucous membranes. Rule-outs include disseminated HSV, enteroviral rashes, and drug eruptions. Diagnosis is typically clinical, but PCR of vesicular fluid or Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells) can confirm. Prompt antiviral therapy with acyclovir or valacyclovir is crucial in these high-risk populations to mitigate severe outcomes, especially varicella pneumonia.

clinical_hallmarks: new or progressive infiltrate on chest X-ray
content: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP) and Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) are serious nosocomial infections. HAP develops >48 hours after hospital admission, while VAP occurs >48 hours after endotracheal intubation. Patients present with new or worsening fever, purulent sputum, new cough, dyspnea, and worsening oxygenation. Physical examination may reveal tachypnea, crackles, dullness to percussion, and signs of sepsis. Risk factors include mechanical ventilation, aspiration, and immunosuppression. Rule-outs include atelectasis, pulmonary edema, ARDS, and pulmonary embolism. Diagnosis involves clinical suspicion, new or progressive infiltrates on chest X-ray/CT, leukocytosis, and cultures from blood, sputum, or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting common hospital pathogens, including MDR organisms, are initiated, with de-escalation based on culture results and susceptibility.

red_flags: severe lower abdominal pain with rebound tenderness
pertinent_negatives: absence of vaginal bleeding (rules out ectopic)
absence of flank pain (rules out pyelonephritis)
absence of severe nausea/vomiting (less likely appendicitis)
absence of acute surgical abdomen signs
content: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) presents with lower abdominal pain, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Physical exam reveals cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, and adnexal tenderness. Rule out appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, and urinary tract infection. Diagnostic workup includes CBC (leukocytosis), ESR/CRP (elevated inflammatory markers), urinalysis (to rule out UTI), pregnancy test (to rule out ectopic), and NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae from cervical swabs. Pelvic ultrasound may show tubo-ovarian abscess or thickened fallopian tubes. Hospitalization is indicated for severe illness, TOA, pregnancy, or failed outpatient therapy. Treatment involves broad-spectrum antibiotics, often ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, with or without metronidazole, per CDC guidelines. Early diagnosis prevents long-term complications like infertility and chronic pelvic pain.

clinical_hallmarks: amenorrhea followed by vaginal bleeding and unilateral lower abdominal pain
disproportionately low or plateauing serum beta-hCG levels
pertinent_negatives: absence of intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound
absence of severe nausea/vomiting (less likely hyperemesis)
absence of urinary symptoms (less likely UTI)
content: Ectopic pregnancy is a life-threatening condition where a fertilized ovum implants outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube. Presentation includes amenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, and unilateral lower abdominal pain. Rupture manifests as sudden, severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, syncope, and signs of hypovolemic shock. Physical exam may reveal adnexal tenderness or mass, and signs of peritoneal irritation. Rule out miscarriage, PID, ovarian torsion, and appendicitis. Diagnostic workup includes quantitative serum beta-hCG (positive, often not doubling appropriately), transvaginal ultrasound (absence of intrauterine gestation with positive hCG, adnexal mass, or free fluid). Management depends on stability and size: stable, unruptured cases may be managed with methotrexate; unstable or ruptured cases require immediate surgical intervention (laparoscopy or laparotomy). Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent maternal mortality.

red_flags: severe acute hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability
bleeding unresponsive to initial medical management
clinical_hallmarks: unpredictable bleeding patterns (heavy, prolonged, frequent, intermenstrual)
content: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) refers to any uterine bleeding outside of normal menstruation. The PALM-COEIN classification aids diagnosis: Structural (Polyps, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/Hyperplasia) and Non-structural (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified). Presentation varies from heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) to intermenstrual bleeding. Physical exam includes pelvic exam to assess for structural abnormalities, cervical lesions, and uterine size. Rule out pregnancy, coagulopathies, thyroid dysfunction, and cervical/endometrial malignancy. Diagnostic workup involves pregnancy test, CBC (anemia), TSH, coagulation profile, cervical cytology, and transvaginal ultrasound. Endometrial biopsy is crucial for women >45 years or with risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma. Management depends on etiology, ranging from hormonal therapy (OCPs, progestins) to surgical interventions like hysteroscopy, myomectomy, or hysterectomy.

red_flags: acute urinary retention from mass effect
clinical_hallmarks: enlarged, irregular uterus on bimanual exam
pertinent_negatives: absence of adnexal mass (rules out ovarian pathology)
content: Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are benign smooth muscle tumors of the uterus, common in reproductive-aged women. They often present with menorrhagia, pelvic pressure, dysmenorrhea, and sometimes urinary frequency or constipation due to mass effect.
