content: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) presents with symmetrical polyarthritis, predominantly affecting small joints of hands and feet, characterized by morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes. Physical examination reveals swollen, tender joints, often with ulnar deviation, swan-neck, or boutonnière deformities. Rheumatoid nodules may be present. Pertinent rule-outs include psoriatic arthritis, SLE, gout, and viral arthritis. Diagnostic workup involves serology (Rheumatoid Factor, anti-CCP antibodies), inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and imaging (X-rays of hands/feet to assess erosions and joint space narrowing). Ultrasound and MRI can detect early synovitis and erosions. Classification criteria (ACR/EULAR) guide diagnosis. Treatment aims for remission, often with DMARDs, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

topic: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (Lupus Nephritis & Malar Rash)
content: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease with diverse manifestations. Patients often present with fatigue, arthralgia, malar rash, photosensitivity, and serositis. Lupus nephritis, a severe complication, presents with proteinuria, hematuria, and declining renal function. Physical examination may reveal skin lesions (discoid, malar), oral ulcers, non-erosive arthritis, and signs of serositis. Rule-outs include drug-induced lupus, infections, and other autoimmune conditions. Diagnostic workup includes ANA (highly sensitive), anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm (highly specific), complement levels (C3, C4), CBC, renal function tests, urinalysis, and liver function tests. Kidney biopsy is crucial for lupus nephritis staging. Imaging like echocardiography or chest X-ray may assess serositis. Management involves immunosuppressants tailored to organ involvement, following Indian and international guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: inflammatory back pain (worse with rest, better with activity)
pertinent_negatives: absence of mechanical back pain features
absence of significant peripheral joint arthritis (initially)
absence of other systemic inflammatory conditions
content: Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the axial skeleton. Patients typically present with inflammatory back pain, characterized by insidious onset, morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes, improvement with exercise, and worsening with rest. Enthesitis and acute anterior uveitis are common extra-articular manifestations. Physical examination reveals reduced spinal mobility (e.g., decreased lumbar flexion via Schober's test, reduced chest expansion). Rule-outs include mechanical back pain, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH), and other spondyloarthropathies. Diagnostic workup includes HLA-B27 testing, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and imaging. X-rays of the sacroiliac joints show sacroiliitis (often bilateral). MRI is more sensitive for early inflammatory changes. Management focuses on NSAIDs, physical therapy, and biologics (TNF inhibitors) for refractory cases, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

red_flags: scleroderma renal crisis (hypertensive emergency, acute renal failure)
pertinent_negatives: absence of other primary autoimmune conditions
absence of isolated Raynaud's phenomenon without other systemic features
content: Systemic Sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by widespread vascular dysfunction and progressive fibrosis of skin and internal organs. Patients often present with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin thickening (sclerodactyly), and digital ulcers. CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias) is a limited form. Physical examination reveals skin induration, telangiectasias, and signs of organ involvement (e.g., crackles in lungs, abnormal heart sounds). Rule-outs include other connective tissue diseases, drug-induced scleroderma-like syndromes, and eosinophilic fasciitis. Diagnostic workup includes ANA, specific autoantibodies (anti-centromere for CREST, anti-Scl-70/topoisomerase I for diffuse), inflammatory markers. Organ-specific assessments include PFTs (pulmonary fibrosis), echocardiogram (pulmonary hypertension), barium swallow (esophageal dysmotility), and renal function tests. Regular monitoring for complications is crucial, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

topic: Polymyalgia Rheumatica & Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis)
red_flags: acute vision loss (amaurosis fugax, permanent blindness)
clinical_hallmarks: bilateral shoulder/pelvic girdle pain and stiffness (PMR)
content: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) presents with bilateral aching and stiffness in the shoulders and pelvic girdle, worse in the morning, in patients typically over 50. Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), a vasculitis often co-occurring with PMR, manifests with new-onset headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual disturbances. Physical examination for PMR shows normal muscle strength but painful range of motion. For GCA, temporal arteries may be tender, thickened, or pulseless. Rule-outs include malignancy, infection, hypothyroidism, and other inflammatory myopathies. Diagnostic workup includes markedly elevated ESR and CRP. Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard for GCA, but urgent steroid therapy should not be delayed. Imaging (ultrasound, MRI, PET) can support GCA diagnosis. Prompt high-dose corticosteroids are critical to prevent irreversible vision loss, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

pertinent_negatives: absence of other primary autoimmune conditions
absence of primary infection of salivary glands
absence of significant malignancy (other than lymphoma risk)
content: Sjögren's Syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease primarily affecting exocrine glands, leading to keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth). Patients often report gritty sensation in eyes, difficulty swallowing dry food, and dental caries. Fatigue and arthralgia are common systemic symptoms. Physical examination may reveal parotid gland enlargement, dental decay, and ocular signs of dryness (e.g., reduced tear film, corneal staining). Rule-outs include medication-induced dryness, sarcoidosis, and other autoimmune diseases. Diagnostic workup includes autoantibodies (ANA, RF, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB), Schirmer's test (tear production), and salivary flow rate. Lip biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis is confirmatory. Management focuses on symptomatic relief, preventing complications, and monitoring for lymphoma development, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

red_flags: septic arthritis (fever, severe systemic illness, purulent joint fluid)
acute kidney injury due to urate nephropathy
clinical_hallmarks: acute monoarthritis (often first MTP joint - podagra)
pertinent_negatives: absence of other crystal arthropathies (e.g., CPPD)
content: Gouty Arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition. Acute attacks typically present as sudden, severe monoarthritis, most commonly affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra), characterized by exquisite pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth. Chronic gout can lead to tophi formation. Physical examination reveals a hot, swollen, tender joint. Rule-outs include septic arthritis, pseudogout, and other inflammatory arthritides. Diagnostic workup involves synovial fluid aspiration and microscopy to identify negatively birefringent, needle-shaped urate crystals. Serum uric acid levels are often elevated but can be normal during an acute attack. Imaging (X-rays) may show characteristic "punched-out" erosions in chronic gout. Management includes NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids for acute attacks, and urate-lowering therapy (e.g., allopurinol, febuxostat) for long-term prevention, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

red_flags: septic arthritis (fever, severe systemic illness, purulent joint fluid)
severe neurological compromise (if cervical spine involvement)
clinical_hallmarks: acute mono- or oligoarthritis (often knee, wrist, shoulder)
positively birefringent rhomboid crystals in synovial fluid
pertinent_negatives: absence of negatively birefringent crystals (rules out gout)
content: Pseudogout, or Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate (CPPD) deposition disease, is an inflammatory arthritis caused by CPPD crystal deposition. It commonly presents as acute mono- or oligoarthritis, frequently affecting large joints like the knee, wrist, or shoulder, mimicking gout but often less severe. Physical examination reveals a swollen, tender, warm joint. Rule-outs include septic arthritis, gout, and osteoarthritis. Diagnostic workup involves synovial fluid aspiration and microscopy, revealing positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped crystals. X-rays often show chondrocalcinosis (calcification of articular cartilage or menisci). Serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium, and iron studies may be indicated to rule out underlying metabolic disorders. Management includes NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids (oral or intra-articular) for acute attacks. There is no specific treatment to remove CPPD crystals, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: chronic widespread pain (WPI ≥ 7 and SS scale ≥ 5, or WPI 3-6 and SS scale ≥ 9)
pertinent_negatives: absence of elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP)
content: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive dysfunction. Patients report pain in multiple body regions, often accompanied by tenderness in specific "tender points." Physical examination is typically normal, with no objective signs of inflammation or joint swelling, but patients exhibit allodynia or hyperalgesia. Rule-outs include inflammatory arthritides, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, sleep apnea, and other chronic pain conditions. Diagnostic workup primarily relies on clinical criteria (Widespread Pain Index and Symptom Severity Scale). Laboratory tests (CBC, ESR, CRP, thyroid function, vitamin D) are usually normal and performed to exclude other conditions. Imaging is generally not indicated unless specific red flags are present. Management involves a multidisciplinary approach including exercise, cognitive behavioral therapy, and pharmacotherapy, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: upper airway involvement (chronic sinusitis, epistaxis, saddle nose deformity)
pertinent_negatives: absence of other primary autoimmune conditions
absence of significant infectious etiology (e.g., fungal infection mimicking granulomas)
absence of isolated organ involvement (typically multi-system)
content: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) is a severe, systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis affecting small-to-medium sized vessels, characterized by granulomatous inflammation. It classically involves the upper respiratory tract (sinusitis, epistaxis, saddle nose), lower respiratory tract (pulmonary nodules, hemoptysis), and kidneys (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis). Physical examination may reveal nasal crusting, lung crackles, or signs of renal impairment. Rule-outs include infections (e.g., fungal, mycobacterial), other vasculitides, and malignancy. Diagnostic workup includes c-ANCA with anti-PR3 antibodies (highly specific), inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), renal function tests, urinalysis, and chest imaging (X-ray, CT scan for nodules/infiltrates). Biopsy of affected tissue (e.g., kidney, lung, sinus) showing granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis is confirmatory. Urgent immunosuppression (corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide/rituximab) is critical to prevent organ damage and improve survival, aligned with Indian and international hospital guidelines.

topic: Organophosphate and Carbamate Poisoning (Cholinergic SLUDGE Toxidrome)
content: Presentation involves acute cholinergic crisis from acetylcholinesterase inhibition, manifesting as SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis) and DUMBBELS (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bronchospasm/Bronchorrhea, Bradycardia, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation). Patients present with miosis, profuse secretions, muscle fasciculations, weakness, bradycardia, and potentially respiratory failure due to bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, and diaphragmatic paralysis. Altered mental status and seizures can occur. Physical exam reveals constricted pupils, wet lung sounds, and muscle twitching. Pertinent rule-outs include other toxidromes (e.g., opioid, sedative-hypnotic withdrawal) and sepsis. Diagnostic workup includes RBC/plasma cholinesterase levels (though treatment is clinical), ABG, electrolytes, ECG, and chest X-ray to assess respiratory compromise. Management involves atropine and pralidoxime (2-PAM) per standard protocols.

Patients present rapidly with severe gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain), followed by profound cardiovascular collapse due to phosphine gas-induced mitochondrial dysfunction. Hallmarks include refractory hypotension, severe metabolic acidosis, and various arrhythmias (often ventricular), leading to cardiogenic shock. A characteristic garlic-like odor may be present on breath. Respiratory distress, acute kidney injury, and altered mental status are common. Physical exam reveals signs of shock, tachypnea, and potentially cyanosis. Pertinent rule-outs include septic shock, myocardial infarction, and other causes of severe metabolic acidosis. Diagnostic workup includes ABG, electrolytes, cardiac enzymes, ECG, echocardiography, and renal function tests. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive, focusing on aggressive fluid resuscitation, vasopressors, and correction of acidosis, often with magnesium sulfate.

topic: Viperine Snake Bite (Vasculotoxic Envenomation with Coagulopathy)
content: Viperine envenomation typically presents with prominent local effects: severe pain, progressive swelling, blistering, and necrosis at the bite site, often with fang marks. Systemically, vasculotoxicity leads to coagulopathy, manifesting as spontaneous bleeding (e.g., gum bleeding, hematuria, epistaxis), and potentially intracranial hemorrhage. Hypotension, acute kidney injury, and shock can develop. Physical exam reveals local tissue damage and signs of bleeding. Pertinent rule-outs include dry bite (no envenomation), other causes of bleeding disorders, and local trauma. Diagnostic workup includes the 20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Time (20WBCT), CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, renal function tests, and urinalysis. Management involves antivenom administration based on evidence of systemic envenomation, along with supportive care.

topic: Elapid Snake Bite (Krait / Cobra Neurotoxic Envenomation with Ptosis & Respiratory Failure)
content: Elapid envenomation (e.g., Krait, Cobra) primarily causes neurotoxicity with minimal local reaction. Patients present with progressive descending flaccid paralysis, starting with ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and diplopia, followed by dysphagia, dysarthria, and ultimately respiratory muscle paralysis leading to respiratory failure. Altered mental status is less common unless hypoxia is severe. Physical exam reveals progressive cranial nerve palsies and muscle weakness. Pertinent rule-outs include other causes of acute flaccid paralysis (e.g., Guillain-Barré Syndrome, botulism, myasthenia gravis crisis) and stroke. Diagnostic workup includes serial neurological assessments, spirometry (FVC), ABG, and a 20WBCT (typically normal) to differentiate from viperine bites. Management involves prompt administration of specific antivenom and aggressive airway management, including mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure ensues.

topic: Scorpion Sting Envenomation & Autonomic Storm (Prazosin Protocol)
content: Scorpion sting envenomation, particularly from highly venomous species, can cause an "autonomic storm" due to massive catecholamine release. Patients present with severe local pain, followed by systemic effects including hypertension, tachycardia, profuse sweating, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Severe cases develop myocarditis, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, and priapism (in males). Neurological symptoms like agitation or seizures can occur. Physical exam reveals local tenderness, signs of sympathetic overactivity, and potentially pulmonary crackles. Pertinent rule-outs include acute coronary syndrome, hypertensive crisis, and other causes of acute heart failure. Diagnostic workup includes ECG, cardiac enzymes, echocardiography, chest X-ray, ABG, and electrolytes. Management involves supportive care, including Prazosin for autonomic manifestations, and antivenom where available and indicated.

topic: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) Overdose & Acute Liver Failure (NAC Protocol)
pertinent_negatives: normal paracetamol level at 4 hours post-ingestion
content: Paracetamol overdose initially presents asymptomatically or with non-specific symptoms like nausea, vomiting, and malaise within the first 24 hours. Hepatotoxicity typically manifests 24-72 hours post-ingestion with right upper quadrant pain, elevated transaminases (AST/ALT), and later jaundice, coagulopathy (elevated INR), and hepatic encephalopathy, indicating acute liver failure. Acute kidney injury can also occur. Physical exam may be unremarkable initially, progressing to signs of liver failure. Pertinent rule-outs include viral hepatitis, other drug-induced liver injury, and sepsis. Diagnostic workup includes serial paracetamol levels (especially 4-hour post-ingestion), LFTs, INR, glucose, renal function tests, and ABG. Management involves N-acetylcysteine (NAC) administration based on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, along with supportive care for liver failure.

topic: Corrosive Acid / Alkali Ingestion & Esophageal Stricture
content: Corrosive ingestion causes immediate chemical burns to the oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, and stomach. Alkali (e.g., lye) causes liquefaction necrosis, leading to deep, penetrating injuries and potential perforation. Acid (e.g., toilet cleaner) causes coagulation necrosis, often forming an eschar. Patients present with severe oral/retrosternal/epigastric pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling, and vomiting. Stridor or hoarseness indicates laryngeal involvement. Signs of perforation (peritonitis, mediastinitis) or shock are red flags. Physical exam reveals oral burns, tenderness, and potentially respiratory distress. Pertinent rule-outs include foreign body ingestion, acute gastritis, or myocardial infarction. Diagnostic workup includes ABCs, NPO, IV fluids, chest/abdominal X-rays (for free air), and urgent endoscopy within 12-24 hours to grade injury and guide management.

Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning presents with non-specific symptoms mimicking viral illness, including headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. Severe poisoning leads to altered mental status, syncope, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and metabolic acidosis. The classic "cherry-red" skin is rare and a late sign. CO binds to hemoglobin with high affinity, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb), impairing oxygen delivery and cellular respiration. Physical exam may reveal tachycardia, tachypnea, or neurological deficits. Pertinent rule-outs include viral syndromes, migraine, stroke, and other causes of altered consciousness. Diagnostic workup includes co-oximetry to measure COHb levels (pulse oximetry is unreliable), ABG, ECG, cardiac enzymes, and neurological assessment. Management involves high-flow 100% oxygen; hyperbaric oxygen therapy is indicated for severe cases.

Heat stroke is a life-threatening condition characterized by a core body temperature >40°C (104°F) and central nervous system dysfunction (e.g., altered mental status, seizures, delirium, coma). Heat exhaustion involves similar symptoms but without significant CNS impairment and with a core temperature typically <40°C. Patients present with headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, muscle cramps, and profound weakness. Skin may be hot and dry (classic) or profusely sweating (exertional). Physical exam reveals hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypotension, and neurological deficits in heat stroke. Pertinent rule-outs include sepsis, meningitis, thyroid storm, and drug-induced hyperthermia. Diagnostic workup includes rectal core temperature, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, CK, coagulation profile, ABG, and ECG. Rapid cooling is paramount, along with fluid resuscitation and supportive care.

topic: Electric Shock and Lightning Injury (Arrhythmias & Deep Tissue Necrosis)
content: Electric shock and lightning injuries can cause a wide spectrum of effects, from minor burns to immediate cardiac arrest. Key concerns include cardiac arrhythmias (ventricular fibrillation, asystole), neurological damage (seizures, paralysis, altered mental status), deep tissue necrosis, rhabdomyolysis, and fractures from tetanic muscle contractions or falls. Entry and exit burns may be present, but internal damage can be extensive without significant external signs. Physical exam focuses on burns, cardiac rhythm, neurological status, and signs of compartment syndrome. Pertinent rule-outs include other causes of trauma, burns, or cardiac arrest. Diagnostic workup includes serial ECGs, cardiac enzymes, CK, renal function tests, urinalysis (for myoglobinuria), neurological assessment, and imaging for fractures or internal injuries. Management is supportive, addressing life-threatening arrhythmias, fluid resuscitation, and wound care.

clinical_hallmarks: non-specific signs of illness in neonate
content: Neonatal sepsis presents with non-specific signs, making early recognition challenging. EOS typically manifests within 72 hours of birth, often linked to maternal infection, while LOS occurs after 72 hours, frequently nosocomial or community-acquired. Physical examination may reveal temperature instability, lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, hypotonia, or jaundice. Pertinent rule-outs include metabolic disorders, congenital heart disease, or non-infectious causes of distress. Diagnostic workup involves complete blood count with differential, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, blood culture, urine culture (for LOS), and cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin and gentamicin/cefotaxime) must be initiated promptly after cultures are obtained, pending sensitivity results. Close monitoring for signs of shock and organ dysfunction is crucial, aligning with international guidelines for neonatal intensive care.

topic: Foreign Body Aspiration in Toddler (Stridor / Unilateral Wheeze)
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset cough or choking episode
unilateral wheeze or decreased breath sounds (lower airway)
pertinent_negatives: normal chest X-ray (though can be normal in FB)
content: Foreign body aspiration in toddlers is a medical emergency. Presentation varies based on location and degree of obstruction. A classic history involves a sudden onset of choking, coughing, or gagging while eating or playing. Upper airway obstruction may cause stridor, hoarseness, or aphonia. Lower airway obstruction often presents with persistent cough, unilateral wheeze, or decreased breath sounds. Pertinent rule-outs include croup, asthma exacerbation, or bronchiolitis. Physical examination focuses on respiratory effort, auscultation, and signs of distress. Diagnostic workup includes a chest X-ray (inspiratory/expiratory films may show air trapping; lateral neck X-ray for upper airway), though a normal X-ray does not rule out aspiration. Bronchoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and removal, requiring urgent consultation with ENT/Pulmonology. Immediate management involves maintaining airway patency and oxygenation.

topic: Intussusception in Infants (Red Currant Jelly Stool & Target Sign)
red_flags: sudden onset severe colicky abdominal pain
clinical_hallmarks: intermittent severe abdominal pain (drawing knees to chest)
pertinent_negatives: no lethargy or signs of dehydration
content: Intussusception is the telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, a common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants. The classic triad includes intermittent severe colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and red currant jelly stools (a late sign of ischemia). Infants may appear well between episodes of pain but become lethargic. Physical examination may reveal a palpable 'sausage-shaped' mass, typically in the right upper quadrant. Pertinent rule-outs include gastroenteritis, appendicitis, or incarcerated hernia. Diagnostic workup involves an abdominal ultrasound, which characteristically shows a 'target sign' or 'pseudokidney sign.' An air or hydrostatic enema is often therapeutic and diagnostic, reducing the intussusception. Surgical consultation is imperative for failed enema reduction, signs of perforation, or peritonitis, aligning with international pediatric surgical guidelines.

topic: Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (Projectile Non-Bilious Vomiting)
red_flags: weight loss or poor weight gain
clinical_hallmarks: visible gastric peristaltic waves across the abdomen
signs of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
content: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically presents between 2-8 weeks of age with progressive, projectile, non-bilious vomiting after feeds. Infants remain hungry despite vomiting. Physical examination may reveal visible gastric peristaltic waves and, crucially, a palpable firm, mobile 'olive-shaped' mass in the epigastrium (the hypertrophied pylorus). Pertinent rule-outs include gastroesophageal reflux, milk protein allergy, or intestinal obstruction. Diagnostic workup involves an abdominal ultrasound, which confirms the diagnosis by measuring pyloric muscle thickness and length. Laboratory findings often show hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to persistent vomiting. Initial management focuses on correcting dehydration and electrolyte imbalances with intravenous fluids. Definitive treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy, a highly successful procedure, typically performed after metabolic stabilization.

topic: Congenital Heart Disease (Cyanotic Spell / Tet Spells in Tetralogy of Fallot)
red_flags: worsening heart murmur or new murmur
clinical_hallmarks: increased cyanosis with rapid, deep breathing
squatting posture in older children to relieve symptoms
pertinent_negatives: no history of congenital heart disease
content: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. 'Tet spells' are paroxysmal hypercyanotic episodes characterized by sudden, profound cyanosis, hyperpnea, and irritability, often triggered by crying, feeding, or defecation. These spells result from increased right-to-left shunting across the ventricular septal defect due to infundibular spasm. Physical examination during a spell reveals severe cyanosis, tachypnea, and often a harsh systolic ejection murmur. Pertinent rule-outs include other causes of cyanosis like pulmonary disease or sepsis. Immediate management involves placing the infant in a knee-chest position, administering oxygen, and potentially morphine, IV fluids, or beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) to relax the infundibular spasm. Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis. Definitive treatment is surgical repair, typically performed in infancy, following established pediatric cardiology guidelines.

topic: Status Epilepticus in Children (Pediatric Convulsive Protocol)
clinical_hallmarks: or recurrent seizures without return to baseline consciousness for >5 minutes
content: Status epilepticus (SE) is a neurological emergency defined as continuous seizure activity lasting >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without regaining consciousness. Prompt intervention is critical to prevent neuronal injury. Initial management focuses on ABCs: airway protection, breathing support (oxygen, ventilation if needed), and circulation (IV access). First-line treatment involves benzodiazepines (e.g., IV lorazepam, IM midazolam, rectal diazepam). If seizures persist, second-line anti-epileptic drugs like fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproate are administered. Pertinent rule-outs for seizure etiology include metabolic derangements, CNS infection, trauma, or drug toxicity. Diagnostic workup includes blood glucose, electrolytes, toxicology screen, and potentially lumbar puncture or neuroimaging. Continuous EEG monitoring is essential for refractory SE. Management follows established pediatric convulsive protocols, emphasizing time-sensitive drug administration and identifying underlying causes.

topic: Pediatric Septic Shock & Cold vs Warm Shock
red_flags: poor capillary refill (>2 seconds) or mottled skin
clinical_hallmarks: signs of systemic infection with cardiovascular dysfunction
tachycardia, altered mental status, poor perfusion
cold shock (vasoconstricted, prolonged CRT, weak pulses)
warm shock (vasodilated, flushed, bounding pulses, rapid CRT)
content: Pediatric septic shock is a life-threatening condition characterized by systemic infection leading to cardiovascular dysfunction. It presents as 'cold shock' (vasoconstricted, prolonged capillary refill, weak pulses) or 'warm shock' (vasodilated, flushed, bounding pulses, rapid capillary refill). Red flags include persistent hypotension despite fluid boluses, altered mental status, and poor perfusion. Pertinent rule-outs include cardiogenic shock, hypovolemic shock, or anaphylaxis. Initial management involves rapid fluid resuscitation (isotonic crystalloids 20 mL/kg boluses), empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within the 'golden hour,' and vasopressors (norepinephrine for cold shock, epinephrine for warm shock) if fluid refractory. Diagnostic workup includes blood cultures, lactate, complete blood count, and inflammatory markers. Source control (e.g., abscess drainage) is crucial. Continuous monitoring of vital signs, urine output, and perfusion parameters is essential, guided by PALS and international sepsis guidelines.

red_flags: uvula deviation away from affected side
drooling or inability to swallow secretions
clinical_hallmarks: acute onset sore throat, fever, exudative tonsillitis (strep pharyngitis)
or severe unilateral throat pain, trismus, uvula deviation, muffled voice (quinsy)
bulging of the soft palate and anterior tonsillar pillar
content: Acute post-streptococcal pharyngitis presents with sore throat, fever, and tonsillar exudates, diagnosed by rapid strep test or culture, treated with antibiotics. Peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy) is a severe complication, presenting with worsening unilateral sore throat, fever, trismus, muffled 'hot potato' voice, and uvula deviation away from the affected side. Airway compromise is a critical concern. Physical examination reveals a bulging soft palate and anterior tonsillar pillar. Pertinent rule-outs include epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess, or severe tonsillitis. Diagnostic workup for Quinsy is primarily clinical, but imaging (ultrasound or CT scan) can confirm the abscess and guide drainage. Management involves urgent needle aspiration or incision and drainage, intravenous antibiotics (e.g., clindamycin or ampicillin-sulbactam), and close airway monitoring, often requiring hospitalization.

pertinent_negatives: diffuse abdominal pain without RLQ localization
content: Pediatric appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency in children. Presentation typically involves periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant (RLQ), followed by anorexia, nausea/vomiting, and low-grade fever. Physical examination reveals localized tenderness at McBurney's point, guarding, and rebound tenderness. Atypical presentations are common in young children, increasing perforation risk. Pertinent rule-outs include gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, Meckel's diverticulitis, or ovarian pathology. Diagnostic workup includes complete blood count (leukocytosis), C-reactive protein (elevated), and imaging. Ultrasound is the preferred initial modality, often showing a non-compressible, dilated appendix. CT scan is highly sensitive and specific, especially if ultrasound is inconclusive or perforation is suspected. Surgical consultation for appendectomy is mandatory. Perforation requires broader antibiotic coverage and may necessitate drainage of abscesses, following established surgical guidelines.

red_flags: drooling due to inability to swallow
clinical_hallmarks: rapid onset high fever, severe sore throat, dysphagia, drooling
preference for tripod position (leaning forward, neck hyperextended)
content: Acute epiglottitis is a life-threatening bacterial infection causing rapid swelling of the epiglottis, leading to acute airway obstruction. It presents with sudden onset high fever, severe sore throat, dysphagia, drooling, and a muffled 'hot potato' voice. Children often adopt a tripod position to maximize airway patency. Pertinent rule-outs include croup (barking cough, hoarseness), peritonsillar abscess, or foreign body aspiration. The most critical aspect of management is securing the airway, often requiring intubation in a controlled environment (e.g., operating room) with an experienced team. Direct visualization of a cherry-red, swollen epiglottis confirms the diagnosis. A lateral neck X-ray, if the child is stable, may show a 'thumbprint sign.' Intravenous antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) are initiated immediately. Hib vaccination has significantly reduced its incidence, but it remains a critical emergency.

topic: Severe Preeclampsia and Eclampsia (Magnesium Sulfate Protocol)
clinical_hallmarks: new-onset hypertension (>160/110 mmHg) with proteinuria or end-organ damage after 20 weeks gestation
content: Severe preeclampsia presents with new-onset hypertension (systolic ≥160 mmHg or diastolic ≥110 mmHg) on two occasions at least four hours apart, accompanied by proteinuria or signs of end-organ damage (e.g., severe headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain, elevated liver enzymes, thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema). Eclampsia is the occurrence of new-onset grand mal seizures in a woman with preeclampsia. Physical examination includes blood pressure monitoring, assessment for edema, hyperreflexia, clonus, and fundoscopy. Pertinent rule-outs include chronic hypertension, HELLP syndrome, TTP, and neurological events like stroke. Diagnostic workup involves CBC, LFTs, creatinine, uric acid, 24-hour urine protein or protein/creatinine ratio, and fetal monitoring. Immediate management includes magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis/treatment, antihypertensives, and timely delivery, often after maternal stabilization, guided by gestational age and severity.

topic: HELLP Syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver Enzymes, Low Platelets)
clinical_hallmarks: laboratory triad (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets)
pertinent_negatives: absence of other causes of liver dysfunction
absence of other causes of thrombocytopenia
absence of severe bleeding diathesis unrelated to platelets
content: HELLP syndrome is a severe variant of preeclampsia characterized by Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets. Patients typically present with severe right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, malaise, and sometimes jaundice. Headache and visual disturbances may also occur. Physical examination reveals abdominal tenderness, possibly jaundice, and signs of preeclampsia. Pertinent rule-outs include acute fatty liver of pregnancy, TTP, HUS, and severe preeclampsia without HELLP. Diagnostic workup confirms the triad: LDH >600 U/L, indirect bilirubin >1.2 mg/dL, schistocytes on smear (hemolysis); AST/ALT >70 U/L (elevated liver enzymes); and platelet count <100,000/µL (low platelets). Coagulation profile and renal function tests are also crucial. Management involves immediate stabilization, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm, and prompt delivery, regardless of gestational age, to prevent maternal and fetal morbidity.

topic: Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH Atony Management & Bakri Balloon)
red_flags: persistent heavy vaginal bleeding despite uterine massage
clinical_hallmarks: cumulative blood loss ≥1000 mL or signs of hypovolemia within 24 hours of birth
content: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is defined as cumulative blood loss ≥1000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs/symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours of birth. Uterine atony is the most common cause. Patients present with heavy vaginal bleeding, often with a soft, boggy uterus. Signs of hypovolemic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, altered mental status) may develop rapidly. Physical examination involves uterine palpation for tone, fundal height, and a thorough genital tract inspection for lacerations or retained placental tissue. Pertinent rule-outs include retained placenta, genital tract trauma, and coagulopathy. Diagnostic workup includes CBC, type & screen, and coagulation studies. Initial management focuses on uterine massage, uterotonics (oxytocin, carboprost, methylergonovine), bimanual compression, and intrauterine balloon tamponade (e.g., Bakri balloon). Surgical interventions like B-Lynch sutures or hysterectomy may be necessary for refractory cases.

red_flags: sudden onset painless bright red vaginal bleeding in 2nd/3rd trimester
clinical_hallmarks: painless, bright red vaginal bleeding, typically in late 2nd or 3rd trimester
content: Placenta previa is the implantation of the placenta over or near the internal cervical os. It typically presents as sudden onset, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding in the late second or third trimester. The bleeding is often recurrent and can range from spotting to severe hemorrhage, potentially leading to maternal hypovolemic shock and fetal distress. Physical examination must *avoid* digital vaginal examination to prevent exacerbating bleeding. Uterine palpation usually reveals a soft, non-tender uterus. Pertinent rule-outs include abruptio placentae, vasa previa, and cervical/vaginal lesions. Diagnostic workup involves transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound for definitive placental localization, CBC, type & screen, and coagulation profile. Fetal monitoring is crucial. Management includes maternal stabilization, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm, and planned cesarean delivery, usually between 36-37 weeks, or immediately for uncontrolled hemorrhage or fetal compromise.

topic: Abruptio Placentae with Concealed / Revealed Hemorrhage
red_flags: dark red vaginal bleeding (or no visible bleeding)
pertinent_negatives: absence of painless bleeding (rules out previa)
absence of other causes of abdominal pain
content: Abruptio placentae is the premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall before delivery. It presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain, often described as tearing or constant, accompanied by dark red vaginal bleeding (revealed hemorrhage) or no visible bleeding (concealed hemorrhage). The uterus is typically tender, rigid, and hypertonic. Signs of maternal hypovolemic shock and fetal distress (e.g., bradycardia, late decelerations) are common. Physical examination reveals uterine tenderness and rigidity; fundal height may increase with concealed hemorrhage. Pertinent rule-outs include placenta previa, uterine rupture, and labor. Diagnostic workup is primarily clinical, supported by ultrasound to rule out previa and sometimes visualize a retroplacental hematoma. Labs include CBC, type & screen, coagulation profile (fibrinogen), and fetal monitoring. Management involves rapid maternal stabilization, blood product transfusion, and prompt delivery, usually via emergent cesarean section, to prevent maternal coagulopathy and fetal demise.

topic: Preterm Premature Rupture of Membranes (PPROM & Chorioamnionitis)
red_flags: confirmed rupture of membranes before 37 weeks
clinical_hallmarks: sudden gush or continuous leakage of clear/yellowish fluid from vagina
pertinent_negatives: absence of cervical mucus plug loss without fluid leakage
content: PPROM is the rupture of amniotic membranes before 37 weeks gestation and prior to the onset of labor. Patients typically report a sudden gush or continuous leakage of clear or yellowish fluid from the vagina. Chorioamnionitis, an intra-amniotic infection, is a serious complication. Signs of chorioamnionitis include maternal fever (>100.4°F/38°C), uterine tenderness, foul-smelling amniotic fluid, and maternal/fetal tachycardia. Physical examination involves a sterile speculum exam to confirm membrane rupture (pooling, nitrazine test, ferning) and assess for cervical dilation; digital exams are avoided unless in active labor. Pertinent rule-outs include urinary incontinence and normal vaginal discharge. Diagnostic workup includes ultrasound for amniotic fluid index, CBC, CRP, and cultures (GBS, STIs). Management involves expectant management with antibiotics, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, and close monitoring for infection. Delivery is indicated if chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise develops.

red_flags: retraction of the fetal head against the perineum (turtle sign)
failure of shoulders to deliver with routine traction
inability to deliver the anterior shoulder
clinical_hallmarks: "turtle sign" (fetal head retracts against the perineum)
failure of shoulders to deliver spontaneously or with gentle traction
pertinent_negatives: easy delivery of shoulders with routine maneuvers
absence of prolonged second stage of labor without shoulder impaction
content: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency where, after delivery of the fetal head, the anterior shoulder fails to pass beneath the maternal pubic symphysis. The classic sign is the 'turtle sign,' where the fetal head retracts against the perineum. This condition requires immediate, systematic intervention to prevent fetal hypoxia, brachial plexus injury, and maternal trauma. Physical examination involves rapid visual assessment and recognition of the turtle sign. There are no pertinent rule-outs as it's a clinical diagnosis of failed shoulder delivery. The HELPERR protocol guides management: Help (call for assistance), Episiotomy (if needed for access), Legs (McRoberts maneuver), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal rotational maneuvers like Rubin or Woods screw), Remove posterior arm, Roll patient (Gaskin maneuver). Time is critical; each step is performed sequentially and rapidly to facilitate delivery and minimize complications.

red_flags: palpable or visible umbilical cord in vagina/introitus after ROM
clinical_hallmarks: sudden, severe, prolonged fetal bradycardia or recurrent variable decelerations
often immediately following rupture of membranes
palpable or visible umbilical cord in the vagina
pertinent_negatives: absence of fetal heart rate abnormalities
absence of palpable cord on vaginal examination
content: Cord prolapse occurs when the umbilical cord descends ahead of the presenting fetal part and through the cervix into the vagina, often after rupture of membranes. This is an obstetric emergency due to potential cord compression, leading to fetal hypoxia and death. Patients may report feeling something in the vagina, but the primary sign is sudden, severe fetal bradycardia or recurrent variable decelerations on fetal heart rate monitoring. Physical examination involves an immediate sterile vaginal examination upon membrane rupture or FHR changes to palpate or visualize the cord. Pertinent rule-outs include placental abruption, uterine rupture, and vasa previa. Diagnostic workup is clinical, confirmed by palpation/visualization and fetal monitoring. Management involves immediate elevation of the presenting part off the cord, placing the patient in Trendelenburg or knee-chest position, administering tocolytics if needed, and emergent cesarean delivery to prevent fetal demise.

red_flags: maternal fever >100.4°F (38°C) on two occasions after 24h postpartum
signs of SIRS or septic shock
pertinent_negatives: absence of other infection sources (e.g., mastitis, UTI)
content: Puerperal sepsis, commonly endometritis, is a bacterial infection of the uterus occurring postpartum, often following cesarean section or prolonged labor. It presents with maternal fever (>100.4°F/38°C) on two occasions after the first 24 hours postpartum, severe pelvic pain, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. Chills, malaise, and tachycardia are common. Physical examination includes abdominal palpation for uterine tenderness and involution, speculum exam to assess lochia characteristics, and inspection of any surgical wounds. Pertinent rule-outs include urinary tract infection, mastitis, wound infection, and DVT. Diagnostic workup involves CBC, CRP, blood cultures, urine culture, and possibly endometrial/wound cultures. Imaging (ultrasound, CT) may be used to rule out retained products or abscesses. Management requires prompt initiation of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, supportive care, and surgical drainage if an abscess forms.

topic: Ruptured Corpus Luteum Cyst with Hemoperitoneum
red_flags: sudden onset severe unilateral lower abdominal pain
signs of hypovolemic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor)
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset severe, sharp, unilateral lower abdominal pain
often occurring mid-cycle or in early pregnancy
signs of peritoneal irritation and sometimes hypovolemia
pertinent_negatives: absence of vaginal bleeding (rules out ectopic/miscarriage)
content: A ruptured corpus luteum cyst with hemoperitoneum is a gynecological emergency, typically presenting with sudden onset, severe, unilateral lower abdominal pain. This often occurs mid-cycle or in early pregnancy, sometimes after intercourse or strenuous activity. Patients may exhibit signs of hypovolemic shock, including tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, and syncope, due to internal bleeding. Physical examination reveals abdominal tenderness, guarding, rebound tenderness, and possibly a palpable adnexal mass on pelvic exam. Pertinent rule-outs include ectopic pregnancy (crucial to exclude), appendicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, ovarian torsion, and renal colic. Diagnostic workup involves CBC, beta-hCG (to rule out ectopic), transvaginal/abdominal ultrasound to identify free fluid in the cul-de-sac and adnexal pathology, and type & screen. Management includes fluid resuscitation, pain control, and often surgical intervention (laparoscopy) for significant hemoperitoneum or ongoing hemorrhage to achieve hemostasis.

topic: Acute Ischemic Stroke (Thrombolysis Window / Alteplase / Tenecteplase Protocol)
content: Acute ischemic stroke presents with sudden onset focal neurological deficits. Rapid assessment using the NIH Stroke Scale is crucial. Standard physical examination focuses on motor, sensory, cranial nerve, and cerebellar functions. Pertinent rule-outs include stroke mimics like hypoglycemia, seizures, migraine with aura, and functional neurological disorder. Diagnostic workup involves immediate non-contrast CT head to rule out hemorrhage, followed by CT angiography/perfusion or MRI for vessel occlusion and penumbra assessment. Labs include glucose, INR/PTT, platelets, and renal function. Time is brain; patients within the thrombolysis window (typically 4.5 hours for IV alteplase/tenecteplase) or thrombectomy window (up to 24 hours for large vessel occlusion) require urgent intervention as per international and Indian guidelines.

topic: Intracerebral Hemorrhage (Basal Ganglia Hematoma with Mass Effect)
clinical_hallmarks: acute onset focal deficit often progressing
pertinent_negatives: absence of clear ischemic changes on early CT
content: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), particularly basal ganglia hematomas, typically presents with acute onset focal neurological deficits, often progressing over minutes to hours, accompanied by severe headache, nausea, and vomiting. Hypertension is a major risk factor. Physical examination may reveal hemiparesis, sensory loss, gaze preference, and signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) such as altered consciousness, pupillary changes, or Cushing's triad. Urgent non-contrast CT head is diagnostic. Pertinent rule-outs include ischemic stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and tumor. Management focuses on airway, breathing, circulation (ABCs), strict blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulation, ICP management, and neurosurgical consultation for potential hematoma evacuation or external ventricular drain placement, aligning with international and Indian guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: abrupt, excruciating headache peaking within seconds/minutes
pertinent_negatives: absence of clear focal deficits (pure SAH vs ICH)
absence of migraine history with similar severity
content: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) from aneurysmal rupture classically presents with a 'thunderclap headache' – the sudden, severe 'worst headache of life,' often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity. Altered consciousness or focal neurological deficits may occur. Physical examination focuses on meningeal signs, cranial nerve function, and level of consciousness. Urgent non-contrast CT head is the initial diagnostic test. If CT is negative but suspicion remains high, a lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is indicated. Pertinent rule-outs include meningitis, migraine, and cervical artery dissection. Subsequent CTA, MRA, or digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is performed to localize the aneurysm. Management includes ABCs, blood pressure control, nimodipine for vasospasm prevention, and neurosurgical/neurointerventional consultation for aneurysm securing, following established protocols.

topic: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST in Puerperium & Hypercoagulable State)
pertinent_negatives: absence of typical arterial stroke signs
absence of clear mass lesion on imaging
content: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST) presents heterogeneously, often with headache (variable in nature), seizures, focal neurological deficits, or signs of increased intracranial pressure like papilledema. High-risk populations include puerperium, oral contraceptive users, and those with hypercoagulable states. Physical examination may reveal focal deficits, papilledema, or altered mental status. Pertinent rule-outs include migraine, tension headache, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and arterial stroke. Diagnosis is confirmed by MRV (Magnetic Resonance Venography) or CTV (CT Venography). Labs include D-dimer, coagulation profile, and thrombophilia screening. Management involves immediate anticoagulation (heparin), symptomatic treatment for seizures and ICP, and investigation for underlying prothrombotic conditions, adhering to international and Indian guidelines for acute management and secondary prevention.

clinical_hallmarks: often preceded by infection (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni)
pertinent_negatives: absence of clear sensory level (spinal cord lesion)
absence of upper motor neuron signs
content: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy characterized by rapidly progressive, symmetric ascending weakness, often preceded by a viral or bacterial infection. Areflexia is a hallmark. Physical examination focuses on motor strength, reflexes, and cranial nerve function, with close monitoring for respiratory and bulbar involvement. Pertinent rule-outs include transverse myelitis, botulism, critical illness polyneuropathy, and tick paralysis. Diagnostic workup includes CSF analysis (albuminocytologic dissociation) and nerve conduction studies/electromyography (NCS/EMG). Management involves close monitoring of vital capacity and bulbar function, ventilatory support if needed, and immunomodulatory therapy with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange (PLEX), as per international and Indian guidelines.

topic: Myasthenia Gravis Myasthenic Crisis vs Cholinergic Crisis
red_flags: acute worsening of bulbar/respiratory muscle weakness
clinical_hallmarks: Myasthenic Crisis: severe generalized weakness, bulbar symptoms, respiratory failure, often triggered by infection/stress.
Cholinergic Crisis: generalized weakness, muscarinic symptoms (salivation, miosis, diarrhea), nicotinic symptoms (fasciculations).
pertinent_negatives: Myasthenic Crisis: absence of muscarinic/nicotinic excess.
Cholinergic Crisis: absence of clear trigger for MG exacerbation (e.g., infection).
Absence of other causes of acute weakness.
content: Myasthenic crisis and cholinergic crisis are life-threatening exacerbations of Myasthenia Gravis, both presenting with acute severe weakness, particularly affecting bulbar and respiratory muscles. Differentiation is critical: Myasthenic crisis results from insufficient acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, often triggered by infection or inadequate medication. Cholinergic crisis results from excessive acetylcholine due to anticholinesterase overmedication. Physical exam focuses on respiratory effort, bulbar function, and autonomic signs. Pertinent rule-outs include other causes of acute flaccid paralysis. Management for both involves airway protection and ventilatory support. Myasthenic crisis is treated with IVIG or plasmapheresis and corticosteroids. Cholinergic crisis requires withholding anticholinesterases and may involve atropine. The Tensilon test can differentiate but is risky in crisis, aligning with international and Indian critical care guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: acute or subacute onset of focal neurological symptoms (e.g., optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, brainstem syndrome)
in a patient with known MS or suggestive history
content: An acute relapse in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) is defined by new neurological symptoms or worsening of old symptoms, lasting at least 24 hours, in the absence of fever or infection (pseudo-relapse). Common presentations include optic neuritis (painful vision loss), transverse myelitis (sensory level, weakness, bladder dysfunction), or brainstem syndromes (diplopia, vertigo, facial numbness). Physical examination focuses on identifying new deficits. Pertinent rule-outs include infection, metabolic disturbances, or vascular events. Diagnostic workup involves neurological examination and MRI brain/spine with contrast to identify new or enhancing lesions. Treatment for acute relapses involves high-dose intravenous corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone) to shorten the duration and severity of the attack, as per international and Indian guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: fluctuating or persistent altered mental status (confusion, stupor, coma)
subtle motor phenomena (e.g., nystagmus, automatisms, myoclonus)
often in patients with known epilepsy or acute brain injury
lack of full recovery between episodes
pertinent_negatives: absence of metabolic derangement fully explaining AMS
absence of structural brain lesion explaining AMS
content: Non-Convulsive Status Epilepticus (NCSE) is a medical emergency characterized by continuous or fluctuating altered mental status due to ongoing seizure activity without prominent motor convulsions. It is often subtle and can manifest as confusion, stupor, coma, or behavioral changes. Physical examination may reveal subtle motor signs like eye deviation, nystagmus, or automatisms. Pertinent rule-outs include metabolic encephalopathy, drug intoxication, stroke, and psychiatric conditions. Definitive diagnosis requires continuous EEG monitoring. Management involves rapid administration of intravenous benzodiazepines, followed by non-benzodiazepine antiepileptic drugs (e.g., fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, valproate) to terminate seizure activity. Identifying and treating the underlying cause is crucial, aligning with international and Indian critical care guidelines for status epilepticus.

clinical_hallmarks: Wernicke: acute triad of encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction (nystagmus, gaze palsies), and gait ataxia.
Korsakoff: severe anterograde and retrograde amnesia, confabulation, apathy, lack of insight.
Often in context of chronic alcohol abuse or malnutrition.
pertinent_negatives: absence of other causes of encephalopathy (e.g., infection, stroke, metabolic)
absence of structural brain lesions explaining symptoms
absence of other causes of ataxia
content: Wernicke Encephalopathy (WE) is an acute neurological emergency due to thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, typically seen in chronic alcoholics or malnourished individuals. The classic triad includes encephalopathy (confusion, apathy), oculomotor dysfunction (nystagmus, gaze palsies), and gait ataxia. Physical examination focuses on these signs. Pertinent rule-outs include stroke, infection, drug intoxication, and other metabolic encephalopathies. Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Urgent treatment with high-dose parenteral thiamine (before glucose administration) is critical to prevent progression to irreversible Korsakoff Syndrome, characterized by severe memory impairment and confabulation. Labs may show thiamine deficiency, but treatment should not be delayed. Management aligns with international and Indian nutritional support guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: chronic daily headache (often worse with Valsalva)
normal neurological exam except for possible CN VI palsy
pertinent_negatives: absence of mass lesion on imaging
normal CSF composition with elevated opening pressure
content: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), or Pseudotumor Cerebri, is characterized by symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) without an identifiable cause, typically affecting obese young to middle-aged women. Presentation includes chronic daily headache, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, and most critically, papilledema. Physical examination focuses on fundoscopy for papilledema and cranial nerve assessment (especially CN VI palsy). Pertinent rule-outs include cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, brain tumor, hydrocephalus, and meningitis. Diagnostic workup involves neuroimaging (MRI brain with venography to rule out structural causes and CVST) and a lumbar puncture to measure elevated CSF opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) with normal CSF composition. Management includes weight loss, acetazolamide, and in severe cases, surgical interventions like optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunting to preserve vision, following international and Indian guidelines.

topic: Acute Necrotizing Pancreatitis (Balthazar CT Severity Index)
red_flags: severe epigastric pain radiating to back
clinical_hallmarks: severe epigastric pain radiating to back
pertinent_negatives: absence of peritonitis in mild cases
content: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and fever. Physical examination may reveal epigastric tenderness, guarding, and in severe cases, signs of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) such as tachycardia, hypotension, and tachypnea. Cullen's or Grey Turner's signs indicate retroperitoneal hemorrhage but are rare. Pertinent rule-outs include perforated viscus, acute cholecystitis, myocardial infarction, and mesenteric ischemia. Diagnostic workup involves serum lipase and amylase (typically >3x upper limit of normal), CBC, LFTs, renal function tests, and inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin). Abdominal CT with contrast is crucial for diagnosis, assessing severity (Balthazar CT Severity Index), and identifying necrosis or complications like pseudocyst or abscess. Management focuses on aggressive fluid resuscitation, pain control, nutritional support, and managing complications, often requiring ICU admission.

topic: Ascending Cholangitis (Charcot Triad & Reynolds Pentad Emergency)
clinical_hallmarks: Reynolds' Pentad (Charcot's Triad + hypotension + altered mental status)
pertinent_negatives: absence of biliary duct dilation on imaging
content: Ascending cholangitis is an acute bacterial infection of the bile ducts, typically due to obstruction. Patients present with Charcot's Triad: fever, right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, and jaundice. In severe cases, Reynolds' Pentad emerges, adding hypotension and altered mental status, indicating septic shock. Physical examination reveals RUQ tenderness, jaundice, and potentially signs of sepsis. Pertinent rule-outs include acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, and liver abscess. Diagnostic workup includes CBC (leukocytosis), LFTs (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, GGT), inflammatory markers, and blood cultures. Imaging, starting with ultrasound, then CT or MRCP, identifies biliary obstruction (e.g., choledocholithiasis, stricture, mass) and ductal dilation. ERCP is therapeutic for stone extraction or stenting. Urgent management involves broad-spectrum antibiotics and prompt biliary decompression, often via ERCP, to prevent progression to multi-organ failure.

topic: Bleeding Esophageal Varices (Terlipressin / Endoscopic Band Ligation)
clinical_hallmarks: acute upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) in a patient with known or suspected cirrhosis/portal hypertension
pertinent_negatives: absence of stigmata of chronic liver disease
normal coagulation profile (though often deranged in cirrhosis)
absence of portal hypertension signs on imaging
content: Bleeding esophageal varices present as acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, typically with hematemesis (bright red blood or coffee-ground emesis) and/or melena, in patients with portal hypertension, most commonly due to cirrhosis. Patients may exhibit signs of hemodynamic instability, including tachycardia, hypotension, and pallor. Physical examination often reveals stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, encephalopathy). Pertinent rule-outs include peptic ulcer disease, Mallory-Weiss tear, and gastritis. Diagnostic workup involves CBC (hemoglobin drop), coagulation profile (INR/PT often elevated), LFTs, and renal function. Urgent upper endoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic (endoscopic band ligation). Initial management includes airway protection, fluid resuscitation, vasoactive drugs (e.g., terlipressin, octreotide) to reduce portal pressure, and prophylactic antibiotics. Transfusion support is guided by hemoglobin levels and clinical status.

clinical_hallmarks: Boerhaave: severe retrosternal chest pain, dyspnea, subcutaneous emphysema (Mackler's Triad) after forceful vomiting
pertinent_negatives: absence of chest pain and systemic signs in Mallory-Weiss
absence of hematemesis in Boerhaave (though can occur)
normal mediastinum on imaging for Mallory-Weiss
content: Mallory-Weiss Syndrome involves a non-transmural esophageal mucosal tear, typically at the gastroesophageal junction, caused by forceful vomiting or retching. Patients present with hematemesis, often preceded by non-bloody emesis. Physical exam is usually benign, with stable hemodynamics. Boerhaave Syndrome is a transmural esophageal rupture, a life-threatening emergency, usually following forceful vomiting. Patients experience sudden, severe retrosternal chest pain, dyspnea, and often subcutaneous emphysema (Mackler's Triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema). Signs of shock and mediastinitis may develop rapidly. Rule-outs for Mallory-Weiss include peptic ulcer, variceal bleed. For Boerhaave, rule-outs include myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, and acute pancreatitis. Diagnosis for Mallory-Weiss is by endoscopy. For Boerhaave, chest X-ray may show pneumomediastinum or pleural effusion; CT chest with oral contrast confirms perforation. Urgent surgical repair is critical for Boerhaave.

topic: Gastric Outlet Obstruction (Peptic vs Malignant Antral Stricture)
clinical_hallmarks: recurrent postprandial vomiting of undigested food (often hours after eating)
pertinent_negatives: absence of weight loss (less likely malignant)
absence of succussion splash (rules out significant obstruction)
content: Gastric outlet obstruction (GOO) presents with recurrent postprandial vomiting of undigested food, often hours after eating, early satiety, and progressive weight loss. Peptic strictures typically result from chronic ulcer disease, while malignant strictures are often due to gastric adenocarcinoma or pancreatic head tumors. Physical examination may reveal a succussion splash, epigastric fullness, and in malignant cases, cachexia or a palpable epigastric mass. Pertinent rule-outs include gastroparesis, rumination syndrome, and high intestinal obstruction. Diagnostic workup includes electrolyte panel (hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis), CBC, and imaging. Upper endoscopy is crucial for direct visualization, biopsy (to differentiate peptic from malignant), and therapeutic dilation. Barium upper GI series can delineate the obstruction site and degree. CT abdomen helps assess for malignancy, nodal involvement, or pancreatic pathology. Management involves gastric decompression, fluid/electrolyte correction, and definitive treatment of the underlying cause.

topic: Acute Liver Failure (Fulminant Hepatic Failure Kings College Criteria)
clinical_hallmarks: rapid onset of severe liver dysfunction (jaundice, coagulopathy) with hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing liver disease
pertinent_negatives: absence of pre-existing chronic liver disease
content: Acute liver failure (ALF) is defined by severe acute liver injury with encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) in a patient without pre-existing liver disease, occurring within 26 weeks of symptom onset. Common etiologies include acetaminophen overdose, viral hepatitis, and idiosyncratic drug reactions. Patients present with jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and rapidly progressive hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis, coma). Physical examination reveals jaundice, signs of encephalopathy, and potentially cerebral edema. Pertinent rule-outs include acute exacerbation of chronic liver disease, sepsis, and metabolic encephalopathies. Diagnostic workup includes LFTs (markedly elevated transaminases, bilirubin), coagulation profile (elevated INR), ammonia, glucose, and viral hepatitis serologies. Imaging (ultrasound, CT) assesses liver size and morphology. Kings College Criteria guide prognosis and liver transplant candidacy. Management focuses on supportive care, managing complications (cerebral edema, infection, renal failure), and urgent evaluation for liver transplantation.

red_flags: signs of toxic megacolon (abdominal distension, tenderness)
clinical_hallmarks: watery diarrhea (often foul-smelling) after antibiotic exposure
content: Clostridioides difficile colitis (CDI), or pseudomembranous colitis, typically presents with watery, often foul-smelling diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and fever, usually following antibiotic exposure. It can range from mild diarrhea to severe, life-threatening toxic megacolon. Physical examination may reveal abdominal tenderness, distension, and signs of dehydration. In severe cases, signs of systemic toxicity or peritonitis may be present. Pertinent rule-outs include other infectious colitides (e.g., viral, bacterial), inflammatory bowel disease flares, and irritable bowel syndrome. Diagnostic workup involves stool testing for C. difficile toxin (EIA) or gene (PCR). CBC typically shows leukocytosis. Abdominal X-ray may show colonic dilation in toxic megacolon. Colonoscopy can confirm pseudomembranes but is usually reserved for refractory cases or when diagnosis is unclear. Management includes discontinuing the inciting antibiotic, initiating specific anti-C. difficile therapy (e.g., oral vancomycin, fidaxomicin), and supportive care.

clinical_hallmarks: positive autoantibodies (ANA, SMA for Type 1; LKM-1 for Type 2)
content: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a chronic inflammatory liver disease, often insidious but can present acutely. Type 1 AIH (most common) is characterized by positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies (SMA). Type 2 AIH, typically affecting children/young adults, involves anti-liver kidney microsomal type 1 (LKM-1) antibodies. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with fatigue, jaundice, anorexia, or signs of chronic liver disease (e.g., spider angiomata, hepatosplenomegaly). Physical examination may reveal jaundice, hepatomegaly, or stigmata of cirrhosis. Pertinent rule-outs include viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and genetic liver diseases. Diagnostic workup involves LFTs (markedly elevated transaminases), immunoglobulin G (IgG) levels, and specific autoantibodies. Liver biopsy is essential for diagnosis, showing interface hepatitis, and for staging fibrosis. Treatment involves immunosuppression, typically with corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) and azathioprine, to achieve remission and prevent progression to cirrhosis.

red_flags: signs of decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleed)
clinical_hallmarks: often associated with other autoimmune diseases
content: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic, progressive autoimmune liver disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts. It predominantly affects middle-aged women. Patients often present with insidious onset of fatigue and intractable pruritus, which can be debilitating. Jaundice is a late manifestation. Physical examination may reveal excoriations from scratching, hepatomegaly, or xanthelasmas. In advanced stages, signs of cirrhosis may be present. Pertinent rule-outs include other cholestatic liver diseases (e.g., primary sclerosing cholangitis, drug-induced cholestasis) and obstructive jaundice. Diagnostic workup involves LFTs (markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT), and the hallmark serological marker: positive antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA). Liver biopsy confirms the diagnosis and stages the disease, showing florid duct lesions. Treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) slows disease progression. Symptomatic management for pruritus and monitoring for complications like osteoporosis are crucial.

topic: Budd-Chiari Syndrome (Hepatic Venous Outflow Tract Obstruction)
clinical_hallmarks: classic triad of abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly
in absence of primary liver disease
pertinent_negatives: absence of portal hypertension signs (e.g., varices) in early stages
content: Budd-Chiari Syndrome (BCS) results from obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, ranging from small intrahepatic veins to the inferior vena cava. It often presents with the classic triad of abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly, with acute, subacute, or chronic onset. Underlying hypercoagulable states (e.g., myeloproliferative neoplasms, oral contraceptives) are common etiologies. Physical examination reveals tender hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema. Jaundice is less common unless severe liver damage occurs. Pertinent rule-outs include congestive heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, cirrhosis with portal hypertension, and veno-occlusive disease. Diagnostic workup includes LFTs (variable), renal function, and screening for hypercoagulable disorders. Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins and IVC is the primary diagnostic tool, showing absent or abnormal flow. CT or MRI with contrast can further delineate obstruction. Angiography is used for definitive diagnosis and intervention. Management involves anticoagulation, diuretics for ascites, and potentially interventional radiology procedures (e.g., angioplasty, stenting, TIPS) or liver transplantation.

topic: Acute Compartment Syndrome (The 6 Ps Surgical Emergency)
clinical_hallmarks: severe pain out of proportion to injury
pain on passive stretch of muscles
content: Acute Compartment Syndrome is a surgical emergency characterized by increased pressure within a confined osteofascial compartment, leading to impaired tissue perfusion and potential irreversible muscle and nerve damage. It typically presents with the '6 Ps': Pain (disproportionate), Pallor, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Pulselessness, and Poikilothermia. Pain with passive stretch of muscles within the affected compartment is a highly sensitive sign. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by direct intracompartmental pressure measurement (delta pressure < 30 mmHg or absolute pressure > 30-40 mmHg). Urgent fasciotomy is the definitive treatment, aiming to decompress the compartment and restore blood flow. Delay can result in Volkmann's ischemic contracture, limb loss, or renal failure from rhabdomyolysis. Rule out DVT, cellulitis, or simple contusion.

topic: Hip Fracture in Elderly (Femoral Neck vs Intertrochanteric Fracture)
red_flags: inability to bear weight after fall
clinical_hallmarks: shortened and externally rotated lower limb
content: Hip fractures in the elderly typically result from low-energy falls, often in osteoporotic individuals. Presentation includes severe groin or hip pain, inability to bear weight, and a classic deformity of a shortened, externally rotated lower limb. Femoral neck fractures (intracapsular) carry a risk of avascular necrosis, while intertrochanteric fractures (extracapsular) are often more comminuted and associated with greater blood loss. Initial assessment includes ABCs, pain control, and neurovascular examination. Diagnosis is confirmed with AP and lateral X-rays of the hip. If X-rays are negative but suspicion remains high, MRI or CT scan is indicated. Urgent surgical fixation (e.g., hemiarthroplasty for displaced femoral neck, intramedullary nail for intertrochanteric) within 24-48 hours is crucial to reduce morbidity and mortality. Rule out pelvic fracture or soft tissue injury.

clinical_hallmarks: skin breach communicating with fracture site
pertinent_negatives: normal neurovascular status distal to injury
content: An open or compound fracture involves a break in the skin and underlying soft tissues, exposing the fracture site to the external environment, significantly increasing infection risk. These are classified by Gustilo-Anderson (Type I: <1cm wound, clean; Type II: 1-10cm wound, moderate contamination; Type III: >10cm wound, severe contamination, extensive soft tissue damage, often high-energy). Initial management includes sterile wound dressing, tetanus prophylaxis, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (e.g., cephalosporin + aminoglycoside for Type III), and pain control. Urgent surgical debridement and irrigation within 6-8 hours are paramount to remove contaminated tissue and bone. Fracture stabilization (internal or external fixation) follows debridement. Neurovascular assessment is critical. Rule out closed fracture or soft tissue laceration without bone involvement.

topic: Acute Anterior Shoulder Dislocation (Bankart & Hill-Sachs Lesion)
red_flags: severe pain and inability to move arm
visible deformity (flattened deltoid, prominent humeral head)
clinical_hallmarks: arm held in slight abduction and external rotation
content: Acute anterior shoulder dislocation typically results from indirect trauma with the arm in abduction and external rotation. Patients present with severe pain, inability to move the arm, and a characteristic deformity: a flattened deltoid contour and a prominent humeral head anteriorly. A thorough neurovascular examination, especially for axillary nerve function (deltoid sensation and contraction), is crucial. X-rays (AP, Y-view, and axillary views) confirm the diagnosis and rule out associated fractures (e.g., greater tuberosity, surgical neck). Bankart lesion (anterior labral tear) and Hill-Sachs lesion (posterolateral humeral head compression fracture) are common complications. Urgent closed reduction under sedation is performed, followed by post-reduction X-rays and immobilization. Rule out rotator cuff tear or AC joint injury.

topic: Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Tear & Meniscal Tear
content: ACL and meniscal tears are common knee injuries, often occurring together, typically from twisting or hyperextension sports injuries. Patients often report an audible 'pop' at the time of injury, followed by immediate swelling (hemarthrosis for ACL) and knee instability or 'giving way.' Meniscal tears can cause joint line pain, locking, or catching. Physical examination reveals a positive Lachman test and anterior drawer test for ACL injury, and positive McMurray test with joint line tenderness for meniscal tears. X-rays rule out fractures. MRI is the gold standard for definitive diagnosis of ligamentous and meniscal injuries. Initial management includes RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation). Definitive treatment varies from conservative management to surgical reconstruction (ACL) or repair/meniscectomy (meniscus), depending on patient activity level and tear characteristics. Rule out collateral ligament injury or patellar dislocation.

topic: Achilles Tendon Rupture (Thompson Squeeze Test Positive)
red_flags: inability to push off foot or stand on toes
clinical_hallmarks: positive Thompson squeeze test (absence of plantarflexion)
content: Achilles tendon rupture typically occurs during sudden plantarflexion or dorsiflexion, often in 'weekend warriors.' Patients describe a sudden sharp pain in the calf or heel, often feeling like they were kicked, accompanied by an audible 'pop' or 'snap.' They experience difficulty with push-off and inability to stand on their toes. The hallmark clinical sign is a positive Thompson squeeze test: squeezing the calf muscle does not produce plantarflexion of the foot. A palpable gap in the tendon may also be present. Ultrasound or MRI can confirm the diagnosis and assess the extent of the tear. Management options include non-operative treatment with casting/boot immobilization in equinus or surgical repair, depending on patient age, activity level, and tear characteristics. Rule out calf muscle strain or ankle sprain.

topic: Cauda Equina Syndrome (Saddle Anesthesia & Sphincter Disturbance)
red_flags: new onset urinary retention or incontinence
clinical_hallmarks: saddle anesthesia (loss of sensation in S2-S5 dermatomes)
bilateral lower extremity motor and sensory deficits
content: Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES) is a rare but severe neurological emergency caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots distal to the conus medullaris. It typically presents with a triad of symptoms: severe low back pain, saddle anesthesia (numbness in the perineal, perianal, and genital areas), and bladder/bowel dysfunction (urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence). Other signs include bilateral lower extremity weakness, sensory deficits, and diminished anal tone. Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine is the diagnostic modality of choice. Immediate surgical decompression is critical, ideally within 24-48 hours of symptom onset, to prevent permanent neurological deficits. Delay in treatment can lead to irreversible bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction. Rule out simple disc herniation or peripheral neuropathy.

red_flags: acute onset monoarticular joint pain, swelling, warmth, erythema
inability to bear weight (in lower limb)
clinical_hallmarks: acute monoarticular arthritis (most commonly knee, hip)
fever and systemic signs of infection
elevated synovial fluid WBC count (>50,000 cells/mm3, >75% PMNs)
content: Septic arthritis is a joint infection, typically bacterial, causing rapid joint destruction if untreated. It presents as acute onset monoarticular arthritis with severe pain, swelling, warmth, erythema, and restricted range of motion. Systemic symptoms like fever and chills are common. In children, Kocher criteria (non-weight bearing, ESR >40, fever, WBC >12,000) aid in diagnosing septic hip.
