Urgent joint aspiration for synovial fluid analysis (cell count, Gram stain, culture, glucose, protein) is critical. Blood cultures and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, WBC) are essential. X-rays may show soft tissue swelling, while MRI can detect early changes. Management involves prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent surgical drainage (arthrotomy or arthroscopic lavage) to remove pus and debris, preventing irreversible cartilage damage. Rule out gout, pseudogout, or inflammatory arthritis.

topic: Acute Osteomyelitis (Pediatric Hematogenous vs Chronic Diabetic)
red_flags: persistent localized bone pain, tenderness, swelling
non-healing wound with exposed bone (diabetic foot)
content: Acute osteomyelitis is a bone infection, often bacterial. Pediatric hematogenous osteomyelitis typically affects long bones, presenting with fever, localized bone pain, and refusal to bear weight. Chronic osteomyelitis, particularly in diabetics, often involves the foot, arising from contiguous spread from ulcers, presenting with a non-healing wound, erythema, and swelling, sometimes without fever. Diagnosis involves elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, WBC), blood cultures (especially for hematogenous), and imaging. X-rays show late changes (periosteal reaction, lucency). MRI is highly sensitive for early diagnosis. Bone scan can also be useful. Management requires prolonged intravenous antibiotics (4-6 weeks) and often surgical debridement of infected and necrotic bone, especially in chronic cases or those with abscess formation. Rule out cellulitis, stress fracture, or tumor.

topic: Pelvic Ring Fracture with Hemodynamic Instability (Tile / Young-Burgess)
red_flags: gross hematuria, rectal or vaginal bleeding
clinical_hallmarks: positive FAST scan for free fluid in abdomen
content: Pelvic ring fractures with hemodynamic instability are life-threatening injuries resulting from high-energy trauma. The primary concern is massive hemorrhage from venous plexuses or arterial injury. Patients present with severe pelvic pain, signs of hypovolemic shock (hypotension, tachycardia), and often pelvic instability on examination. Initial management focuses on ABCDE, aggressive fluid resuscitation, and immediate application of a pelvic binder or sheet to reduce pelvic volume and tamponade bleeding. AP pelvis X-ray is initial imaging; CT scan provides detailed fracture assessment and identifies hemorrhage sources. Angioembolization or preperitoneal packing may be required for arterial bleeding. External fixation or C-clamp application provides definitive stabilization and further hemorrhage control. Close monitoring for associated genitourinary, gastrointestinal, and neurological injuries is crucial. Rule out isolated hip fracture or sacral fracture without instability.

Ludwig's Angina is a rapidly progressive, aggressive cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, typically arising from odontogenic infections. It is a medical emergency due to its potential for rapid airway compromise. Patients present with fever, malaise, severe neck pain, bilateral submandibular swelling, and a characteristic 'woody' induration of the floor of the mouth and neck. Physical examination reveals elevated tongue, drooling, and trismus. Pertinent rule-outs include deep neck abscesses and necrotizing fasciitis. Diagnostic workup involves urgent CT scan of the neck with contrast to assess the extent of infection and airway patency. Management includes aggressive broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (e.g., penicillin G plus metronidazole or clindamycin), meticulous airway monitoring, and potential for surgical airway (tracheostomy) if obstruction is imminent. Surgical drainage is generally not indicated unless a true abscess forms.

topic: Deep Neck Space Infection (Retropharyngeal & Parapharyngeal Abscess)
content: Deep neck space infections, including retropharyngeal and parapharyngeal abscesses, are serious infections of the fascial planes of the neck, often originating from odontogenic, tonsillar, or pharyngeal infections. Patients typically present with fever, severe neck pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, and torticollis. Physical examination may reveal unilateral neck swelling, trismus (parapharyngeal), or a posterior pharyngeal bulge (retropharyngeal). These infections can rapidly spread, leading to life-threatening complications like airway obstruction, mediastinitis, or septic thrombophlebitis (Lemierre's syndrome). Pertinent rule-outs include simple cellulitis or lymphadenitis. Diagnostic workup necessitates an urgent CT scan of the neck with intravenous contrast to delineate the extent of infection and identify abscess formation. Management involves aggressive broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and often surgical incision and drainage, particularly for mature abscesses or those causing airway compromise.

topic: Malignant Otitis Externa (Skull Base Osteomyelitis in Diabetics)
red_flags: granulation tissue at bony cartilaginous junction
clinical_hallmarks: granulation tissue in external auditory canal
pertinent_negatives: absence of typical fungal elements (though can be fungal)
content: Malignant Otitis Externa (MOE) is a severe, necrotizing infection of the external auditory canal and skull base, predominantly affecting elderly diabetic or immunocompromised patients. It is typically caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Patients present with unrelenting, deep-seated otalgia, purulent otorrhea, and often granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the external auditory canal. Progression can lead to cranial nerve palsies, particularly facial nerve paralysis, and osteomyelitis of the temporal bone and skull base. Pertinent rule-outs include simple otitis externa or cholesteatoma. Diagnostic workup includes high-resolution CT scan of the temporal bone to assess bone erosion, MRI for soft tissue and intracranial extension, and Technetium-99m bone scan for early diagnosis. Treatment involves prolonged courses (weeks to months) of high-dose intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics, with surgical debridement reserved for refractory cases or sequestrum formation.

topic: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL Golden Window Steroid Therapy)
clinical_hallmarks: acute onset (>30 dB SNHL over 3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours)
content: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL) is defined as an acute onset of hearing loss of at least 30 dB in three contiguous frequencies over a period of 72 hours or less. It is often idiopathic but can be caused by viral infections, vascular events, or autoimmune conditions. Patients typically present with unilateral hearing loss, often accompanied by tinnitus and sometimes vertigo. The 'golden window' for treatment is crucial, ideally within 2 weeks of onset. Physical examination should rule out conductive causes (e.g., cerumen impaction, middle ear effusion). Diagnostic workup includes urgent pure-tone audiometry to confirm SNHL. MRI of the internal auditory canal and brain is essential to rule out retrocochlear pathology, such as a vestibular schwannoma. Treatment involves systemic corticosteroids, with intratympanic steroid injections as an alternative or salvage therapy, and close follow-up.

topic: Severe Posterior Epistaxis (Sphenopalatine Artery Bleed / Epistaxis Packing)
clinical_hallmarks: inability to control bleeding with anterior pressure
content: Severe posterior epistaxis typically originates from branches of the sphenopalatine artery in the posterior nasal cavity and can lead to significant blood loss and hemodynamic instability. Patients present with profuse bleeding, often perceived as blood dripping down the back of the throat, which is not controlled by anterior nasal pressure. Risk factors include hypertension, coagulopathies, and anticoagulant use. Initial management focuses on ABCs, vital sign stabilization, and assessment of blood loss. Physical examination involves careful anterior rhinoscopy after suctioning to identify the bleeding source. If anterior packing fails, posterior nasal packing (e.g., balloon catheter, gauze pack) is required. Pertinent rule-outs include trauma or underlying tumors. Diagnostic workup may include CBC, coagulation profile, and type and cross-match. Refractory cases may necessitate endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolization. Hospital admission is often required for observation and management of underlying causes.

topic: Foreign Body Bronchus vs Foreign Body Esophagus (Coin vs Button Battery)
content: Foreign body (FB) aspiration into the bronchus or ingestion into the esophagus are common pediatric emergencies. Bronchial FBs present with sudden choking, coughing, wheezing, or stridor, potentially leading to respiratory distress. Esophageal FBs cause dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling, or refusal to eat. Button battery ingestion is a critical emergency due to rapid liquefaction necrosis and perforation risk. Coins are common FBs. Physical examination includes assessing respiratory status and auscultating the chest for unilateral findings. Pertinent rule-outs include croup or asthma. Diagnostic workup begins with plain radiographs (AP and lateral neck/chest/abdomen) to localize the FB. Bronchial FBs appear vertically oriented on AP view, esophageal FBs appear horizontally. Management involves urgent endoscopic removal: rigid bronchoscopy for airway FBs and esophagoscopy for esophageal FBs. Button batteries require immediate removal.

clinical_hallmarks: postauricular erythema, tenderness, swelling, and fluctuance
recent history of acute otitis media
content: Acute mastoiditis is an inflammatory process of the mastoid air cells, typically a complication of inadequately treated acute otitis media. When a subperiosteal abscess forms, it indicates pus accumulation beneath the mastoid periosteum. Patients present with persistent otalgia, fever, and postauricular pain, erythema, and swelling, often causing the auricle to protrude downwards and outwards. Physical examination reveals tenderness and fluctuance over the mastoid process. Pertinent rule-outs include cellulitis or lymphadenitis. Diagnostic workup includes a high-resolution CT scan of the temporal bone with contrast to confirm mastoiditis, identify bone erosion, and delineate any abscesses or intracranial complications. Management involves aggressive intravenous antibiotics. Surgical intervention, typically myringotomy with tympanostomy tube placement and/or cortical mastoidectomy with abscess drainage, is often required, especially with abscess formation or signs of intracranial spread.

topic: Vestibular Neuritis & Labyrinthitis (HINTS Exam Central vs Peripheral)
clinical_hallmarks: spontaneous horizontal nystagmus (unidirectional, suppressed by fixation)
positive head impulse test (peripheral), no hearing loss (neuritis)
content: Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis are acute peripheral vestibulopathies causing sudden, severe vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. Labyrinthitis additionally involves hearing loss. The critical distinction is differentiating peripheral from central causes of vertigo, especially stroke, using the HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew). A 'HINTS-plus' exam (adding hearing loss) is highly sensitive for central lesions. Peripheral findings include a positive head impulse test, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus suppressed by fixation, and no skew deviation. Central findings include a negative head impulse, vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation. Pertinent rule-outs include posterior circulation stroke or cerebellar hemorrhage. Diagnostic workup involves clinical assessment; MRI brain is indicated if HINTS suggests a central lesion. Management is symptomatic (antiemetics, vestibular suppressants) and vestibular rehabilitation.

topic: Nasal Bone Fracture with Septal Hematoma
clinical_hallmarks: intranasal examination revealing septal hematoma (bluish, boggy swelling)
content: Nasal bone fractures are the most common facial fractures, typically resulting from direct trauma. Patients present with nasal pain, swelling, epistaxis, and often visible deformity. The most critical complication to identify is a septal hematoma, which appears as a bluish, boggy swelling on intranasal examination. Untreated, a septal hematoma can lead to avascular necrosis of the septal cartilage and subsequent 'saddle nose' deformity or septal abscess. Physical examination involves palpation for crepitus and deformity, and careful anterior rhinoscopy. Pertinent rule-outs include other facial fractures or intracranial injury. Diagnostic workup is primarily clinical; imaging (CT facial bones) is reserved for suspected concomitant fractures, orbital involvement, or for surgical planning. Management includes urgent incision and drainage of any septal hematoma, pain control, and closed reduction of the nasal fracture, ideally within 7-14 days of injury.

topic: Vocal Cord Paralysis (Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Palsy)
clinical_hallmarks: direct visualization of immobile vocal cord on laryngoscopy
pertinent_negatives: no obvious mass on initial exam
content: Vocal cord paralysis, often due to recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy, results in impaired vocal cord mobility. Unilateral paralysis typically presents with hoarseness, a breathy voice, and sometimes aspiration, particularly with liquids. Bilateral paralysis is a life-threatening emergency causing severe airway obstruction and stridor. Common etiologies include iatrogenic injury (e.g., thyroid or neck surgery), malignancy (lung, thyroid, esophageal), neurological disorders, or idiopathic causes. Physical examination includes flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy to directly visualize vocal cord mobility and identify the affected side. Pertinent rule-outs include vocal cord mass or cricoarytenoid joint fixation. Diagnostic workup involves imaging from the skull base to the diaphragm (CT neck and chest) to identify any lesion compressing or invading the RLN. Management includes voice therapy, and for persistent dysphonia or aspiration, surgical options like injection laryngoplasty or medialization thyroplasty.
